sections.title: The science of microbiology: subject, branches and tasks

blocks.text: **Microbiology** (Gr. *mikros* — small, *bios* — life, *logos* — study) is the science that studies the structure, vital activity, heredity and ecology of tiny living organisms that cannot be seen with the naked eye, and their relationship with humans, animals, plants and the environment. The world of microorganisms includes **bacteria, archaea, fungi, protozoa** (eukaryotes) and the acellular forms — **viruses** and **prions**.

**Medical microbiology** studies the microorganisms that cause disease in humans (pathogenic and opportunistic) and the diagnosis, treatment and prevention of the infectious diseases they cause. It is divided into the following branches:

items: **bacteriology** — studies bacteria;
**virology** — viruses;
**mycology** — fungi;
**protozoology** — disease-causing protozoa;
**immunology** — the body’s defense system.

sections.title: History of microbiology and the contribution of Uzbek scientists

blocks.text: Several stages are distinguished in the development of microbiology:

items: **Empirical (heuristic) period** — before the discovery of microbes, speculation about the “invisible causes” of diseases (Hippocrates; Avicenna (Ibn Sina) wrote in *“The Canon of Medicine”* about tiny particles that spread disease).
**Morphological period** — Antonie van **Leeuwenhoek** (1676) was the first to see “animalcules” (bacteria) in a microscope he built himself.

**Physiological period** — Louis **Pasteur** proved that fermentation and putrefaction are the work of microbes and laid the foundations of sterilization and vaccination; Robert **Koch** developed methods of isolating pure cultures, solid culture media, immersion microscopy and “Koch’s postulates.”
**Immunological period** — I.I. **Mechnikov** created the theory of phagocytosis and P. **Ehrlich** created the theory of humoral immunity.
**Molecular-genetic period** — the discovery of antibiotics (A. Fleming) and the development of virology, genetics and biotechnology.

sections.title: The microbiological laboratory: structure, equipment and safety

blocks.text: Because a microbiological laboratory works with infectious materials, it has a special regime. It usually consists of the following rooms: specimen reception, preparation (staining, media preparation), inoculation (transfer boxes), incubator room, autoclave (sterilization) and washing room.
**Main equipment:**

items: **immersion microscope** — for examining stained smears;
**incubator** — for growing inoculated media at 37 °C;
**autoclave** — sterilization under steam pressure (121 °C, 1 atm of excess pressure);
**dry-heat sterilizer (oven)** — for sterilizing glassware at 160–180 °C;
**bactericidal lamps (UV)**, **laminar-flow box** — for disinfecting the air and the work area;
**centrifuge, refrigerator, pH meter, bacteriological loop and Petri dishes.**

parts.text: Biosafety is divided into 4 levels (BSL-1 to BSL-4). Work with especially dangerous infections (cholera, plague, anthrax, hemorrhagic fevers) is done only in special laboratories of the highest levels (BSL-3/4). An ordinary diagnostic laboratory is BSL-2.

blocks.text: **Working rules (in brief):** work wearing a lab coat and gloves; treat all inoculated material as potentially infectious; sterilize the loop each time by flaming; after work, disinfect the work area and wash the hands; discard used material only after decontaminating it in an autoclave; eating and touching the face are forbidden in the laboratory.

Because bacteria are very small (0.5–10 µm), they can be seen only under a microscope. The resolving power of the light microscope is ≈ 0.2 µm; the maximum useful magnification is ≈ 1000× (10× eyepiece × 100× immersion objective).

items: **Cocci** (spherical): depending on the plane of division and whether the cells separate afterward — micrococcus (single), **diplococcus** (pair: pneumococcus, gonococcus, meningococcus), **streptococcus** (chain), **staphylococcus** (grape-like cluster), tetracoccus (group of four), **sarcina** (packet of 8–16 cells).
**Rod-shaped**: single (monobacterium), paired (diplobacterium), chain (streptobacterium). The ends may be blunt, pointed or thickened.
**Curved**: **vibrio** (comma-shaped — causative agent of cholera), **spirillum** (1–3 large coils), **spirochete** (many fine coils — syphilis, leptospirosis).

skills.title: Practical skill: examining a smear under immersion microscopy

blocks.text: Algorithm:

items: Point the microscope toward the light source, raise the condenser to its upper position and open the diaphragm.
Secure the stained and dried smear on the stage.
Place **one drop of immersion oil** on the smear.
Rotate the nosepiece so that the **immersion objective (90–100×)** touches the oil (the objective is immersed in the oil).
Looking from the side, carefully bring the objective close to the smear with the coarse focus knob, then looking through the eyepiece bring the image into sharp focus with the **fine focus knob**.
Move the field of view and assess the shape, arrangement and staining of the cells.
When finished, clean the objective with a soft tissue.

parts.text: When working with the immersion objective, use only the **fine focus knob** — if you turn the coarse focus knob sharply, the objective will break the slide and damage the lens.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A smear taken from a purulent wound was stained by the Gram method; under the microscope, spherical cells arranged in grape-like clusters and stained dark purple were found.
cases.ask: What morphological group and what probable causative agent can be considered?
cases.answer: Spherical (coccus), staphylococcal arrangement, gram-positive cells — probably *Staphylococcus aureus*. A frequent causative agent of purulent infections.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A patient is suspected of having syphilis (lues). Fluid taken from the base of an ulcerative lesion must be examined alive, without staining.
cases.ask: Which microscopy method is used and why?
cases.answer: Dark-field microscopy. *Treponema pallidum* is a delicate, motile spirochete that takes ordinary dyes poorly; against a dark background it is seen alive as a bright spiral.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: While working with the immersion objective, a student is looking for the image by sharply turning the coarse focus knob without looking through the eyepiece. As a result, the slide broke.
cases.ask: Which rule was violated?
cases.answer: When working with the immersion objective, bring the objective close carefully while watching from the side, and perform fine focusing only with the fine focus knob. Sharp turning of the coarse focus knob damages the lens and the specimen.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The bacterial ribosome is **70S** (30S + 50S), the human ribosome is **80S**. Aminoglycosides and tetracyclines act on 30S, macrolides and chloramphenicol (levomycetin) on 50S, stopping only bacterial protein synthesis.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The **LPS (endotoxin)** of gram-negative bacteria is released when the cell breaks down and causes fever, a fall in blood pressure, DIC syndrome and septic shock. Gram-positive bacteria, in contrast, mainly release exotoxins (proteins).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The most important and most commonly mishandled step is **decolorizing with alcohol**. If left in alcohol for too long, Gram+ cells also lose their color and give a false Gram− result; if decolorized too briefly, Gram− cells stay purple and give a false Gram+ result.

sections.title: Permanent structures of the bacterial cell

blocks.text: A bacterium is a **prokaryote**: it has no nucleus enclosed by a nuclear membrane and no membrane-bound organelles (mitochondria, ER, Golgi).

blocks.label: Figure 2.1
blocks.caption: Structure of the bacterial cell: capsule, cell wall, periplasmic space and membrane, nucleoid, ribosomes, mesosome, inclusions, flagellum. Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

blocks.text: **Permanent structures** (present in almost all bacteria):

items: **Cell wall** — determines shape, provides resistance to osmotic pressure, and determines Gram staining and many antigenic properties. Its basis is **peptidoglycan (murein)**.

**Cytoplasmic membrane (CPM)** — a phospholipid bilayer; selective permeability, transport of nutrients, respiratory enzymes and ATP synthesis (bacteria have no mitochondria — energy is produced in the CPM). Its inward folding is the **mesosome**.
**Cytoplasm** — a colloidal medium; enzymes, RNA, reserve substances.
**Nucleoid** — a single circular double-stranded DNA (chromosome), without histones and without a nuclear membrane.
**Ribosomes** — of the **70S** type (30S + 50S subunits); the site of protein synthesis. Their difference from the eukaryotic ribosome (80S) is the basis for the selective action of many antibiotics.
**Plasmids** — small circular DNA outside the chromosome that replicates independently (antibiotic resistance, toxin genes — in detail in topic 11).

parts.text: The bacterial ribosome is **70S** (30S + 50S), the human ribosome is **80S**. Aminoglycosides and tetracyclines act on 30S, macrolides and chloramphenicol (levomycetin) on 50S, stopping only bacterial protein synthesis.

blocks.text: **Chemical composition:** water (≈ 80%), proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates, lipids and minerals. The composition of the cell wall (peptidoglycan, teichoic acids or LPS) depends on the Gram group.

sections.title: The cell wall: gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria

blocks.text: **Peptidoglycan (murein)** — alternately linked chains of N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid; they are cross-linked by short peptide bridges to form a net-like layer. This cross-linking is carried out by the enzyme **transpeptidase** (penicillin-binding protein) — the target of beta-lactam antibiotics.

head: Feature
Gram-positive (Gram +)
Gram-negative (Gram −)
rows: The outer membrane is a barrier — more resistant

blocks.label: Figure 2.3

parts.text: The **LPS (endotoxin)** of gram-negative bacteria is released when the cell breaks down and causes fever, a fall in blood pressure, DIC syndrome and septic shock. Gram-positive bacteria, in contrast, mainly release exotoxins (proteins).

blocks.text: **Special cases:**

items: **Acid-fast** bacteria (mycobacteria — tuberculosis, leprosy): their wall contains a lot of **mycolic acid** and wax; they stain poorly by Gram, so they are stained by the **Ziehl–Neelsen** method (red rods on a blue background).
**Mycoplasmas** — have no cell wall at all; variable shape, naturally resistant to beta-lactam antibiotics.
**L-forms** — temporary forms whose wall is partially lost (for example, under the action of penicillin).

blocks.text: The Gram method (1884, Christian Gram) is the most important differential stain in bacteriology. The difference in staining is based on the structure of the cell wall: thick peptidoglycan is dehydrated by alcohol, its pores narrow, and it retains the **gentian violet–iodine** complex (Gram+); Gram− cells, with thin peptidoglycan and an outer membrane that dissolves in alcohol, lose this complex and then turn red with the counterstain (fuchsin).

blocks.label: Figure 2.4
blocks.caption: Steps of Gram staining (the algorithm from the laboratory manual). Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

blocks.text: **Steps:** 1) gentian violet (1–2 min) — all cells turn purple; 2) Lugol’s solution (iodine — the fixative, 1 min) — the dye–iodine complex forms; 3) alcohol (decolorizer, 10–20 s) — Gram− cells are decolorized; 4) rinse with water, then fuchsin (counterstain, 1–2 min) — Gram− cells turn red. Result: **Gram+ — purple, Gram− — red (pink).**

parts.text: The most important and most commonly mishandled step is **decolorizing with alcohol**. If left in alcohol for too long, Gram+ cells also lose their color and give a false Gram− result; if decolorized too briefly, Gram− cells stay purple and give a false Gram+ result.

sections.title: Classification and nomenclature of bacteria and Bergey’s Manual

blocks.text: Bacteria are classified by **taxonomic units**: domain → phylum → class → order → **family** → **genus** → **species**.

**Nomenclature is binomial (two-name):** each species is named with two Latin words: the first is the genus name (capitalized), the second is the species name (lowercase), both in italics: for example, *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Escherichia coli*, *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*.

**Bergey’s Manual** (*Bergey’s Manual of Determinative Bacteriology*) is the main reference that helps identify bacteria by their morphological, tinctorial (Gram), cultural and biochemical features. In practice, bacteria are identified by following this sequence of features.
**Variants within a species.** Although they are not formally part of the classification, in practice bacteria within one species are distinguished by the following features:

skills.title: Practical skill: the Gram staining algorithm

items: Place a drop of physiological saline on a clean slide, prepare a smear from the culture to be examined with a loop, and air-dry it.
**Fix** the smear by passing it 2–3 times over the flame (this fixes the cells to the glass and kills them).
Stain with gentian violet for 1–2 minutes.
Pour off the dye and apply Lugol’s solution for 1 minute.
Decolorize with alcohol for 10–20 seconds, until no more color comes off; rinse immediately with water.
Counterstain with fuchsin for 1–2 minutes, rinse and dry.
Examine with the immersion objective (100×): purple — Gram+, red — Gram−; record the shape and arrangement.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A smear was stained by the Gram method, and red (pink) rods were seen under the microscope. The patient has signs of an intestinal infection.
cases.ask: Which Gram group does the bacterium belong to and what is its wall structure?
cases.answer: A gram-negative (Gram−) rod — it has thin peptidoglycan, an outer membrane and LPS (endotoxin). Enteric rods (Enterobacteriaceae — for example, *E. coli*) are gram-negative.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: While performing Gram staining, a student kept the alcohol decolorization step far too long (1 minute). As a result, a known gram-positive culture was also stained red.
cases.ask: What error occurred and how is the result assessed?
cases.answer: Over-decolorization with alcohol — the thick peptidoglycan also lost the gentian violet–iodine complex, and the gram-positive cells looked falsely gram-negative (red). The result is incorrect; the staining must be repeated.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A patient was prescribed an antibiotic of the penicillin group, but it had no effect on the causative agent (a mycoplasma).
cases.ask: Why was penicillin ineffective?
cases.answer: Mycoplasmas have no cell wall (peptidoglycan), while penicillin blocks peptidoglycan synthesis (transpeptidase). With no wall, the drug has no target — which is why mycoplasmas are naturally resistant to beta-lactams (macrolides and tetracyclines act on them).

topics.title: Nonpermanent structures of bacteria: spore, capsule, flagella, inclusions. Complex staining methods. Fungi

goals.text: To know the structure and function of the nonpermanent (optional) structures of bacteria — spore, capsule, flagellum, pili and inclusions;
to explain the importance of these structures as differential features in identifying the species;
to master the complex (differential) staining methods — Ozheshko, Burri–Hiss, Neisser, Ziehl–Neelsen — and the methods of determining motility;
Independent work: to know the morphology and structure of fungi and the methods of studying them.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: A spore does not take up an ordinary dye: in an ordinary smear it appears as an **unstained white space**. With the Ozheshko method, however, the **spore is red and the vegetative cell is blue**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Remember the location by the shape: **terminal — drumstick** (tetanus), **subterminal — racket** (botulism), **central — the shape does not change** (anthrax).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: In a cerebrospinal fluid smear, encapsulated gram-positive diplococci raise suspicion of pneumococcal meningitis; in sputum, large encapsulated gram-negative rods (a slimy, dome-shaped colony) raise suspicion of Klebsiella pneumonia.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In a hanging drop, **true motility** must be distinguished from **Brownian motion**: in Brownian motion the cells merely vibrate in place, whereas in true motility they cross the field of view and change position.

blocks.text: Permanent structures (cell wall, cytoplasmic membrane, cytoplasm, nucleoid, ribosomes) are present in every bacterium. **Nonpermanent structures**, by contrast, occur only in some species or only under certain conditions. They are not essential for the bacterium’s survival, but they serve as an **important differential feature in identifying the species**, and for this reason they are studied separately in the practical class.

blocks.title: Table 3.1. Nonpermanent structures and their detection

blocks.label: Figure 3.1
blocks.caption: Preparations stained by complex methods: a) Burri–Hiss (capsule), b) Ziehl–Neelsen (acid-fast rods), c) Neisser (volutin granules), d) Ozheshko (spore). Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

blocks.text: **Spore** — a resting form produced under unfavorable conditions by some gram-positive rods (*Bacillus* — aerobes, *Clostridium* — anaerobes). It is a form of **preservation, not reproduction**: one spore forms from one cell, and one vegetative cell grows back from the spore.

**Structure.** In the center are dehydrated cytoplasm and the nucleoid, surrounded by the cortex, a multilayered coat and sometimes an exosporium. There is almost no free water, and there is a lot of the **calcium salt of dipicolinic acid** — because of this, metabolism in the spore stops and it is much more resistant than the vegetative cell. That is why in medicine the reliability of sterilization is assessed precisely by the **destruction of spores** (see topic 9: autoclave and biological indicators).
**Spore location** — a morphological feature used in identifying the species:

items: **central** — in the middle of the cell, does not change the shape of the cell (anthrax bacillus);
**subterminal** — near the end, giving a “tennis racket” appearance (the causative agent of botulism);
**terminal** — at the very end, giving a **“drumstick bacillus”** appearance (the causative agent of tetanus).

blocks.text: If the spore diameter is greater than the width of the cell, the cell swells and takes the **clostridial (spindle-shaped)** form; if smaller, the **bacillus** form is retained.

parts.text: A spore does not take up an ordinary dye: in an ordinary smear it appears as an **unstained white space**. With the Ozheshko method, however, the **spore is red and the vegetative cell is blue**.
Remember the location by the shape: **terminal — drumstick** (tetanus), **subterminal — racket** (botulism), **central — the shape does not change** (anthrax).

blocks.text: The Ozheshko method (spore staining) — procedure

items: A smear is prepared and air-dried.
A 0.5% solution of hydrochloric acid is dropped onto the preparation and heated for 1–2 minutes — the spore coat becomes permeable to the dye.
The acid is washed off with water and the smear is fixed.
It is stained with carbol fuchsin, heated until steam rises (5–7 minutes), and rinsed.
It is counterstained with methylene blue (3–5 minutes), rinsed and dried.
It is examined under the immersion objective: **red spore + blue vegetative cell**.

blocks.text: **Capsule** — a mucous layer with a distinct border on top of the cell wall. If thicker than 0.2 µm it is a **macrocapsule** (visible with a light microscope); a thinner one is called a **microcapsule**. A layer without a distinct border that is easily removed is the **slime layer (glycocalyx)**; it forms the basis of the biofilm and is important in infections associated with catheters, prostheses and implants.
**Chemical composition:** a polysaccharide in most bacteria (pneumococcus, Klebsiella, meningococcus, *Haemophilus influenzae*), a polypeptide in the anthrax bacillus.
**Significance:**

items: resists phagocytosis — a **virulence factor** (unencapsulated strains are not virulent);
determines the **serovars within a species**: pneumococcus has more than 90 capsular serotypes, and vaccines are made precisely from these polysaccharides;
protects against desiccation and immune factors.

blocks.text: Most bacteria form the capsule **in the body** or on media with added serum, and lose it on ordinary artificial media. That is why a smear prepared from **pathological material** (sputum, CSF, blood) is usually used to see the capsule.

**Burri–Hiss method:** India ink is added to the material and smeared (the background becomes black); after fixation, it is stained with fuchsin. As a result, a **red cell** on a **black background** is seen, and around it a **colorless halo — the capsule**.

parts.text: In a cerebrospinal fluid smear, encapsulated gram-positive diplococci raise suspicion of pneumococcal meningitis; in sputum, large encapsulated gram-negative rods (a slimy, dome-shaped colony) raise suspicion of Klebsiella pneumonia.

blocks.text: **Flagellum** — a filamentous appendage made of flagellin protein and anchored to the cytoplasmic membrane; it gives the bacterium motility and **chemotaxis** (toward nutrients, away from harmful substances). The flagellum is used as the **H-antigen** in serological identification.

blocks.text: **Methods of determining motility:**

items: **Hanging drop** — living cells in a drop between a concave slide and a coverslip are observed by phase-contrast or dark-field microscopy.
**Crushed (wet-mount) drop** — a coverslip is placed over a drop on an ordinary slide; simpler, but the drop dries quickly.

**Stab inoculation into semisolid agar** — motile bacteria spread sideways from the stab line and make the medium cloudy; nonmotile ones grow only along the stab line. This method is the most widely used in routine practice.

parts.text: In a hanging drop, **true motility** must be distinguished from **Brownian motion**: in Brownian motion the cells merely vibrate in place, whereas in true motility they cross the field of view and change position.

blocks.text: **Pili (fimbriae)** — numerous protein appendages that are shorter and thinner than flagella. They are divided into two groups:

items: **common-type pili (adhesins)** — ensure attachment of the cell to the epithelium; this is the first step of infection (for example, the P pili of E. coli in urinary tract infection, gonococcal pili);
**sex (F) pili** — ensure the transfer of DNA between donor and recipient cells during conjugation (topic 11).

blocks.text: **Inclusions** — reserve substances in the cytoplasm: **volutin (metachromatic granules)**, glycogen, starch, lipid droplets, sulfur granules. The most important for diagnosis is **volutin**: it is located at the ends of the diphtheria bacillus, and with the **Neisser** stain the cell appears yellow-brown while the volutin granules appear **dark blue-black**. This is the classic sign in the bacterioscopic diagnosis of diphtheria.

blocks.label: Figure 3.3
blocks.caption: Diphtheria bacillus stained by the Neisser method: dark volutin granules at the ends of the cells. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

parts.text: **NEI**sser — **NEI**ther end is clear: the tips are black, because of **volutin**. Diphtheria + granules at the ends = a “matchstick” appearance, and the cells lie at an angle to one another (in the shape of the **Latin letters V and X**).

sections.title: Independent work: Fungi — morphology, structure and methods of study

blocks.text: **Fungi** — **eukaryotic**, chlorophyll-free, heterotrophic organisms. They differ from bacteria in having a formed nucleus, membrane-bound organelles, **80S** ribosomes, a cell wall made of **chitin and glucan**, and **ergosterol** in the membrane (the target of antifungal drugs). That is why antibacterial antibiotics do not act on fungi.

blocks.title: Table 3.3. Main morphological forms of fungi

blocks.text: **Mycelium** may be septate or nonseptate. Reproduction: **asexual** — conidia, sporangiospores, blastospores, chlamydospores, arthrospores; **sexual** — asco-, basidio- and zygospores.
**Methods of study:**

items: **Microscopic:** examining the material (hair, nail, skin scrapings) cleared in 10–20% KOH solution; staining smears with Gram, Romanowsky–Giemsa, PAS or calcofluor white.
**In culture:** inoculation onto **Sabouraud** medium and growth at 22–28 °C (and 37 °C) for several days to several weeks; identification by colony appearance, pigment and microscopic structure.
**Serological and molecular:** antigen detection (cryptococcal capsular antigen, galactomannan), ELISA, PCR.

parts.text: *Candida albicans* is a member of the normal microflora; against a background of antibiotics, diabetes mellitus or reduced immunity it turns into candidiasis (oral cavity — thrush, esophagus, urinary tract, generalized form). That is why finding a fungus in the material is not enough by itself — its quantity is assessed together with the clinical picture.

skills.title: Practical skill: choosing complex staining methods

blocks.text: In the laboratory, the staining method is chosen according to the **structure being sought**:

items: Shape, arrangement and Gram group needed → **Gram method**.
Acid-fast rods (tuberculosis, leprosy) → **Ziehl–Neelsen** (red rods, blue background) or the fluorescent method with auramine.
Spore → **Ozheshko** (red spore, blue cell).
Capsule → **Burri–Hiss** (black background, colorless halo).
Volutin granules (diphtheria) → **Neisser**.
Spirochetes → **Romanowsky–Giemsa**, **Morozov** (silver impregnation) or dark-field.
Fungi → **KOH preparation**, PAS, calcofluor.

parts.text: In complex methods, the order of steps and the timing must be strictly observed. In the Ozheshko method, the spore is not stained unless it is treated with acid; in the Neisser method, if the counterstain is held too long, the volutin granules merge with the background and become invisible.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: In a smear of material taken from a deep, soil-contaminated wound, gram-positive rods were found; at their ends there is a thick round structure, and the cell has a “drumstick bacillus” appearance.
cases.ask: What is this structure and which causative agent should be considered?
cases.answer: A terminally located spore; the morphological appearance is typical of the causative agent of tetanus (*Clostridium tetani*). To confirm the diagnosis, culture under anaerobic conditions and toxin detection are needed (topic 17).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: In a preparation made with India ink from the sputum smear of a patient with pneumonia, red rods on a black background and wide colorless halos around them were seen.
cases.ask: Which method was used, what is the colorless halo and which causative agent is likely?
cases.answer: The Burri–Hiss method; the colorless halo is the macrocapsule. Large encapsulated gram-negative rods are typical of *Klebsiella pneumoniae*. Culture and identification are needed for a final answer.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A student, seeing small vibrations of cells in place in a hanging drop preparation, judged the culture “motile.” But when it was stab-inoculated into semisolid agar, growth occurred only along the stab line.
cases.ask: What is the error?
cases.answer: The student mistook Brownian motion for true motility. In true motility, the cell crosses the field of view. The result in semisolid agar confirms that the culture is nonmotile (atrichous).

goals.text: To know the morphology and biological features of the groups that differ in structure from ordinary bacteria — spirochetes, mycoplasmas, chlamydiae, rickettsiae and actinomycetes;
to explain the special methods of studying these groups (dark-field, silver impregnation, cell culture);
to be able to name the main diseases caused by each group and the principle of their laboratory diagnosis;
Independent work: to know the morphology and structure of protozoa and the methods of studying them.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Prokaryotes that **multiply only inside cells** — **chlamydiae and rickettsiae** (they do not grow at all on artificial media). **No cell wall** — **mycoplasmas** (and therefore naturally resistant to penicillin).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: By the number of coils: **B**orrelia — **b**ig, loose coils (few and large); **T**reponema — **t**ight and tiny (regular, fine coils); **L**eptospira — **l**ots of coils + hooked ends.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: *Treponema pallidum* takes ordinary dyes poorly (hence its name — “pale”). Therefore in primary syphilis a preparation made from the discharge of the hard chancre is examined **alive, in dark field**. In late stages, diagnosis relies mainly on **serological** methods (RPR, TPHA, ELISA) (topic 25).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Chlamydiae and rickettsiae **cannot be cultured on ordinary nutrient media**. If a report states “chlamydia was grown on blood agar,” this is an error. They are propagated in living cell culture, chick embryo or laboratory animals.

sections.title: General description: why these groups are studied separately

blocks.text: Although the groups listed above are prokaryotes (apart from fungi and protozoa), each of them has a **feature that differs markedly from an ordinary bacterium**: one is extremely thin and coiled, one has lost its cell wall, one multiplies only inside cells. These differences directly affect practice — they do not grow on ordinary media, they stain poorly by Gram, and beta-lactam antibiotics do not always act on them.

parts.text: Prokaryotes that **multiply only inside cells** — **chlamydiae and rickettsiae** (they do not grow at all on artificial media). **No cell wall** — **mycoplasmas** (and therefore naturally resistant to penicillin).

blocks.text: **Spirochetes** — thin, long, spiral-shaped, motile bacteria. Their structure differs from ordinary bacteria: in the center is the **protoplasmic cylinder** (cytoplasm + nucleoid, surrounded by the cell wall), around it are the **axial fibrils** (axial filaments), and the **outer sheath** covers the whole cell. It is the contraction of the axial fibrils that allows the spirochete to move by rotating and flexing.

blocks.caption: Structure of a spirochete: a) external appearance; b) cross-section — protoplasmic cylinder, axial fibrils, outer sheath. Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

blocks.title: Table 4.2. Spirochetes of medical importance

parts.text: By the number of coils: **B**orrelia — **b**ig, loose coils (few and large); **T**reponema — **t**ight and tiny (regular, fine coils); **L**eptospira — **l**ots of coils + hooked ends.

*Treponema pallidum* takes ordinary dyes poorly (hence its name — “pale”). Therefore in primary syphilis a preparation made from the discharge of the hard chancre is examined **alive, in dark field**. In late stages, diagnosis relies mainly on **serological** methods (RPR, TPHA, ELISA) (topic 25).

blocks.text: **Mycoplasmas** — the smallest self-replicating prokaryotes (0.1–0.3 µm). Their main feature is the **complete absence of a cell wall**; they are surrounded only by a three-layered cytoplasmic membrane, and, unlike other bacteria, the membrane contains **sterols**.
**Consequences:**

items: the shape is not constant (**pleomorphism**): round, pear-shaped, filamentous forms;
**practically not stained by the Gram method** (Romanowsky–Giemsa is used);
**naturally resistant to beta-lactam antibiotics** (penicillin stops cell wall synthesis, and there is no wall) — macrolides, tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones are used in treatment;
can pass through bacterial filters;
grows slowly on specially enriched medium and forms tiny colonies with a depressed center, a **“fried-egg”** appearance.

blocks.text: Medically important: *Mycoplasma pneumoniae* (atypical pneumonia), *Mycoplasma hominis* and *Ureaplasma urealyticum* (urogenital infections).

**Chlamydiae** — gram-negative prokaryotes that have a cell wall but little peptidoglycan; **obligate intracellular parasites**, because they cannot synthesize ATP themselves (“energy parasites”). Their developmental cycle consists of alternation between two forms:

items: **Elementary body (EB)** — a small, dense, metabolically inactive, **infectious** form that lives outside the cell; it enters the cell.
**Reticulate body (RB)** — a large, metabolically active form that divides inside the cell, but is not infectious.

blocks.text: Cycle: EB enters the cell → prevents phagolysosome formation → turns into RB and multiplies → turns into new EBs → the cell breaks down and EBs are released. The whole cycle lasts 48–72 hours.

blocks.label: Figure 4.2
blocks.caption: Developmental cycle of *Chlamydia trachomatis*: alternation of elementary and reticulate bodies. Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

blocks.text: **Main species and diseases:** *C. trachomatis* — trachoma, urogenital chlamydiosis, neonatal conjunctivitis; *C. psittaci* — ornithosis (from birds); *C. pneumoniae* — respiratory infection.

**Diagnosis:** inoculation into cell culture (the reference method, rarely used in practice), **PCR** (the main method today), direct immunofluorescence, antibody detection by ELISA; seeing intracellular inclusions in a smear with Romanowsky–Giemsa.

parts.text: Chlamydiae and rickettsiae **cannot be cultured on ordinary nutrient media**. If a report states “chlamydia was grown on blood agar,” this is an error. They are propagated in living cell culture, chick embryo or laboratory animals.

blocks.text: **Rickettsiae** — small, polymorphic (coccoid or rod-shaped) gram-negative bacteria, **obligate intracellular parasites**. Most are transmitted by **arthropods** (lice, ticks, fleas) — which is why the infections they cause are called **vector-borne** (topic 26).
Main ones: *Rickettsia prowazekii* — epidemic typhus (via lice); *R. typhi* — endemic (murine, rat) typhus (via fleas); *Coxiella burnetii* — Q fever (also transmitted by the airborne route).
**Staining:** Romanowsky–Giemsa, the **Zdrodovsky** method (rickettsiae red, cell cytoplasm blue). **Diagnosis** is made mainly by serological methods (CFT, PHA, ELISA) and PCR.

**Actinomycetes** — gram-positive bacteria that form branching filamentous outgrowths (mycelium). They were formerly considered fungi, but their prokaryotic structure (a wall with peptidoglycan, 70S ribosomes, no nucleus) places them among the bacteria; they are sensitive to antibacterial antibiotics.

items: *Actinomyces israelii* — a member of the normal oral microflora; when immunity falls or after injury it causes **actinomycosis** (chronic granulomatous inflammation, fistulas). Yellow **druses** (sulfur granules; clumps of mycelium) visible to the naked eye are found in the pus — this is the classic diagnostic sign.
*Nocardia* — partially acid-fast; pulmonary and cutaneous nocardiosis, often in patients with reduced immunity.

parts.text: A chronic, indurated infiltrate with fistulous openings in the maxillofacial region + yellow granules (druses) in the pus — a picture typical of actinomycosis. Seeing the druses on ordinary microscopy speeds up the diagnosis.

blocks.text: **Protozoa** — unicellular **eukaryotic** organisms: a formed nucleus, membrane-bound organelles, 80S ribosomes. Most exist in two forms: the **vegetative (trophozoite)** — the active, multiplying form, and the **cyst** — the form resistant to the external environment and infectious.

parts.text: In malaria, the gold standard of diagnosis is the **thick smear** (to find the parasite) and the **thin smear** (to identify the species), stained with Romanowsky–Giemsa.

skills.title: Practical skill: choosing the right material and method

items: **Suspected primary syphilis** → ulcer discharge → **dark-field** microscopy (live, unstained preparation).
**Suspected relapsing fever** → **blood smear** taken at the height of fever → Romanowsky–Giemsa.
**Suspected atypical pneumonia** → throat–nasal swab/sputum → **PCR** (mycoplasma, chlamydia).
**Suspected urogenital chlamydiosis** → urethral/cervical canal **scraping** (it must contain epithelial cells, not the discharge alone) → PCR or IF.
**Suspected actinomycosis** → fistula discharge → look for druses + culture.
**Suspected trichomoniasis** → **warm native preparation** of the discharge → look for motile flagellated cells.

parts.text: The Trichomonas preparation must be examined **immediately and warm**: in a cooled preparation the parasite stops moving and it becomes difficult to distinguish it from an epithelial cell.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: In a 25-year-old patient, a painless hard ulcer appeared on the genitalia. In a preparation made from the ulcer discharge, bright, tiny, regularly coiled motile microorganisms that flex at an angle were seen on a dark background.
cases.ask: Which method was used and which causative agent should be considered?
cases.answer: Dark-field microscopy; the morphology is typical of *Treponema pallidum* — primary syphilis. Serological reactions (RPR and treponema-specific tests) are performed for confirmation.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 19-year-old patient has had a dry cough and subfebrile fever for several weeks; the chest X-ray shows bilateral interstitial changes. Sputum culture showed no growth, and treatment with penicillin gave no result.
cases.ask: Which causative agent is most likely, and why is penicillin ineffective?
cases.answer: *Mycoplasma pneumoniae* (atypical pneumonia). Mycoplasmas have no cell wall, and penicillin blocks wall synthesis — so it has no effect. Diagnosis is by PCR/serology, treatment with a macrolide or tetracycline.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A discharge taken from the cervical canal was sent for PCR, and the result was negative. On repeat testing, when a scraping (with epithelial cells) was taken, the result was positive.
cases.ask: Why was the first test negative?
cases.answer: Chlamydia is an intracellular parasite; the material must contain **epithelial cells**. When only the discharge is taken, the causative agent does not get into the sample and gives a false-negative result.

goals.text: To know the chemical composition of bacteria, the types of nutrition and the growth factors;
to explain the stages of the growth curve of a bacterial population in liquid medium and their practical importance;
to know the classification of nutrient media, the requirements for their composition and their role in diagnosis;

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: All bacteria that cause disease in humans are **chemoorganoheterotrophs**: they obtain both carbon and energy from ready-made organic substances.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: *Haemophilus influenzae* needs **factor X (hemin)** and **factor V (NAD)** to grow. That is why it does not grow on ordinary blood agar, but grows well on **chocolate agar** (heated blood — the erythrocytes break down and release the factors). This requirement is taken into account directly in routine laboratory work.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In determining antibiotic susceptibility and testing a disinfectant, a **24-hour (young, logarithmic-phase)** culture is used. In an old culture the cells are polymorphic, and the result comes out wrong.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Remember the types of media by function: **S**elective — **S**ingles out the one you want to grow; **D**ifferential — **D**istinguishes (tells organisms apart); **T**ransport — **T**o carry the specimen safely.

blocks.text: **Water** makes up 75–85% of the bacterial cell (the larger part of it is free water — the medium and solvent for reactions). The main components of the dry residue:

items: **proteins** (50–80%) — structural proteins, enzymes, toxins, antigens;
**nucleic acids** — DNA (nucleoid, plasmid) and RNA (r-, m-, t-RNA);
**carbohydrates** — cell wall, capsule, reserve substances;
**lipids** — membrane, mycolic acid in mycobacteria, lipid A in gram-negative bacteria;
**minerals** — phosphorus, potassium, magnesium, iron, sulfur and trace elements.

sections.title: Types of nutrition and growth factors

blocks.text: Bacteria are classified by their source of **carbon** and **energy**:

head: Criterion
Type
Description
Example
blocks.title: Table 5.1. Types of nutrition

parts.text: All bacteria that cause disease in humans are **chemoorganoheterotrophs**: they obtain both carbon and energy from ready-made organic substances.

blocks.text: **Entry of substances into the cell** occurs by passive diffusion, facilitated diffusion, **active transport** (spending energy, against the concentration gradient) and group translocation. Active transport is the main route.

**Growth factors** — substances that the bacterium cannot synthesize itself and must obtain ready-made: some amino acids, vitamins (B group), purine and pyrimidine bases, heme. Bacteria that need them are called **auxotrophs**, and those that do not are called **prototrophs**.

parts.text: *Haemophilus influenzae* needs **factor X (hemin)** and **factor V (NAD)** to grow. That is why it does not grow on ordinary blood agar, but grows well on **chocolate agar** (heated blood — the erythrocytes break down and release the factors). This requirement is taken into account directly in routine laboratory work.

blocks.text: Bacteria multiply by **binary fission**. The time between two cell divisions is the **generation time**; in *E. coli* it is 20–30 minutes under favorable conditions, and in *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* up to 14–24 hours.
The **growth curve in liquid medium** consists of four phases:

items: **Lag phase (adaptation)** — the number of cells does not increase; the enzyme system adapts to the new medium.

**Logarithmic (exponential) phase** — the number of cells increases in geometric progression; the bacteria are most active, their morphology is typical, and they are most sensitive to antibiotics and disinfectants. Cultures for research are taken from this phase.
**Stationary phase** — balance between multiplication and death; the cell count is at its maximum (M-concentration). Many secondary metabolites, toxins, pigments and spores are formed in this phase.
**Death (decline) phase** — nutrients run out, metabolites accumulate, the number of living cells falls, and forms change (pleomorphism, involution forms).

parts.text: In determining antibiotic susceptibility and testing a disinfectant, a **24-hour (young, logarithmic-phase)** culture is used. In an old culture the cells are polymorphic, and the result comes out wrong.

blocks.text: **Growth on solid medium** — in the form of colonies. A colony is a visible collection of cells that has arisen by multiplication from a single cell; therefore **a single colony = a source of pure culture**.

**Requirements for a nutrient medium:** it must be sterile; contain the necessary nutrients and growth factors; have an optimal pH (7.2–7.6 for most pathogens); be isotonic; have moisture and transparency; have a standard composition.

blocks.title: Table 5.3. Stages of pure culture isolation

blocks.text: **Tasks of day 1:**

items: **Taking the material correctly** — before antibiotics are given, from the organ appropriate to the stage of the disease, into a sterile container, in sufficient quantity. Each material has its own rule (blood — at the height of fever, urine — the midstream portion, sputum — morning, deep).
**Preliminary microscopy** — a smear stained by the Gram method helps in choosing the next step.
**Choosing the medium and inoculating** — the material is inoculated onto selective and differential media suited to its composition.
**Isolation streaking** — the main technique for obtaining a separate colony.

blocks.label: Figure 5.2
blocks.caption: The technique of taking the material and inoculating it onto a Petri dish with a bacteriological loop: flaming the loop, taking the material, streaking by sectors and, as a result, obtaining separate colonies. Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

blocks.text: A **prion** is an infectious particle that has no nucleic acid and consists of **protein** alone. In the brains of humans and animals the normal protein **PrP^C^** is normally present; the pathological form **PrP^Sc^** refolds the normal protein to resemble itself (changes its conformation). As a result, insoluble aggregates accumulate in the brain and the tissue becomes porous — **spongiform encephalopathy**.

**Features:** they do not provoke an immune response (no inflammation and no fever), are extremely resistant to ordinary sterilization regimens and to irradiation, the incubation period is measured in years, the disease develops gradually and has no cure.
**Prion diseases:** Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease, kuru, Gerstmann–Sträussler–Scheinker syndrome, fatal familial insomnia; in animals — bovine spongiform encephalopathy, scrapie.

parts.text: A prion is an infectious agent **without nucleic acid**. This is an exception to the classic “central dogma” in microbiology, and for this reason it is studied separately.

blocks.text: **Chromogenic media** are modern differential media that contain a colorless **chromogenic substrate**. If a bacterium has a particular enzyme, it breaks down the substrate and a colored product is released — the colony is stained a **characteristic color**.
**Advantages:**

items: the species can be preliminarily identified **by colony color** — the answer is 18–24 hours faster;
it becomes easier to separate species in mixed growth (for example, in a urine culture);
the number of additional biochemical tests is reduced.

blocks.text: Examples used in practice: chromogenic agar for urine culture (E. coli — pink-red, enterococcus — blue-green colonies), chromogenic agar for distinguishing *Candida* species, and special chromogenic media for screening for MRSA and Salmonella.

parts.text: A chromogenic medium gives a quick **preliminary** answer, but it does not replace final identification: a biochemical or molecular method (in modern laboratories, mass spectrometry or PCR) is still used for confirmation.

skills.title: Practical skill: the algorithm for streaking by sectors (quadrant method)

items: Draw 4 sectors on the back of the plate and mark them; write the patient information and the date.
Flame the bacteriological loop in the alcohol burner **until red-hot** and cool it for 10–15 seconds.
Take the material with the loop and spread it in a dense zigzag in **sector 1**.
**Flame and cool the loop again**; draw it 3–4 times from the edge of sector 1 and spread into **sector 2**.
Continue in the same way into sectors 2→3 and 3→4. The loop is flamed before each transition — the number of cells decreases in each sector.
Place the plate **upside down** (so that condensation drops do not fall on the streak) in the incubator at 37 °C for 18–24 hours.

parts.text: Touching the material with the loop **without cooling** it after flaming is the most common mistake: a hot loop kills the cells and the result becomes a false negative. The loop can be cooled by touching it to an empty area of the medium.

blocks.text: **Pasteur’s dilution method** and **Koch’s plate method** (serially diluting the material and pouring it mixed with molten agar) are other classic variants of isolation; in current practice, streaking by sectors is used more often.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: Material taken from the CSF was inoculated onto blood agar, but after 24 hours there was no growth. In the smear, however, small gram-negative rods had been seen. Growth appeared when it was inoculated onto chocolate agar.
cases.ask: Why was there no growth on ordinary blood agar?
cases.answer: The causative agent needs growth factors (factors X and V) — probably *Haemophilus influenzae*. These factors are present only in blood agar in which the erythrocytes have been broken down, that is, heated blood (chocolate) agar.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: To determine antibiotic susceptibility, a student used a culture that had stood in the incubator for three days. The results differed sharply from previous tests.
cases.ask: What is the error?
cases.answer: A three-day culture is in the death phase; the cells are polymorphic and some have died. For susceptibility testing, a young culture in the **24-hour, logarithmic phase** and a standard turbidity (for example, 0.5 McFarland) must be used.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A urine culture was inoculated onto chromogenic medium; after 18 hours pink-red and blue-green colonies grew at the same time.
cases.ask: What does this result mean and what is the next step?
cases.answer: Two different causative agents have grown (judging by the colors, probably E. coli and enterococcus). The next step is to subculture each colony separately, assess the quantity (CFU/mL), confirm the identification and set up a separate antibiogram for each.

topics.title: Catabolic metabolism: types of respiration. Isolation of pure cultures of aerobes and anaerobes. Cultural properties — day 2

goals.text: To know the ways of obtaining energy and the types of respiration (aerobic, anaerobic, facultative) in bacteria;
to divide bacteria into groups by their relation to oxygen and to explain the methods of creating anaerobic conditions;
to acquire the skill of fully describing the cultural properties of colonies;
to perform day 2 of pure culture isolation (studying the colonies, subculturing onto an agar slant);
Independent work: to gain an understanding of modern molecular-genetic methods of rapid diagnosis.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **The main feature of fermentation** is that the electron acceptor is an **organic substance** and oxygen does not take part. That is why fermentation yields little ATP, but allows life in the absence of oxygen.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **Catalase present → tolerates oxygen.** The catalase test is also used in practice to distinguish staphylococci (catalase +) from streptococci (catalase −): if bubbles appear when hydrogen peroxide is dropped on, the catalase is positive.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: When choosing a colony, **only an isolated colony** is picked. Material taken from a confluent (“fused”) area gives a mixed culture, and all the following steps (biochemical, serological, antibiogram) will show wrong results.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Small beta-hemolytic colonies on blood agar + gram-positive cocci in chains + material taken from the throat → suspicion of group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus; this is important in view of tonsillitis and its complications (rheumatic fever, glomerulonephritis) (topic 16).

sections.title: Catabolism and ways of obtaining energy

blocks.text: **Metabolism** consists of two directions: **catabolism** (breakdown, release of energy) and **anabolism/constructive metabolism** (synthesis, expenditure of energy — topic 7). In bacteria, energy is stored as **ATP** and is produced in the **cytoplasmic membrane** (there are no mitochondria).

The main pathways of carbohydrate breakdown: **glycolysis (Embden–Meyerhof–Parnas pathway)** — the most widespread; the **pentose phosphate pathway**; the **Entner–Doudoroff pathway** (for example, in *Pseudomonas*). The product of glycolysis is pyruvate, and its further fate depends on the type of respiration.

blocks.text: **Why is oxygen toxic to anaerobes?** In oxygen metabolism, toxic intermediate products form — the **superoxide anion (O₂⁻)** and **hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂)**. Aerobes have enzymes that neutralize them — **superoxide dismutase** and **catalase**; obligate anaerobes lack these enzymes or have very little, so they die in the presence of oxygen.

parts.text: **Catalase present → tolerates oxygen.** The catalase test is also used in practice to distinguish staphylococci (catalase +) from streptococci (catalase −): if bubbles appear when hydrogen peroxide is dropped on, the catalase is positive.

blocks.text: **Methods of creating anaerobic conditions:**

items: **Physical:** anaerostat (replacing the air with a gas mixture), boiling the medium to drive off oxygen and sealing it with a layer of oil, deep inoculation (a tall column of medium).
**Chemical:** gas-generating packs, oxygen-absorbing substances (pyrogallol + alkali).
**Biological:** Fortner’s method — an aerobe and an anaerobe are inoculated side by side on one plate; the aerobe consumes the oxygen and the anaerobe begins to grow.
**Special media:** Kitt–Tarozzi medium (with liver pieces and a layer of oil), thioglycolate medium.

blocks.text: The appearance of a colony is a species-specific feature that allows **preliminary identification**. A colony is described by the following features:

head: Feature
Variants
rows: Small (up to 1 mm), medium (1–3 mm), large (more than 3 mm)
Smooth (S form), rough (R form), mucoid (M form)
Flat, convex, with a depressed center, dome-shaped
Colorless, white, yellow, golden, blue-green, red
Soft, dry, sticky, easily picked up with a loop
Hemolysis, change in the color of the medium, diffusion of pigment into the medium
blocks.title: Table 6.3. Scheme for describing a colony

blocks.text: **S and R form colonies.** **S (smooth)** colonies are smooth, convex and moist; they are usually typical of encapsulated strains or those with complete LPS, which are more virulent. **R (rough)** colonies are dry with an uneven edge; in some species (tubercle bacillus, anthrax bacillus, diphtheria bacillus), by contrast, the R form is typical and is considered virulent.
**Hemolysis on blood agar** — the main feature in distinguishing streptococci:

items: **alpha-hemolysis** — a green-gray zone around the colony (partial breakdown of hemoglobin);
**beta-hemolysis** — a completely clear, colorless zone (the erythrocytes are completely lysed);
**gamma** — no hemolysis.

blocks.label: Figure 6.1
blocks.caption: Pure culture and colonies of pathogenic cocci: streptococcus (stained with methylene blue) and staphylococcus (by Gram), and their colonies on nutrient medium. Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

blocks.text: **Types of growth in liquid medium:** uniform turbidity (most facultative anaerobes), sediment at the bottom (streptococcus, species that settle out), a pellicle on the surface (obligate aerobes — the tubercle bacillus, *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*), pellicle + sediment.

sections.title: Isolation of a pure culture: day 2

blocks.text: **Goal** — to choose the needed colony from the inoculated plate and accumulate a pure culture.
**Work to be done:**

items: Examine the plate: whether there is growth, the number of colony types, and record the cultural properties of each.
**Prepare a smear and stain it by the Gram method** from the chosen (suspicious) colony — check that the morphology and tinctorial property match the colony description.
Take the remainder of that colony with the loop and subculture it onto a **meat-peptone agar slant** (or a selective medium) — this is the stage of accumulating the pure culture.
Place in the incubator at 37 °C for 18–24 hours.

blocks.text: Day 2 is slightly different **for anaerobes**: inoculation is done in an anaerostat or on Kitt–Tarozzi medium; because growth is slower, the result is assessed after 48–72 hours.

parts.text: When choosing a colony, **only an isolated colony** is picked. Material taken from a confluent (“fused”) area gives a mixed culture, and all the following steps (biochemical, serological, antibiogram) will show wrong results.

Small beta-hemolytic colonies on blood agar + gram-positive cocci in chains + material taken from the throat → suspicion of group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus; this is important in view of tonsillitis and its complications (rheumatic fever, glomerulonephritis) (topic 16).

sections.title: Independent work: Modern methods of rapid diagnosis of bacteria

blocks.text: The classic bacteriological method is reliable, but it takes **3–4 days**. Modern methods can give an answer within hours.

**1. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR).** A specific fragment of the pathogen’s DNA (or RNA — via reverse transcription) is amplified in vitro. Steps: **denaturation** (≈95 °C) → **primer binding (annealing)** (50–65 °C) → **elongation** (72 °C); the cycle is repeated 30–40 times and the target sequence multiplies exponentially. **Real-time PCR** measures the result during amplification by fluorescence and gives a quantitative assessment.

*Advantages:* very sensitive and specific; indispensable for pathogens that do not grow or grow slowly (chlamydia, mycoplasma, tuberculosis, viruses); gives a result even after antibiotics have been started.
*Limitations:* does not distinguish live from dead microbes; does not give full antibiotic susceptibility (detects only known resistance genes); sensitive to contamination.

**2. Sequencing the 16S ribosomal RNA gene.** The 16S rRNA gene is present in all bacteria; within it, regions common to all species (conserved) alternate with species-specific (variable) ones. Primers are placed on the common regions to amplify the gene, then its sequence is read and compared with a database. This method is used to identify **uncultivable or unusual** microorganisms, and also to study the composition of the microbiota.

**3. Electromigration methods.** **Capillary zone electrophoresis** — separates particles by charge and size in a thin capillary; **capillary isoelectric focusing** — separates proteins by their isoelectric point. They allow microbial proteins and nucleic acids to be analyzed with high accuracy.

**4. Mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF).** The spectrum of proteins in a colony is compared with a reference database, and the species is identified **in a few minutes**. It has now become the main method of identification in many laboratories.

parts.text: Rapid methods **complement, not replace,** classic culture: a live culture is still needed for full assessment of antibiotic susceptibility and for epidemiological analysis.

skills.title: Practical skill: describing a colony and accumulating a pure culture

items: Take the plate out of the incubator and, **without turning it over**, hold it up to the light and examine it: determine whether there is growth and how many kinds of colonies there are.
Describe each type of colony according to the scheme: size, shape, edge, surface, profile, color, transparency, consistency and change in the medium (hemolysis, pigment).
Assess the type of hemolysis on blood agar: clear zone (beta), green zone (alpha), no zone (gamma). Look at the zone from the bottom of the plate, holding it up to the light.
Write the description in the notebook and mark the suspicious colony — **only an isolated** colony is chosen.
Prepare a smear from part of that colony and stain it by the Gram method: the morphology must match the colony description.
Take the rest of the colony with the loop and inoculate it in a zigzag onto a **meat-peptone agar slant** (to accumulate a pure culture).
Label the tube (patient, date, colony number) and place it in the incubator at 37 °C for 18–24 hours.

parts.text: Touching a neighboring colony when picking a colony with the loop is the most common mistake: as a result a mixed culture accumulates and all the following steps give a wrong answer.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: Material taken from a deep, ulcerated wound was inoculated onto ordinary blood agar and incubated for 24 hours under aerobic conditions — there was no growth. In the smear, however, a large number of gram-positive rods had been seen.
cases.ask: What mistake was made and how is it corrected?
cases.answer: The causative agent may be an obligate anaerobe. The material must be inoculated under anaerobic conditions (anaerostat, Kitt–Tarozzi medium) and observed for 48–72 hours.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: Material taken from the throat was inoculated onto blood agar. After 24 hours, a completely clear zone appeared around small, transparent colonies; gram-positive cocci in chains were seen in the smear. The catalase test is negative.
cases.ask: What is the preliminary conclusion?
cases.answer: Beta-hemolytic streptococcus (catalase-negative, gram-positive cocci in chains). To determine the group, bacitracin susceptibility and serological grouping (for group A) are carried out.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: Material was taken after antibiotics had been started in the patient. Culture gave no growth, but PCR showed a positive result.
cases.ask: How is this explained and how should the PCR result be interpreted?
cases.answer: Under the action of the antibiotic the microbes have died or cannot grow, but their DNA has been preserved. PCR does not distinguish live from dead microbes — so the result confirms the presence of the causative agent, but in assessing the effect of treatment it is interpreted together with the clinical picture.

topics.title: Constructive metabolism: enzymes and products of vital activity. Identification of a pure culture — day 3

goals.text: To know the constructive metabolism of bacteria, their enzymes and their classification;
to explain the products of bacterial vital activity (enzymes, pigments, aromatic substances, toxins, antibiotics) and their diagnostic significance;
to master the methods of identifying a pure culture by its biochemical properties (Hiss, Kligler, oxidase, catalase, indole, urease);
to perform day 3 of pure culture isolation and prepare for the final report;
Independent work: to know the forms of obtaining energy in microorganisms, the types of fermentation and the pathways of carbohydrate fermentation.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Constitutive** enzymes — “permanent staff” (always working); **inducible** — “on call” (synthesis begins when the substrate arrives). The lac operon is the classic example of induction.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Aggression enzymes are themselves pathogenicity factors: **plasmacoagulase** (*S. aureus*) forms a fibrin shell that protects against phagocytosis and is the main test for distinguishing *S. aureus* from *S. epidermidis*; **hyaluronidase** “dissolves” the intercellular space of the tissue and makes spread easier (the “spreading factor”); **lecithinase** destroys the cell membrane.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Pigment and odor are only **auxiliary** signs. They speed up identification, but a final answer is not given without biochemical and serological confirmation.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Remember Kligler as a “**traffic light**”: **yellow = acid** (sugar fermented), **red = alkaline** (not fermented), **black = H₂S**, **crack/bubble = gas**.

blocks.text: **Constructive metabolism** is the process of synthesizing cell components (protein, nucleic acid, polysaccharide, lipid); energy is expended. It is closely linked to catabolism: catabolism provides **ATP and intermediate metabolites** (carbon skeletons), and anabolism uses them. Reactions common to both directions are called **amphibolic pathways** (for example, the Krebs cycle).
The bacterial cell synthesizes very quickly: under favorable conditions the entire cell content doubles in 20–30 minutes. The direction and rate of synthesis are controlled by **enzymes**.

An **enzyme** is a biological catalyst of protein nature. Enzymes serve as the main feature in the identification of bacteria, because **each species has its own characteristic set of enzymes** and it is passed on from generation to generation.

Type
Description and example
rows: Secreted outside the cell; break down large molecules (protease, lipase, amylase, hyaluronidase)
Work inside the cell (respiratory and synthetic enzymes)
Always synthesized, independent of the substrate (glycolytic enzymes)
Synthesized only when the substrate is present (if lactose is present — beta-galactosidase)
Hyaluronidase, plasmacoagulase, fibrinolysin, lecithinase, neuraminidase, collagenase

parts.text: **Constitutive** enzymes — “permanent staff” (always working); **inducible** — “on call” (synthesis begins when the substrate arrives). The lac operon is the classic example of induction.

Aggression enzymes are themselves pathogenicity factors: **plasmacoagulase** (*S. aureus*) forms a fibrin shell that protects against phagocytosis and is the main test for distinguishing *S. aureus* from *S. epidermidis*; **hyaluronidase** “dissolves” the intercellular space of the tissue and makes spread easier (the “spreading factor”); **lecithinase** destroys the cell membrane.

items: **Enzymes** — discussed above; the basis of identification.

**Pigments** — species-specific colored substances: *S. aureus* — golden-yellow (carotenoid), *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* — **pyocyanin** (blue-green, diffuses into the medium) and pyoverdine (fluorescent), *Serratia marcescens* — red prodigiosin. Functions of pigment: protection from UV rays, participation in respiration, antibiotic action.

**Aromatic (odorous) substances** — some species give off a characteristic smell: *P. aeruginosa* — a jasmine (hyacinth) smell, *Proteus* — a foul, putrid smell; in practice noted as an auxiliary sign.
**Toxins** — exotoxins (protein, species-specific, potent) and endotoxin (LPS) — in detail in topic 11.
**Antibiotics and bacteriocins** — substances that inhibit other microbes (topic 9).
**Vitamins and organic acids** — synthesized by the normal intestinal microflora (topic 10) and used in industry.

parts.text: Pigment and odor are only **auxiliary** signs. They speed up identification, but a final answer is not given without biochemical and serological confirmation.

blocks.text: For identification, the pure culture is tested for **saccharolytic** (carbohydrate breakdown), **proteolytic** (protein breakdown), **oxidation–reduction** and other enzyme activities.
5.1. Saccharolytic activity

**Hiss media (the “variegated series”)** — each tube contains one carbohydrate (glucose, lactose, maltose, sucrose, mannitol) + an indicator + a gas-collecting float (Durham tube). If the carbohydrate is broken down, acid forms → the indicator changes color (**A — acid**); if gas is also released, a bubble is seen in the tube (**AG — acid + gas**).

**Kligler medium (two-sugar iron medium)** — a medium that gives a lot of information in one tube. It contains glucose (little), lactose (much), an iron salt and an indicator; the tube consists of a slant (aerobic) and a butt (anaerobic) part.

blocks.text: 5.2. Proteolytic activity

The breakdown of proteins and amino acids is tested: gelatin liquefaction, milk coagulation, and production of **indole**, **hydrogen sulfide (H₂S)** and **ammonia**. To detect indole, Kovacs reagent is added — if a red ring appears, the result is positive (typical of E. coli).

sections.title: Isolation of a pure culture: day 3

blocks.text: **Goal** — to confirm the purity of the accumulated pure culture and determine its species.

items: **Checking purity:** a smear is prepared from the growth on the slant and stained by the Gram method. All cells must have the same morphology and tinctorial property.
**Biochemical identification:** the Hiss series, Kligler, indole, H₂S, urease and other tests are set up; modern laboratories use ready-made test systems or automated analyzers.
**Serological identification:** a **slide agglutination** reaction with diagnostic sera (dividing enteric bacteria into serovars — topic 22).
**Antibiogram:** set up by disk diffusion or another method (topic 9).
If necessary, additional tests: typing with phages, determination of toxigenicity, biological test.

blocks.text: **Day 4** — all the results are put together and the final report is given: **the species of the causative agent (if necessary — the serovar) and its susceptibility to antibiotics.**

parts.text: Biochemical results must be read **at the specified time**. Kligler is read after 18–24 hours: if read too early, the breakdown of lactose is not seen; if read too late, the acid in the slant turns alkaline and a lactose-negative result may be misinterpreted as falsely “lactose-positive.”

sections.title: Independent work: Forms of energy production and types of fermentation

blocks.text: **Forms of cell energy:** **ATP** (the chemical form) and the **proton gradient across the membrane (proton-motive force)**. The respiratory chain pumps protons out through the membrane, and the gradient formed is converted into ATP by **ATP synthase** (chemiosmotic theory). The proton gradient is also used directly for flagellar rotation and active transport.
**Ways of producing energy:** substrate-level phosphorylation (in fermentation, in a direct reaction), oxidative phosphorylation (in the respiratory chain), photophosphorylation (in phototrophs).
**Pathways of carbohydrate fermentation:** glycolysis (EMP), the pentose phosphate pathway, the Entner–Doudoroff pathway.

parts.text: In Enterobacteriaceae, **mixed (formic acid) fermentation** is exactly the reason **gas** forms in Hiss and Kligler media — this result is seen in daily identification.

skills.title: Practical skill: the algorithm for reading a biochemical series

items: Take the tubes out of the incubator at the specified time (usually 18–24 hours).
Compare with a control (uninoculated) tube — to see the color difference clearly.
For each carbohydrate: write **A** if the color has changed, **AG** if there is a bubble in the Durham tube, and **−** if there is no change.
In Kligler, assess the slant and the butt separately and note H₂S (black) and gas (cracks).
Perform the additional tests (indole, urease, oxidase, catalase).
Compare the set of results with an identification table or with **Bergey’s Manual** and determine the species.
In doubtful cases, confirm by serological identification or a molecular method.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A pure culture isolated from stool on Kligler medium: the slant is red, the butt is yellow, there is gas, and black color appeared in the butt. It is motile, oxidase-negative and does not break down lactose.
cases.ask: Which group should be considered and what is the next step?
cases.answer: A lactose-negative, H₂S-positive, motile gram-negative rod — **Salmonella** is highly likely. The next step is serological identification with diagnostic agglutinating sera (by O and H antigens).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: Gram-positive cocci isolated from pus are catalase-positive and plasmacoagulase-positive.
cases.ask: Which causative agent is this and what do these tests prove?
cases.answer: Catalase-positive — staphylococcus (not streptococcus); plasmacoagulase-positive — *Staphylococcus aureus*. Coagulase is the main pathogenicity and differential feature of this species.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A student read the Hiss series after 48 hours and wrote “lactose-positive,” but on serological testing the culture turned out to be Shigella.
cases.ask: What is the error related to?
cases.answer: Reading the result later than the specified time. Some shigellae can break down lactose **late** (after 48 hours); the standard reading time is 18–24 hours. A result read late misleads identification.

topics.title: Distribution of microbes in the environment. The microbiota of water, air and soil. Basics of sanitary microbiology

goals.text: To know the composition of the microbiota of water, air, soil and dwellings and its effect on human health;
to explain the aim of sanitary microbiology, the concept of sanitary indicator microorganisms and the requirements for them;
to master the methods of determining the total microbial count (TMC) and the coli index;
Independent work: to know the principles of sanitary-bacteriological assessment of milk and meat products.

summary.label: Remember

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: In sanitary examination, looking for the pathogen itself takes a long time and is often ineffective (pathogens are present in small numbers). That is why an **indirect indicator** — coliforms — is used: where they are found, the conclusion is drawn that intestinal pathogens may also be present.

summary.label: Caution

sections.title: General concept of the ecology of microorganisms

blocks.text: Microorganisms are distributed in all layers of the biosphere. They play a decisive role in **biogeochemical cycles** (the cycles of nitrogen, carbon, sulfur and phosphorus), break down organic residues and maintain soil fertility. From the medical point of view, however, the external environment can be a **source of infection and a factor of transmission**.

Relationships of microorganisms in the external environment: **symbiosis** (mutualism), **commensalism**, **neutralism**, **antagonism** (one species inhibits another — the natural basis of antibiotics and bacteriocins), **parasitism**.

Soil is the environment richest in microorganisms (billions of cells in 1 g of fertile soil). They are mainly **saprophytes**: bacteria, actinomycetes, fungi, algae, protozoa. The most microbes are at a depth of 10–20 cm; at the surface they decrease under the action of UV rays and drying.
**Function:** mineralization of organic residues, nitrogen fixation (*Azotobacter*, nodule bacteria), nitrification and denitrification, cellulose breakdown.

**Medical significance.** Most pathogenic microorganisms die quickly in soil, but **spore forms** persist for a long time; for this reason soil is a natural reservoir for the causative agents of tetanus, gas gangrene and anthrax. The causative agents of intestinal infections enter the soil with feces and can persist for several days to weeks.

**Sanitary indicators:** the total number of microbes, the **coli titer** and **perfringens titer** (the smallest amount of soil in which *E. coli* and *C. perfringens* are found), the number of thermophilic bacteria. A small coli titer is a sign of fresh fecal contamination, a small perfringens titer — of old contamination.

The composition of microbes in water depends on the source: **artesian waters** are almost sterile; **open water bodies** (river, lake) are contaminated from soil, precipitation and wastewater. Water has a capacity for self-purification (sunlight, sedimentation, microbial antagonism, grazing by protozoa), but it is limited.

**Waterborne infections:** cholera, typhoid and paratyphoid fevers, dysentery, escherichiosis, leptospirosis, tularemia, hepatitis A and E, poliomyelitis, rotavirus gastroenteritis, giardiasis and amebiasis.

Meaning

blocks.text: Air is not a favorable environment for microbes: there are no nutrients, it dries out, and sunlight acts on it. Therefore the microbes in the air are temporary and float together with **dust particles and droplets**.
**Two kinds of aerosol:**

items: **droplet (large-droplet) phase** — formed by coughing and sneezing, settles quickly; ensures transmission at close range;
**droplet-nuclei and dust phase** — fine, stays suspended for a long time; resistant pathogens (tubercle bacillus, streptococcus, fungal spores) spread by this route.

blocks.text: **Airborne infections:** influenza and other acute respiratory viral infections, COVID-19, measles, chickenpox, whooping cough, diphtheria, meningococcal infection, tuberculosis, streptococcal tonsillitis.

**Sanitary indicators:** per 1 m³ of air, the **total microbial count**, and the number of **hemolytic streptococci** and **Staphylococcus aureus** (an indicator of contamination from the human respiratory tract). In enclosed rooms the indicators are standardized according to the summer–winter season and the density of people; the requirements are strictest for operating rooms and children’s institutions.

**Methods of taking an air sample:** sedimentation (Koch’s method — leaving an open Petri dish for a certain time; simplified, approximate) and **aspiration** (the Krotov apparatus and similar devices — blowing a certain volume of air onto the surface of the medium; quantitative and accurate).
**Sanitary microbiology** is the branch that assesses the microbiological state of environmental objects (water, air, soil, food, objects, hands) and their danger to human health.
**Two main directions:**

items: Determining the **total microbial count** — the overall level of contamination of the object.
Determining **sanitary indicator microorganisms** — **indirect** evidence of contamination with human or animal excretions.

blocks.text: **Requirements for a sanitary indicator microorganism:**

items: it must live permanently in the human (animal) body and be excreted with discharges;
it must not multiply in the external environment, but survive for no shorter a time than pathogens;
the method of detection must be simple and reliable;
there must be no natural “native” representative of it in the external environment.
