sections.title: Independent work: Sanitary-bacteriological assessment of milk and meat products

blocks.text: **Milk.** After milking, milk contains natural microflora; the main cause of spoilage is the multiplication of lactic acid bacteria (souring). Sanitary indicators: **TMC (CFU/mL)**, coliforms (coli titer), somatic cell count, absence of pathogens (Salmonella, *S. aureus*, Listeria). The **reductase test** is a method for rapidly assessing the number of microbes in milk by the time it takes methylene blue or resazurin to decolorize: the faster the color disappears, the more microbes there are.

Infections that can be transmitted through milk: brucellosis, tuberculosis, salmonellosis, listeriosis, staphylococcal poisoning, campylobacteriosis. **Pasteurization** (for example, 72 °C for 15 s or 63 °C for 30 minutes) destroys vegetative pathogens.

**Meat.** The muscle tissue of a healthy animal is practically sterile; contamination occurs during slaughter, processing and storage. Indicators: TMC per 1 g, coliforms, sulfite-reducing clostridia, absence of Salmonella and Listeria in 25 g. In assessing freshness, organoleptic and chemical tests (ammonia, hydrogen sulfide reaction) are also used.

parts.text: The microbiological safety of food consists of three indicators: **total contamination (TMC)** + **sanitary indicator microbes (coliforms)** + **absence of pathogens in the specified mass**.

skills.title: Practical skill: microbiological examination of water

blocks.text: 7.1. Determining the total microbial count (pour plate method)

items: The water sample is collected in a sterile container and examined within 2 hours (or within 6 hours if kept cooled).
1 mL of water is placed in a sterile Petri dish.
10–12 mL of melted meat-peptone agar cooled to 45 °C is poured over it and mixed by rotating the dish.
After the agar sets, the dish is inverted and incubated at 37 °C for 24 hours.
The colonies that have grown are counted — the result is expressed in **CFU/mL** (colony-forming units).

blocks.text: 7.2. Membrane filter method (determining coliforms)

items: A certain volume of water (usually 100–333 mL) is passed through a **membrane filter** — the bacteria are retained on the surface of the filter.
The filter is removed with sterile forceps and placed on the surface of **Endo medium**.
It is incubated at 37 °C for 24 hours.
The **red colonies with a metallic sheen** that have grown on the filter are counted as lactose-positive coliforms; they are confirmed with a smear and an oxidase test.
The coli index is calculated from the result.

blocks.label: Figure 8.1
blocks.caption: The membrane filter apparatus used in the microbiological examination of water and how it is used. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

parts.text: Pouring agar that is **hotter than 45 °C** kills the microbes, and the TMC comes out falsely low. Placing the plate upside down prevents condensation drops from “spreading” the colonies.

blocks.text: 7.3. Titration (fermentation) method

Different volumes of water are inoculated into lactose medium; from the tubes with gas formation, subcultures are made onto Endo medium, and the coli index is calculated from the confirmed results using a special table (most probable number).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A well-water sample was examined: the coli index was sharply elevated and thermotolerant coliforms were found. Cases of acute intestinal infection have increased in the village.
cases.ask: What does the result mean and what measures are taken?
cases.answer: The water is contaminated with fresh feces; intestinal pathogens are likely to be present. Use of the water is stopped, the source of contamination is identified, the well is cleaned and disinfected, and use is permitted after repeat testing.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: An operating-room air sample was examined: the total microbial count was above the norm and hemolytic streptococcus was found.
cases.ask: What does this indicate?
cases.answer: The room air is contaminated with the microflora of the human respiratory tract (staff, ventilation, violation of the sanitary regime). The air exchange, disinfection and UV irradiation regimens are reviewed, and the staff are examined.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In the laboratory, agar was poured while still hot when determining the TMC of a water sample. The result was very low, but many coliforms were found by the membrane filter method.
cases.ask: Why do the results contradict each other?
cases.answer: Hot agar killed the microbes, so the TMC came out falsely low. The agar should have been cooled to 45 °C. The result of the membrane filter method is reliable.

summary.text: **Low temperature does not kill, it preserves.** That is why freezing is not a method of disinfection; on the contrary, it is used to store cultures and samples.

For this reason, the groups acting on the wall are usually considered the least toxic.

blocks.title: Table 9.1. Effect of physical factors on microorganisms

parts.text: **Low temperature does not kill, it preserves.** That is why freezing is not a method of disinfection; on the contrary, it is used to store cultures and samples.

blocks.text: **Sterilization** is the complete elimination of **all** microorganisms, including spores, from an object.
**Disinfection** is the elimination of pathogenic and opportunistic microbes (mainly vegetative forms) to reduce the risk of transmission; spores may survive.

head: Method
Regimen
Used for
rows: Nutrient media, used materials, fabrics, rubber
blocks.title: Table 9.2. Main sterilization methods

blocks.text: **Asepsis** is a system of measures to **prevent** microbes from entering a wound, tissue or an object that must be sterile (sterilized instruments, gloves, mask, laminar flow cabinet, preparation of the operative field).
**Antisepsis** is the elimination or reduction of microbes **already present** in a wound or living tissue (treatment of skin and mucous membranes).

**Groups of disinfectant and antiseptic substances:** halogens (chlorine and iodine preparations), alcohols (70% ethanol is the most effective), oxidizing agents (hydrogen peroxide, potassium permanganate), aldehydes (formaldehyde, glutaraldehyde), phenols, salts of heavy metals, surfactants (chlorhexidine, quaternary ammonium compounds), dyes (brilliant green).

parts.text: **95% alcohol disinfects less effectively than 70% alcohol**: high-concentration alcohol immediately coagulates the protein on the cell surface, forms a crust and cannot penetrate inside.

blocks.text: **Antibiotics** are substances produced by microorganisms, plants or animals, or obtained synthetically or semisynthetically, that stop the growth of other microorganisms or kill them.
**Classification:**

items: **By origin:** natural (penicillin, streptomycin), semisynthetic (ampicillin, amoxicillin), synthetic (sulfonamides, fluoroquinolones).

**By the nature of action:** **bactericidal** (kill — beta-lactams, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, vancomycin) and **bacteriostatic** (stop multiplication — tetracyclines, macrolides, chloramphenicol (levomycetin), sulfonamides).
**By spectrum of action:** narrow-spectrum (mainly Gram-positive or mainly Gram-negative) and broad-spectrum.

head: Target
Mechanism
Groups
rows: Inhibition of DNA gyrase, RNA polymerase
Stopping the steps of folate synthesis
blocks.title: Table 9.3. Groups of antibiotics by mechanism of action

parts.text: Remember the targets of protein synthesis inhibitors: **“30 — AT, 50 — CLM”**: **A**minoglycoside and **T**etracycline — **30S**; **C**hloramphenicol, **L**incosamide, **M**acrolide — **50S**.

The selective action (selective toxicity) of an antibiotic is based on the difference between the bacterial and the human cell: humans have no peptidoglycan wall (which is why beta-lactams are relatively safe) and the ribosome is 80S (not 70S). For this reason, the groups acting on the wall are usually considered the least toxic.

blocks.text: 5.1. Disk diffusion method (Kirby–Bauer)

items: A suspension of standard turbidity (0.5 McFarland) is prepared from a pure culture.
The suspension is spread evenly (in three directions) over the surface of **Mueller–Hinton agar** with a swab.
**Disks** impregnated with antibiotics are placed with forceps at specified distances.
It is incubated at 35–37 °C for 16–18 hours.

The **diameter of the zone of growth inhibition** around the disk is measured with a ruler and interpreted using a standard table: **S — susceptible**, **I — intermediate (susceptible at an increased dose)**, **R — resistant**.

blocks.label: Figure 9.1
blocks.caption: Determining susceptibility to antibiotics: zones of growth inhibition around the disks in the disk diffusion method and reading of the result. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

parts.text: The diameter of the zone by itself does not mean “good or bad”: every antibiotic and every species has its **own cutoff value**. That is why the result is interpreted only according to the current standard table.

blocks.text: 5.2. Dilution method — MIC and MBC

**MIC (minimum inhibitory concentration)** is the lowest concentration of an antibiotic that stops visible growth. **MBC (minimum bactericidal concentration)** is the lowest concentration that kills a specified proportion of the microbes. MIC is determined by serial dilution in liquid or solid medium; in practice the E-test (gradient strip) is also used.

**Clinical significance:** MIC helps in choosing the drug dose and route of administration; in severe infections (sepsis, endocarditis, meningitis) a quantitative MIC value is preferable to a qualitative “S/I/R” answer.

**Bacteriocins** are protein substances produced by bacteria that act against **closely related species**. They are named after the producing species: colicins (*E. coli*), staphylococcins, pyocins. They are encoded on plasmids.

**Significance:** a factor of competition (antagonism) between microbial populations; **bacteriocin typing** is a method of distinguishing strains in epidemiological investigation; a natural preservative in the food industry (nisin); being studied as new antibacterial agents.

sections.title: Independent work: Mechanisms of resistance to antibiotics

blocks.text: **Types of resistance:**

items: **Natural (innate)** — arises from the structure of the species and is present in all its representatives (mycoplasmas — to beta-lactams; the outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria — to many drugs).
**Acquired** — arises as a result of mutation or gene transfer; this is the type that causes clinical problems.

blocks.text: **Genetic basis of acquired resistance:** chromosomal mutations and **horizontal gene transfer** — conjugation (R plasmids), transduction, transformation, transposons and integrons (topic 11).

head: Mechanism
Meaning
Example
rows: An enzyme that destroys the antibiotic
An altered penicillin-binding protein in MRSA; ribosome methylation
The antibiotic cannot enter the cell
A pump pushes the antibiotic out
blocks.title: Table 9.4. Biochemical mechanisms of resistance

blocks.text: **Factors that lead to the spread of resistance:** unjustified prescription of antibiotics (in viral infections), not completing the course of treatment, wrong choice of dose, mass use in livestock farming, spread of resistant strains inside hospitals.
**Prevention:** prescribing antibiotics **based on an antibiogram**, completing the course, infection control and hand hygiene, antibiotic stewardship programs, monitoring of resistance.

**Bacteriological assessment of sterilization and disinfection.** The quality of sterilization is monitored with **biological indicators** (an ampoule or strip containing spores of a resistant test microorganism): after the cycle is finished, the indicator is cultured and there must be no growth. Physical (temperature, pressure, time record) and chemical (indicator strips) monitoring are also used in addition. The quality of disinfection is assessed by culturing wash samples taken from treated surfaces — no sanitary indicator microbes should be found.

parts.text: Only **biological monitoring** fully confirms the reliability of sterilization: physical and chemical indicators show that the regimen was carried out, but they do not directly prove the result.

skills.title: Practical skill: setting up and reading the disk diffusion method

items: From a 24-hour pure culture, prepare a suspension in sterile saline and adjust its turbidity to the **0.5 McFarland** standard.
Dip a sterile swab into the suspension and press out the excess liquid against the wall of the tube.
Spread the swab evenly over the surface of **Mueller–Hinton agar** in **three directions** (rotating the dish 60° each time); also cover the edges.
Wait 3–5 minutes until the surface is dry.
Place the antibiotic disks with sterile forceps at least 24 mm apart and press them lightly so that they stick to the surface.
Invert the dish and incubate at 35–37 °C for 16–18 hours.
Measure the diameter of the zone of growth inhibition from the bottom of the dish with a ruler in **mm**; take the whole diameter of the zone.
Compare the result with the current standard table, mark it as **S / I / R** and write it in the report.

parts.text: If the suspension is denser than the standard, the zone becomes smaller (false resistance); if it is thinner, the zone becomes larger (false susceptibility). That is why adjusting the turbidity is the main condition for a reliable result.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A patient has a purulent infection; the *S. aureus* isolated was found to be oxacillin-resistant in the antibiogram.
cases.ask: What does this result mean and what is important in treatment?
cases.answer: A methicillin (oxacillin)-resistant staphylococcus — MRSA. The resistance is linked to an altered penicillin-binding protein, so **all beta-lactams** are considered ineffective. Treatment is carried out according to the antibiogram with drugs of another group; the patient is placed under infection control measures.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: In a laboratory, after the autoclave cycle was finished, the color of the chemical indicator changed, but growth was detected when the biological indicator was cultured.
cases.ask: What is the conclusion?
cases.answer: Sterilization was in fact not achieved. The chemical indicator only shows that the temperature reached the set value; the exposure time or the penetration of steam into the material may have been insufficient. The autoclave is sent for technical inspection and the material is re-sterilized.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: For an acute respiratory viral infection, a doctor prescribed a broad-spectrum antibiotic to a patient; when the patient felt better, he stopped the drug on day 3.
cases.ask: What two mistakes are there here, and what is the consequence?
cases.answer: First, an antibiotic in a viral infection is unjustified (it does not act on viruses). Second, the course was not completed. Both mistakes lead to the selection of resistant strains and to disruption of the normal microflora (dysbacteriosis).

topics.title: The normal microflora of the human body. Dysbacteriosis. Probiotics

goals.text: To know the concept of the normal microflora (microbiota), its formation and its composition by organ;
to explain the functions of the normal microflora for the body;
to master the causes, degrees and laboratory diagnostic methods of dysbacteriosis (dysbiosis);
Independent work: to have an understanding of probiotics, prebiotics and synbiotics.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: If a microorganism is isolated from a site that should normally be **sterile** (blood, cerebrospinal fluid), this is almost always a sign of **pathology** — even if the isolated species is “a member of the normal microflora.”

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: In the large intestine **anaerobes predominate**: **BI-BA** — **Bi**fidobacteria and **Ba**cteroides. Although *E. coli* is mentioned often, it makes up **less than 1%** of the total mass.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: When colonization resistance is disrupted (especially after a broad-spectrum antibiotic), the vacated place is taken by resistant or opportunistic species. Antibiotic-associated diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis caused by *Clostridioides difficile* are the clinical expression of this condition.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: A stool culture reflects only part of the **luminal** microflora of the intestine, and not all anaerobes can be cultured. That is why the result of a “dysbacteriosis analysis” is interpreted together with the clinical picture; prescribing treatment on the basis of the analysis alone is not correct.

sections.title: General concept of the normal microflora

blocks.text: **The normal microflora (microbiota)** is the totality of microorganisms that permanently inhabit the organs and tissues of a healthy body that are in contact with the external environment. The number of microbial cells in the human body is comparable to the number of body cells; most of them are located in the large intestine.
**Two parts:**

items: **Resident (permanent, obligate) microflora** — of stable composition, characteristic of the organ (bifidobacteria, lactobacilli, bacteroides, *E. coli*);
**Transient microflora** — species that come from the external environment and do not persist for long; among them there are also opportunistic pathogens.

blocks.text: **Sterile sites (microbe-free in the norm):** blood, cerebrospinal fluid, internal organs, synovial fluid, the bladder and the upper parts of the urinary tract, the uterine cavity, the alveolar part of the lung.

parts.text: If a microorganism is isolated from a site that should normally be **sterile** (blood, cerebrospinal fluid), this is almost always a sign of **pathology** — even if the isolated species is “a member of the normal microflora.”

parts.text: In the large intestine **anaerobes predominate**: **BI-BA** — **Bi**fidobacteria and **Ba**cteroides. Although *E. coli* is mentioned often, it makes up **less than 1%** of the total mass.

items: **Colonization resistance (protection)** — occupies the space and the nutrients, preventing pathogens from settling; produces bacteriocins, organic acids and hydrogen peroxide.
**Shaping immunity** — stimulates the gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT), supports the production of secretory IgA, provides “training” of the immune system.

**Metabolic and digestive function** — ferments undigested carbohydrates, forms short-chain fatty acids (an energy source for the intestinal epithelium), takes part in the metabolism of bile acids and cholesterol.
**Vitamin synthesis** — vitamin K, B vitamins (B₁₂, folate, biotin).
**Detoxification** — breaks down certain toxic substances and speeds up their excretion.
**Morphokinetic effect** — influences the normal development of the intestinal mucosa and peristalsis.

parts.text: When colonization resistance is disrupted (especially after a broad-spectrum antibiotic), the vacated place is taken by resistant or opportunistic species. Antibiotic-associated diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis caused by *Clostridioides difficile* are the clinical expression of this condition.

blocks.text: **Dysbacteriosis** is a persistent disturbance in the qualitative and quantitative composition of the normal microflora: the resident representatives decrease, and opportunistic pathogens and unusual species increase. It is not an independent nosological entity but a **syndrome** — the cause must always be sought.

**Causes:** antibiotics and other drugs (chemotherapy, immunosuppressants), acute intestinal infections, chronic gastrointestinal diseases, improper nutrition, operations, immunodeficiency, stress and irradiation; in a newborn — disruption of the breastfeeding regimen.

head: Degree
Laboratory picture
Clinical picture
rows: Bifido-/lactobacilli slightly decreased, the amount of *E. coli* changed
Anaerobes markedly decreased, opportunistic pathogens increased, lactose-negative and hemolytic *E. coli* have appeared
Opportunistic pathogens (Proteus, Klebsiella, staphylococcus, fungi) predominate
Profound disturbance, risk of overgrowth and spread of opportunistic pathogens
Severe clinical picture, possibility of generalization
blocks.title: Table 10.2. Conventional degrees of intestinal dysbacteriosis

blocks.text: **Laboratory diagnosis:**

items: **Classic bacteriological method** — serial dilution of stool (from 10⁻¹ to 10⁻⁹) and culture on selective and differential media; for each group (bifidobacteria, lactobacilli, *E. coli* and its variants, enterococci, staphylococci, Proteus, Klebsiella, fungi) the **CFU/g** is calculated and compared with the norm.
**Gas-liquid chromatography** — assessing the state of the anaerobic microbiota from the spectrum of short-chain fatty acids in stool.
**Molecular methods** — PCR, sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene; they also cover species that cannot be cultured and show the composition of the microbiota more fully.
**Additional** — examination of biopsy material from the intestinal mucosa (mucosa-associated microflora).

parts.text: A stool culture reflects only part of the **luminal** microflora of the intestine, and not all anaerobes can be cultured. That is why the result of a “dysbacteriosis analysis” is interpreted together with the clinical picture; prescribing treatment on the basis of the analysis alone is not correct.

sections.title: Independent work: Probiotics, prebiotics and synbiotics

blocks.text: **Probiotics** are **live microorganisms** that, when taken in adequate amounts, have a beneficial effect on health. By composition:

items: **monocomponent** — a single strain (bifidumbacterin, lactobacterin, colibacterin);
**polycomponent (symbiotic)** — several strains (Bifiform and similar preparations);
**self-eliminating antagonists** — species that do not multiply in the intestine but displace pathogens (preparations based on *Bacillus*, *Saccharomyces boulardii*);
**sorbed** — strains immobilized on a sorbent.

blocks.text: **Mechanism of action:** restoring colonization resistance, producing organic acids and bacteriocins, strengthening the barrier function of the epithelium, stimulating local immunity (secretory IgA).
**Prebiotics** are substances that are not digestible but stimulate the growth of the beneficial microflora (lactulose, inulin, oligofructose).
**Synbiotics** are combined preparations of a probiotic and a prebiotic.
**Use:** prevention of antibiotic-associated diarrhea, recovery after acute intestinal infections, supporting the formation of the microbiota in newborns.

parts.text: The effect of a probiotic is **strain-specific**: a benefit proven for one strain is not automatically transferred to the whole species or to another preparation. In patients with severely reduced immunity, preparations of live microorganisms are used with caution.

skills.title: Practical skill: algorithm for examining stool for dysbacteriosis

items: Stool is collected into a **sterile container**, before antibiotics are taken (or 2–3 days after stopping them); the sample is delivered to the laboratory within 2 hours.
1 g of stool is mixed in 9 mL of sterile solution — a 10⁻¹ dilution; serial dilutions are made in the same way up to 10⁻⁹.

From each dilution, the appropriate media are inoculated: Blaurock (bifidobacteria), MRS (lactobacilli), Endo/Levine (E. coli and enterobacteria), egg-yolk salt agar (staphylococci), enterococcus agar, Sabouraud (fungi), blood agar (hemolytic variants).
For anaerobes, culture is done under anaerobic conditions for 48–72 hours; aerobes for 24–48 hours, at 37 °C.
The colonies are counted and multiplied by the dilution factor — the result is given in **CFU/g**.
Identification is done (Gram stain, biochemical tests); hemolytic and lactose-negative variants are recorded separately.
The results are compared with age norms and a conclusion is given on the degree of dysbacteriosis.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: After a patient took a broad-spectrum antibiotic for 10 days, frequent loose stools and abdominal pain appeared. In the stool culture, bifidobacteria were sharply decreased, while hemolytic *E. coli* and fungi had increased.
cases.ask: How do you assess the condition and what must be taken into account?
cases.answer: Antibiotic-associated dysbacteriosis. Colonization resistance is disrupted. In severe cases, colitis associated with *C. difficile* must be excluded (special testing). Treatment consists of eliminating the cause and, if necessary, agents that support the microbiota; the prescription is determined by the physician.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: *Staphylococcus epidermidis* was isolated from a blood culture. The patient has a central venous catheter and a raised temperature.
cases.ask: Is it correct to assess this result as “skin microflora, insignificant”?
cases.answer: No. Blood is sterile in the norm. Although *S. epidermidis* is a member of the normal skin microflora, when a catheter is present it can form a biofilm and cause a true catheter-related infection. It is assessed together with a repeat culture and clinical data.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: On examination of a woman’s vaginal discharge, lactobacilli are almost absent, the pH is above 5.5, and various opportunistic anaerobes have increased.
cases.ask: What does this picture mean?
cases.answer: Disruption of the vaginal microbiota (the picture of bacterial vaginosis). The decrease in lactobacilli stops the production of lactic acid, the pH rises and anaerobes multiply. The diagnosis is made on the basis of the clinical picture, pH, a smear (clue cells) and other criteria.

topics.title: The doctrine of infection. Pathogenicity and virulence. Genetics and variability of microorganisms

goals.text: To distinguish the concepts of infection, infectious process and infectious disease;
to know the factors of pathogenicity and virulence and the types of toxins;
to explain the stages, forms and routes of transmission of the infectious process;
to know systematically the main methods of diagnosing infectious diseases;
to master the genetics of bacteria, the types of variability and the ways genetic material is transferred;
Independent work: to know the significance of plasmids, transposons, IS elements and temperate phages in medicine.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Toxoid (anatoxin)** is an exotoxin that has lost its toxicity under the action of formalin and heat but has retained its immunogenicity. It is the basis of the vaccines against tetanus and diphtheria.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Paired sera rule:** in serological diagnosis, serum is taken at the beginning of the illness and after 10–14 days. For diagnosis, a **rise in titer of at least 4-fold** is significant; a positive result in a single serum can often also indicate a past infection or vaccination.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Remember the three routes by their source: **Trans-FOR-mation** — **free DNA** (from the environment); **Trans-DUC-tion** — a **phage** carries it; **Conjugation** — **contact** (through a pilus).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Horizontal gene transfer is the main reason for the **rapid spread of antibiotic resistance among species**. That is why a resistant strain that has arisen in one ward can pass the resistance gene to other species and become a problem throughout the hospital.

blocks.text: **Infection (infectious process)** is the totality of interactions between a microorganism and a macroorganism under certain environmental conditions. **Infectious disease** is the form of the infectious process that is manifested by clinical signs; that is, not every infection ends in disease.

head: Form
Description
rows: Acute, chronic, recurrent; typical or atypical course
No clinical signs, but an immunological shift is present
Healthy, convalescent (after recovery), acute or chronic
Long-term retention of the pathogen in the body
The pathogen “sleeps” and is activated when conditions change (herpes, tuberculosis)
blocks.title: Table 11.1. Forms of the infectious process

blocks.text: **By origin:** exogenous (from outside) and **endogenous** (from the body’s own opportunistic microflora, when immunity falls). By the number of pathogens: monoinfection and **mixed infection**. By repeat infection: **reinfection** (infection again with the same species after recovery), **superinfection** (infection again without having recovered), **relapse** (recurrence due to the pathogen that remained in the body).

**Periods of the disease:** incubation → prodromal (initial, vague signs) → peak (typical clinical picture) → recovery (convalescence). For each period, **the appropriate material and method** are chosen — this is the main rule of laboratory diagnosis.
**Pathogenicity** is the ability of a species to cause disease; it is a **species trait**, genetically fixed, a qualitative concept.

**Virulence** is the **strain-specific quantitative** expression of pathogenicity (“the power to cause disease”); the units of measurement are DLM (minimum lethal dose), LD₅₀ (the dose that kills 50% of animals) and ID₅₀ (infectious dose).

head: Group
Factors
Task
rows: Attachment to the epithelium — the first stage of infection
Capsule, plasmacoagulase, catalase, protein A, IgA protease
Protection from phagocytosis and immune factors

parts.text: **Paired sera rule:** in serological diagnosis, serum is taken at the beginning of the illness and after 10–14 days. For diagnosis, a **rise in titer of at least 4-fold** is significant; a positive result in a single serum can often also indicate a past infection or vaccination.

blocks.text: **Genetic apparatus:** a circular **chromosome** (nucleoid) and extrachromosomal elements — **plasmids**, **transposons**, **IS elements**, and the genome of a temperate phage (prophage).
**Genotype** is the totality of genes; **phenotype** is the expression of the genotype under particular conditions.

head: Type
Mechanism
Heritable?
Example
rows: The genotype does not change, the expression changes
Formation of a capsule or pigment depending on the composition of the medium
Acquiring a gene from another cell
blocks.title: Table 11.6. Types of variability

blocks.text: **Mutations:** spontaneous (natural, low frequency) and induced (under the action of mutagens — UV light, chemicals); point (a single nucleotide) and genomic (large rearrangements). Under conditions of **selection** (for example, antibiotic pressure), mutations come to predominate in the population.
6.1. Ways of transfer of genetic material (recombination)

items: **Transformation** — a bacterium takes up **free DNA** from the environment. For this the cell must be in a special state (competence). Historical significance: the experiments of Griffith (1928) and Avery proved that DNA is the hereditary material.

**Transduction** — the transfer of genes by a **bacteriophage**. In **general (generalized)** transduction any piece of the chromosome is transferred; in **specialized** transduction, particular genes next to the prophage are transferred.
**Conjugation** — two cells in direct contact transfer DNA (often a plasmid) through a **sex (F) pilus**. The donor is an F⁺ or Hfr cell, the recipient is F⁻.

parts.text: Remember the three routes by their source: **Trans-FOR-mation** — **free DNA** (from the environment); **Trans-DUC-tion** — a **phage** carries it; **Conjugation** — **contact** (through a pilus).

Horizontal gene transfer is the main reason for the **rapid spread of antibiotic resistance among species**. That is why a resistant strain that has arisen in one ward can pass the resistance gene to other species and become a problem throughout the hospital.

sections.title: Independent work: Plasmids, transposons, IS elements and temperate phages

blocks.text: **Plasmids** are extrachromosomal, independently replicating circular DNA. Properties: they are not essential for the life of the cell but give it additional capabilities; they can pass to another cell by conjugation; they can also be lost (elimination).

head: Plasmid
Encoded property
Significance
blocks.title: Table 11.7. Plasmids of significance in medicine

blocks.text: **IS elements (insertion sequences)** are the simplest transposable elements, containing only the gene required for their own transposition. They move from place to place in the genome and can inactivate genes or, conversely, activate them.

**Transposons**, unlike IS elements, carry **additional genes** besides the transposition genes (often an antibiotic resistance gene or a toxin gene). They move between the chromosome and plasmids and speed up the spread of resistance genes. **Integrons** are systems that “collect” resistance gene cassettes and play an important role in the development of multidrug resistance.

**Temperate phages and lysogeny.** A temperate phage does not lyse the bacterium immediately but integrates its genome into the chromosome and is passed from generation to generation as a **prophage** (a **lysogenic culture**). If the prophage genes give the bacterium a new property, this is called **phage conversion**.

**The most important clinical examples:** toxin production by the diphtheria agent is controlled by a prophage gene — **only lysogenic strains are toxigenic**; the toxin genes of the cholera vibrio and of some *Shigella*/*E. coli* strains are also phage-associated.

parts.text: The toxigenicity of the diphtheria bacillus is a classic example of **phage conversion**. That is why, in the diagnosis of diphtheria, it is essential to **determine the toxigenicity** of the isolated culture separately (topic 18).

skills.title: Practical skill: choosing the method and material according to the stage of the disease

items: **Determine the stage of the disease:** incubation, prodromal, peak or recovery. At each stage the pathogen is in different places in the body.
**In the early stage**, look for the pathogen itself: take the material **before antibiotics** and choose a bacteriological or molecular method.
**From week 2**, assess the body’s response: for the serological method take **paired sera** (at the beginning of the illness and after 10–14 days).
**Choose the material:** according to where the pathogen is multiplying — blood (bacteremia), stool (intestine), sputum (respiratory tract), cerebrospinal fluid (CNS), urine, wound discharge.
**Collect and transport the sample correctly:** a sterile container, a transport medium if necessary; for fragile pathogens (meningococcus, gonococcus) — warm and fast.
**Fill in the referral:** clinical diagnosis, date of onset of the illness, whether antibiotics have been taken, vaccination history.
**Interpret the result:** not a single positive serological result but the **dynamics of the titer**; and with PCR, take into account that live and dead microbes are not distinguished.

parts.text: There is no single universal method: the method is matched to **the stage of the disease**. Material taken at the wrong time gives a false-negative result even in the best laboratory.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A patient has fever, a sharp drop in blood pressure and signs of DIC. A gram-negative rod grew in the blood culture. After antibiotics were started, the condition at first worsened.
cases.ask: What is this picture related to?
cases.answer: The effect of **endotoxin (LPS)** in the wall of gram-negative bacteria — a picture of septic shock. When bacteria break down under the action of the antibiotic, a large amount of endotoxin is released, and the condition may temporarily worsen. Treatment is carried out in intensive care.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A culture resembling the diphtheria bacillus, isolated from the throat, matched morphologically and biochemically, but the toxigenicity test was negative.
cases.ask: How should the result be interpreted?
cases.answer: The culture may be a **nontoxigenic** strain: toxin production depends on prophage genes (phage conversion). A nontoxigenic strain does not produce the typical clinical picture of diphtheria. That is why the diagnosis is made together with determining toxigenicity.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In an intensive care unit, various gram-negative bacteria isolated from several patients proved resistant to the same group of antibiotics.
cases.ask: How is such a picture explained?
cases.answer: The resistance genes may have spread among species by **horizontal gene transfer** (R plasmids, transposons, integrons). Measures: infection control, hand hygiene, rational use of antibiotics and monitoring of resistance.

topics.title: General virology: the structure, reproduction and classification of viruses. Bacteriophages. Isolation, indication and identification of viruses

goals.text: To know the structure, chemical composition and principles of classification of viruses;
to explain the stages of virus reproduction and the types of virus–cell relationships;
to master the methods of culturing viruses (cell culture, chick embryo, laboratory animals), indication and identification;
to know the structure, life cycle and practical uses of bacteriophages;
Independent work: the use of bacteriophages in treatment, identification and prophylaxis.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Enveloped (supercapsid)** viruses are unstable in the external environment: they are sensitive to lipid solvents, alcohol and soap. **Non-enveloped** viruses are much more resistant and adapted to transmission by the fecal-oral route (enteroviruses, hepatitis A, rotavirus).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Remember the stages in order: **A–P–U–S–A–R**: **A**dsorption → **P**enetration → **U**ncoating → **S**ynthesis → **A**ssembly → **R**elease.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The basis of modern virological diagnosis is **PCR** (and real-time PCR): it is fast and sensitive, detects the virus without culturing it and quantitatively assesses the viral load. The classic virological method (isolation) has remained mainly for scientific purposes and for selecting vaccine strains.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In virology, **the time of collecting the material** is decisive: virus shedding is often highest in the first days of the illness. In material taken late, even PCR may be negative, so it is supplemented with serology.

sections.title: The structure and chemical composition of viruses

blocks.text: **Viruses** are acellular forms of life; they are **obligate intracellular parasites**. Their main distinguishing features:

items: they contain only **one** type of nucleic acid — **DNA or RNA** (not both together);
they have no protein-synthesizing system (ribosomes) or energy-producing system of their own — they use those of the host cell;
they multiply not by binary fission but by the **disjunctive (separated)** method: the components are synthesized separately and then assembled;
they pass through bacterial filters;
they are not susceptible to antibiotics.

blocks.text: **Virion** is the mature, extracellular virus particle. Structure:

items: **Nucleoid (genome)** — DNA or RNA; single-stranded or double-stranded, linear or circular, whole or segmented.
**Capsid** — the protein shell, built of **capsomers**; it protects the genome and takes part in attachment to the cell and in antigenic properties.
**Supercapsid (outer envelope)** — present in some viruses; it is formed from the host cell membrane and equipped with viral glycoproteins (spikes).

blocks.text: **Types of symmetry:** **helical** (the nucleocapsid is coiled in a spiral — influenza, rabies), **cubic (icosahedral)** (adenovirus, poliovirus, herpes), **complex (mixed)** (smallpox virus, most bacteriophages).

blocks.label: Figure 12.1
blocks.caption: The structure of the influenza virus: supercapsid, hemagglutinin and neuraminidase spikes, matrix protein, nucleoprotein with segmented RNA. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

parts.text: **Enveloped (supercapsid)** viruses are unstable in the external environment: they are sensitive to lipid solvents, alcohol and soap. **Non-enveloped** viruses are much more resistant and adapted to transmission by the fecal-oral route (enteroviruses, hepatitis A, rotavirus).

blocks.label: Figure 12.2
blocks.caption: The main virus families that cause disease in humans: classification into DNA and RNA viruses and enveloped and non-enveloped groups. Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

blocks.text: **Principles of classification:** type of nucleic acid (DNA/RNA), strandedness (single/double), type of symmetry, presence of an envelope, virion size, site of replication (nucleus or cytoplasm), antigenic properties.

sections.title: The interaction of a virus with the cell

blocks.text: **Three kinds of outcome:**

items: **Productive (lytic)** — the full cycle is completed, new virions form, and the cell often dies.
**Abortive** — the cycle stalls (the cell is unsuitable or the virus is defective); no new virions form.
**Integrative (virogeny)** — the viral genome integrates into the cell chromosome and replicates with it (retroviruses, hepatitis B, some oncoviruses).

blocks.text: Stages of the productive cycle

items: **Adsorption** — binding of the viral spikes to **specific receptors** on the cell surface. This very stage determines the tissue and species specificity (tropism) of the virus.
**Penetration (entry)** — endocytosis through the receptor, or fusion of the envelope with the cell membrane.
**Uncoating (“undressing”)** — the genome is freed from the envelope and capsid and exposed.
**Eclipse (hidden) period and synthesis** — the viral genome and proteins are synthesized in the host cell’s systems; during this time no whole virion can be found in the cell.
**Assembly (morphogenesis)** — the nucleocapsid is assembled from the components.
**Release** — by cell lysis (non-enveloped viruses) or by **budding** (enveloped viruses take their envelope from the membrane).

parts.text: Remember the stages in order: **A–P–U–S–A–R**: **A**dsorption → **P**enetration → **U**ncoating → **S**ynthesis → **A**ssembly → **R**elease.

blocks.text: Viruses do not grow in artificial nutrient media, so **living systems** are needed:

head: System
Use
Methods of indication (detecting presence)
rows: Cytopathic effect (CPE), plaques, hemadsorption, color test, immunofluorescence
Embryo death, plaques on the chorioallantoic membrane, hemagglutination test
Signs of disease, paralysis, pathomorphological changes
blocks.title: Table 12.1. Systems for culturing viruses

blocks.text: **Types of cell cultures:** primary (directly from tissue, limited lifespan), semi-continuous (diploid strains) and **continuous (permanent) lines** (unlimited growth — HeLa, Vero and others).

blocks.label: Figure 12.3
blocks.caption: Cytopathic effect of viruses on cell culture: a) perinuclear inclusions; b) hemadsorption reaction; c) virus colonies (plaques). Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

blocks.label: Figure 12.4
blocks.caption: The structure of a chick embryo (8–10 days old) and the routes of infecting viruses: onto the chorioallantoic membrane, into the amniotic and allantoic cavities, into the yolk sac. Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

blocks.text: **Methods of detecting the presence of a virus (indication):**

items: **Cytopathic effect (CPE)** — rounding of cells, formation of syncytia (multinucleated cells), appearance of inclusions, breakdown of the cell layer;
**Intracellular inclusions** — characteristic of certain viruses (**Babes–Negri** bodies in rabies, **Guarnieri** bodies in smallpox);
**Hemadsorption** — adhesion of erythrocytes to the surface of infected cells (influenza, parainfluenza);
**Hemagglutination (HA)** — fluid containing the virus causes erythrocytes to agglutinate;
**Plaque method** — counting virus colonies under an agar overlay (quantitative assessment).

blocks.text: **Identification** — determining the type of virus — is done with **specific immune sera** in serological reactions: the **hemagglutination inhibition test (HI)**, the **neutralization test (NT)**, the complement fixation test (CFT), ELISA, immunofluorescence, as well as PCR and sequencing.

parts.text: The basis of modern virological diagnosis is **PCR** (and real-time PCR): it is fast and sensitive, detects the virus without culturing it and quantitatively assesses the viral load. The classic virological method (isolation) has remained mainly for scientific purposes and for selecting vaccine strains.

blocks.text: **Bacteriophage (phage)** — a virus that infects bacteria. It was discovered in 1915–1917 by F. Twort and F. d’Hérelle.
**Structure** (in the example of T-even phages): an icosahedral **head** (DNA inside), a **tube (tail)** and a contractile sheath, a **baseplate** and **tail fibers** (for adsorption).

blocks.label: Figure 12.5
blocks.caption: The structure of the T4 coliphage: head, tube, baseplate and tail fibers. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **The life cycle of a phage runs in two ways:**

head: Feature
**Lytic cycle (virulent phage)**
**Lysogenic cycle (temperate phage)**
rows: Bacterial lysis, release of new phages
The phage DNA integrates into the chromosome (prophage)
Lives, passes the prophage to its progeny at division

blocks.text: **The stages of the phage cycle** are like those of the viral cycle: adsorption (through the tail fibers, onto a species-specific receptor) → injection of the nucleic acid into the cell → synthesis → assembly → lysis of the bacterium.
**Specificity of the phage:** polyvalent (for several genera), monovalent (for a single species), type-specific (for particular variants within a species) phages.

sections.title: Independent work: Uses of bacteriophages in practice

blocks.text: **1. Identification and epidemiological typing (phage typing).** A set of type-specific phages is applied to the isolated culture; from which phages produce lysis, the **phagovar** (phage type) is determined. This helps to distinguish strains within the same species and to find the source of infection (for example, in identifying the focus of a hospital staphylococcal infection).
**2. Phage diagnosis.** Isolating **the phage itself** from the material being examined also indirectly shows the presence of the pathogen (for example, detection of coliphages in water).

**3. Phage therapy.** Preparations of live virulent phages are used to treat infections (staphylococcal, streptococcal, dysentery, typhoid fever, Proteus, *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* phages, polyvalent pyobacteriophage). Advantages: narrow and precise action (does not disturb the normal microflora), and it may also act on antibiotic-resistant strains. Limitations: narrow spectrum (the phage must match the strain), development of phage resistance in bacteria, problems of standardization. The order of prescribing and using the preparation is determined by the physician.
**4. Phage prophylaxis.** Used on epidemic indications (for contacts in a focus).
**5. Genetic engineering and research.** Phages are a means of transferring genetic material (transduction), vectors, and also a classic model of molecular biology.

parts.text: The main difference between phage therapy and an antibiotic: an antibiotic is a **chemical substance with broad action**; a phage is a **live, highly selective** biological agent that lyses only the bacteria it matches.

skills.title: Practical skill: the general algorithm of a virological examination

items: **Collecting material** — according to the stage of the disease and the tropism of the virus: nasopharyngeal wash/swab for respiratory viruses, stool for enteroviruses, vesicle fluid for herpes, cerebrospinal fluid for neuroinfections, blood serum for serology.
**Transport** — on ice (2–8 °C), in a special transport medium, fast; many viruses are unstable in the external environment.
**Rapid diagnosis** — detecting **viral antigen** (ELISA, immunofluorescence, immunochromatography) or **nucleic acid** (PCR) in the material.
**Virological method** — inoculation into cell culture/chick embryo → indication (CPE, HA, hemadsorption) → identification with specific sera (HI, NT).
**Serological method** — a ≥4-fold rise in antibody titer in **paired sera**; IgM — recent infection, IgG — past infection or a sign of immunity.
**Interpreting the result** — together with clinical and epidemiological data.

parts.text: In virology, **the time of collecting the material** is decisive: virus shedding is often highest in the first days of the illness. In material taken late, even PCR may be negative, so it is supplemented with serology.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: After 48 hours, cells in a cell culture infected with the material rounded up and the cell layer began to break up; when erythrocytes were added, they stuck to the cell surface.
cases.ask: What phenomena were observed and what do they mean?
cases.answer: Cytopathic effect (CPE) and hemadsorption indicate that a virus is present in the material. To determine its type, HI or the neutralization test is set up with specific immune sera.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: In a nasopharyngeal swab taken on day 8 of a respiratory infection, PCR was negative, but the clinical picture fits a viral infection.
cases.ask: How should the result be interpreted and what is the next step?
cases.answer: Virus shedding is usually highest in the first days; in material taken late the result may be negative. The next step is serological examination with **paired sera** (a ≥4-fold rise in titer or detection of IgM).

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: *S. aureus* was isolated from several patients in a hospital ward. All the strains proved to belong to the same phagovar.
cases.ask: What does this conclusion mean epidemiologically?
cases.answer: The strains have most likely spread from a single source (a common source or a carrier). Phage typing is used precisely to establish such an epidemiological link; the measures are to find the source and to apply infection control.

topics.title: Immunity. The structure and functions of the immune system. Innate immunity: complement, phagocytes. Antigen-presenting cells

goals.text: To know the concept and types of immunity and the structure of the immune system;
to explain the factors of innate (nonspecific) immunity — barriers, phagocytosis, complement, interferons, NK cells;
to master the stages of phagocytosis and the pathways of complement activation;
to know the antigen-presenting cells and their role in linking innate and adaptive immunity;
Independent work: to have an understanding of the theories of immunity and of the major histocompatibility complex class I (HLA-A, -B, -C).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Innate immunity is the **first line of defense** — it limits the infection and buys time until the adaptive response forms; in addition, through antigen presentation it **triggers** the adaptive response.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Incomplete phagocytosis** is seen with *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, *Brucella*, gonococci and *Leishmania*. This explains the long persistence of the pathogen in the body, the chronic course and the relapses of the disease.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The stages of phagocytosis: **C–A–E–P–D**: **C**hemotaxis → **A**dhesion → **E**ndocytosis → **P**hagolysosome → **D**igestion.

blocks.text: **Immunity** is the body’s way of defending itself against genetically foreign substances (microorganisms, altered own cells, foreign proteins) and of maintaining the constancy of the internal environment.

head: Criterion
Type
Description
rows: Hereditary, present from birth; acts quickly, leaves no memory
Forms during life; slow, but specific and leaves **memory**
From mother to child (IgG, IgA via the placenta and milk)
When serum or immunoglobulin is administered
blocks.title: Table 13.1. Types of immunity

head: Feature
Innate
Adaptive
rows: General (recognizes structures characteristic of groups of microbes)
Present (the secondary response is rapid and strong)
Barriers, phagocytes, NK cells, complement, interferons
Pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) — through Toll-like receptors
blocks.title: Table 13.2. Comparison of innate and adaptive immunity

parts.text: Innate immunity is the **first line of defense** — it limits the infection and buys time until the adaptive response forms; in addition, through antigen presentation it **triggers** the adaptive response.

blocks.text: **Central (primary) organs** — lymphocytes mature here:

items: **Bone marrow** — the source of all blood cells; **B lymphocytes** mature here.
**Thymus** — **T lymphocytes** mature here; positive and negative selection take place here (cells directed against the body’s own tissue are eliminated).

blocks.text: **Peripheral (secondary) organs** — the encounter with antigen and the immune response take place here: **lymph nodes**, **spleen**, mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT; in the intestine — **GALT**, Peyer’s patches, tonsils, appendix), and free lymphocytes in the blood and lymph.
**Immunocompetent cells:** T lymphocytes, B lymphocytes, NK cells, macrophages, dendritic cells, neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils and mast cells.
4.1. Barriers and humoral factors

items: **Mechanical barriers:** intact skin, mucous membranes, movement of the ciliated epithelium, the cough and sneeze reflex, the flow of urine.
**Chemical factors:** fatty acids and sweat acids of the skin, gastric hydrochloric acid, vaginal lactic acid, bile acids.
**Biological barrier:** the normal microflora (colonization resistance — topic 10).

**Humoral factors:** **lysozyme** (breaks down peptidoglycan; abundant in tears, saliva, mucus), **complement**, **interferons**, **C-reactive protein** and other acute-phase proteins, properdin, beta-lysins, lactoferrin.

blocks.text: 4.2. Phagocytosis
**Phagocytosis** is the process by which a cell engulfs and digests particles; it was discovered by I.I. Mechnikov.
**Phagocytes:**

items: **Microphages** — neutrophils (abundant in the blood, arrive quickly, short-lived);
**Macrophages** — arise from monocytes; located in tissues (Kupffer cells in the liver, alveolar macrophages in the lung, osteoclasts in bone tissue, microglia in the brain).

blocks.text: **Stages of phagocytosis:**

items: **Chemotaxis** — the movement of a phagocyte toward the object along chemical signals (bacterial products, complement C5a, cytokines).
**Adhesion (attachment)** — sticking to the object; **opsonins** (IgG antibodies, complement C3b) sharply speed up this stage.
**Endocytosis (engulfment)** — enclosure with pseudopodia, formation of a **phagosome**.
**Formation of the phagolysosome** — fusion with a lysosome.

**Digestion (killing)** — oxygen-dependent mechanisms (the oxidative burst: superoxide, hydrogen peroxide, hypochlorite) and oxygen-independent mechanisms (lysozyme, defensins, lactoferrin, proteases).

blocks.text: **By outcome:**

items: **Complete phagocytosis** — the microbe is digested;
**Incomplete phagocytosis** — the microbe stays alive inside the phagocyte and even multiplies.

parts.text: **Incomplete phagocytosis** is seen with *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, *Brucella*, gonococci and *Leishmania*. This explains the long persistence of the pathogen in the body, the chronic course and the relapses of the disease.
The stages of phagocytosis: **C–A–E–P–D**: **C**hemotaxis → **A**dhesion → **E**ndocytosis → **P**hagolysosome → **D**igestion.

blocks.text: 4.3. The complement system
**Complement** is a system of more than 30 proteins in the blood serum that are activated in sequence (a cascade). Activation proceeds by **three pathways**:

head: Pathway
What starts it
Role in the immune response
rows: Binding of mannose-binding lectin to microbial carbohydrates
blocks.title: Table 13.3. Pathways of complement activation

blocks.text: All three pathways converge at the **cleavage of C3** and finally form the **membrane attack complex (MAC, C5b–C9)** — it opens a pore in the cell membrane and causes lysis.
**Main effects of complement:**

items: **Lysis** (through the MAC);
**Opsonization** (C3b — enhances phagocytosis);
**Chemotaxis and inflammation** (C3a, C5a — anaphylatoxins; release of histamine from mast cells, recruitment of leukocytes);
**Clearance of immune complexes**.

parts.text: **C3 — the central component**: all three pathways converge here. **C3b — opsonin**, **C3a and C5a — anaphylatoxin and chemoattractant**, **C5b–C9 — MAC (lysis)**.

blocks.text: 4.4. Interferons and NK cells

**Interferons (IFN)** are the main innate factor of antiviral defense; they are protein cytokines. Types: **IFN-α** (leukocyte) and **IFN-β** (fibroblast) — mainly antiviral; **IFN-γ** (immune) — mainly regulates immunity and activates macrophages.

**Mechanism of action:** interferon does not kill the virus directly; acting on **neighboring cells**, it switches on enzymes in them that stop the synthesis of viral nucleic acid and proteins — the cell enters a “resistant” state against the virus.

**NK (natural killer) cells** destroy virus-infected cells and tumor cells in an antigen-independent manner. They detect **a decrease in MHC class I molecules** on the surface of the target cell (“missing-self recognition”): many viruses and tumors try to hide MHC I, and NK cells kill exactly such cells. They release perforin and granzymes and trigger apoptosis.
**Antigen-presenting cells:** **dendritic cells** (the most effective, “professional”), **macrophages**, **B lymphocytes**.

**Function:** to engulf an antigen, break it into fragments (peptides) and show it to a T lymphocyte on the cell surface together with an **MHC (HLA in humans)** molecule. A T lymphocyte recognizes an antigen **only together with MHC** — this is called **MHC-restricted recognition**.

head: Feature
**MHC I (HLA-A, -B, -C)**
**MHC II (HLA-DR, -DQ, -DP)**
rows: Only in APCs (dendritic cells, macrophages, B lymphocytes)
Taken up from outside (bacterial, foreign protein)
The immune response is regulated, B cells receive help
blocks.title: Table 13.4. MHC class I and class II

parts.text: The **“8 × 1 = 8, 4 × 2 = 8”** rule: **CD8** — **MHC I**; **CD4** — **MHC II** (the product is always 8).

blocks.text: **The dendritic cell takes a central place in starting the immune response:** it engulfs the antigen in the tissue → migrates to the lymph node → there it shows the antigen to a “naive” T lymphocyte → the adaptive response begins. That is why APCs are the **bridge linking innate and adaptive immunity**.

sections.title: Independent work: Theories of immunity and class I HLA molecules

blocks.text: **Development of the theories:**

items: **Phagocytic (cellular) theory** — I.I. Mechnikov (1883): the basis of defense is phagocytes.
**Humoral theory** — P. Ehrlich: defense is due to antibodies in the blood; the “side-chain” theory was the first attempt to explain antibody formation.
**Instructive (template) theories** — assumed that the antigen acts as a “template” in antibody synthesis; later rejected.

**Clonal selection theory** — F. Burnet (1957): every lymphocyte has **in advance** a receptor matching one specific antigen; the antigen **selects** the matching clone and expands it. This is the foundation of modern immunology and explains both immunological memory and tolerance to self (clones that respond to the body’s own tissue are eliminated during maturation).

blocks.text: The theories of Mechnikov and Ehrlich do not exclude each other — it was later confirmed that they are the two arms of immunity (cellular and humoral); both scientists shared the Nobel Prize in 1908.

**Major histocompatibility complex class I (HLA-A, -B, -C).** These molecules are encoded on chromosome 6 and are extremely **polymorphic** (almost every person has a unique set). Structure: a heavy chain (α1, α2, α3 domains) + **β₂-microglobulin**; the peptide-binding groove lies between the α1 and α2 domains and holds a peptide of 8–10 amino acids.
**Functions:**

items: presenting peptides synthesized inside the cell (viral, tumor-specific) to **CD8⁺ cytotoxic T lymphocytes**;
serving as a “self-recognition” signal for NK cells (if MHC I decreases, the NK cell kills the cell);
determining tissue compatibility in **transplantation** — donor and recipient are matched by HLA;
some HLA alleles are linked to susceptibility to particular diseases (for example, HLA-B27 and certain rheumatologic diseases).

parts.text: A virus multiplies inside the cell, so the main defense against it is the **MHC I + CD8⁺ T lymphocyte** pathway. For this very reason, antibodies alone are not enough in intracellular infections.

skills.title: Practical skill: assessing phagocytic activity

blocks.text: **Procedure for setting up the phagocytic reaction:**

items: A suspension of leukocytes is prepared from the patient’s blood.
A certain amount of test culture (usually killed staphylococci or standard particles) is added to it.
The mixture is incubated at 37 °C for 30 minutes.
A smear is prepared and stained by the Romanowsky–Giemsa method.
100 neutrophils are viewed under the microscope and counted:

blocks.text: - **phagocytic activity (percentage)** — the percentage of cells that have engulfed microbes;
- **phagocytic number (index)** — the average number of microbes per phagocyte;
- **completion index** — the proportion of microbes digested (also assessed by repeat culture).

**NBT test (nitroblue tetrazolium test)** — assesses the oxygen-dependent killing ability of phagocytes: in an activated neutrophil the colorless dye is converted into blue formazan granules. The test is used to detect defects of the phagocytic system (for example, chronic granulomatous disease).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A child has recurrent purulent infections. When the NBT test was done, formazan granules did not form in the neutrophils.
cases.ask: Which stage is impaired?
cases.answer: The **digestion (killing)** stage of phagocytosis — the oxygen-dependent mechanism is not working. This picture is characteristic of a defect of the phagocytic system (a condition of the chronic granulomatous disease type); the engulfment stage may be preserved.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A patient was found to have repeated episodes of meningococcal infection. Examination found a deficiency of the terminal complement components (C5–C9).
cases.ask: Why do exactly these infections recur?
cases.answer: The terminal components form the **MAC**; the MAC is decisive in lysing *Neisseria* (meningococcus, gonococcus). Their deficiency creates susceptibility to exactly this group of infections.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A virus-infected cell reduced the MHC I molecules on its surface and in this way “hid” from CD8⁺ T lymphocytes.
cases.ask: Which other defense mechanism is triggered in the body?
cases.answer: **NK cells.** By the principle of “missing-self recognition,” they detect a cell with decreased MHC I and trigger apoptosis through perforin and granzymes.

topics.title: Antigens and antibodies. Serological (immunological) reactions. Diagnosticums and diagnostic sera

goals.text: To know the concept of antigen, its properties and the types of bacterial antigens;
to explain the structure, classes and functions of immunoglobulins;
to master the principle, components and purpose of setting up serological reactions;
to acquire the skill of setting up the main reactions (agglutination, precipitation, CFT, ELISA, immunoblot, immunofluorescence) and interpreting the result;
Independent work: to know monoclonal antibodies, how they are obtained and their use in practice.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **IgM — “Most recent”** (first, a new infection); **IgG — “Gestation”** (crosses the placenta, protects the newborn) and long-term immunity; **IgA — “At the surfaces”** (mucous membranes); **IgE — “Eczema/allergy”**.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Prozone phenomenon:** if there is too much antibody (the serum is only slightly diluted), the reaction may not be visible. That is why the serum is set up in **serial dilutions** and the result is assessed by titer.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Remember the result of CFT: **“No hemolysis — reaction present”** (positive); **“Hemolysis — no reaction”** (negative). This is where students make the most mistakes.

blocks.text: **Antigen (Ag)** — a genetically foreign substance that, on entering the body, can provoke an immune response (antibody formation and/or a cellular response) and can bind **specifically** with the products of that response.
**Main properties:**

items: **Antigenicity** — the ability to bind with the products of the immune response;
**Immunogenicity** — the ability to provoke an immune response (it is high if the molecular mass is large and the chemical structure is complex);
**Specificity** — determined by the **epitope (antigenic determinant)**, the small part of the antigen molecule that binds directly to the antibody.

blocks.text: **Types:**

items: **Complete antigens** — both immunogenic and antigenic (proteins);

**Haptens** — small molecules; they do not provoke an immune response by themselves but do so when joined to a carrier protein; they bind to antibody independently (many drugs can cause allergy as haptens).

head: Antigen
Location/nature
Property
Significance
rows: A type of K antigen (typhoid fever)
blocks.title: Table 14.1. The main antigens of bacteria

blocks.text: **Immunologically important concepts:** **superantigens** (activate a large proportion of T lymphocytes at once — toxic shock syndrome); **cross-reactive (shared) antigens** — similarity between microbial and human tissue antigens (group A streptococcus and heart tissue — important in the pathogenesis of rheumatic fever); **autoantigens** and **alloantigens** (blood groups, HLA).
**Antibody** — a protein (immunoglobulin, Ig) produced by B lymphocytes and plasma cells in response to an antigen, which binds specifically with the antigen.

**Structure:** two **heavy (H)** and two **light (L)** chains; the **Fab fragment** binds antigen (variable — V domains), the **Fc fragment** carries out the effector function (activating complement, binding to phagocytes, crossing the placenta). On cleavage with enzymes, papain gives 2 Fab + 1 Fc.

head: Class
Structure
Share in blood serum
Main properties
rows: The main serum antibody; **crosses the placenta**; opsonization, activates complement (classical pathway); a sign of the **secondary response**
Appears **first in the primary response**; the strongest activator of complement; does not cross the placenta; a sign of new infection
Protection of mucous membranes, saliva, tears, breast milk
Binds to mast cells; **immediate-type allergy**, defense against helminths
Receptor on the surface of B lymphocytes
blocks.title: Table 14.2. Classes of immunoglobulins

parts.text: **IgM — “Most recent”** (first, a new infection); **IgG — “Gestation”** (crosses the placenta, protects the newborn) and long-term immunity; **IgA — “At the surfaces”** (mucous membranes); **IgE — “Eczema/allergy”**.

blocks.text: **Dynamics of the immune response.** **Primary response:** latent period 3–5 days, first **IgM**, then IgG; the titer is low and falls quickly. **Secondary response (due to memory):** the latent period is short (1–2 days), a large amount of **IgG** forms at once, and the titer is high and persists for a long time. For this reason **revaccination** is done in vaccination.
**Serological reactions** are reactions based on the specific binding between antigen and antibody *in vitro*.
**They are set up for two purposes:**

items: **Detecting an unknown antigen with a known antibody** (identifying the pathogen) — for this a **diagnostic serum** is needed;
**Detecting unknown antibodies with a known antigen** (in the patient’s serum) — for this a **diagnosticum** is needed.

blocks.text: **Reagents:**

items: **Diagnostic serum** — serum containing known antibodies, obtained by immunizing animals with a known antigen (agglutinating, precipitating, luminescent, enzyme-conjugated and others).
**Diagnosticum** — a preparation of a known antigen (a suspension of killed microbes, an erythrocyte diagnosticum, an antigen extract).

blocks.text: **General conditions of the reaction:** the antigen and antibody must match, an electrolyte (physiological saline) must be present, the pH and temperature must be optimal (often 37 °C), and the ratio of the components must be correct.

parts.text: **Prozone phenomenon:** if there is too much antibody (the serum is only slightly diluted), the reaction may not be visible. That is why the serum is set up in **serial dilutions** and the result is assessed by titer.

blocks.text: 5.1. Agglutination reaction (AR)
**Principle:** a corpuscular (large, particulate) antigen — bacterial cells, erythrocytes — sticks together under the action of antibody and forms a visible granular precipitate.
**Variants:**

items: **On a glass slide (preliminary, rapid)** — mixing the isolated culture with diagnostic serum → granularity appears; for identification;
**Extended (in a tube)** — serially diluting the patient’s serum and adding a diagnosticum → the **titer** is determined (Widal reaction — in typhoid fever; Wright reaction — in brucellosis);
**Indirect (passive) hemagglutination (PHA)** — the antigen is “loaded” onto the surface of erythrocytes; high sensitivity;
**Coagglutination** — antibodies are attached to staphylococcal protein A;
**Latex agglutination** — antibodies are attached to latex particles (rapid tests).

blocks.label: Figure 14.1
blocks.caption: Agglutination reactions: the mechanism, the titration series in a tube and the preliminary reaction on a glass slide; positive and negative result. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: 5.2. Precipitation reaction (PR)

**Principle:** a **soluble (molecular)** antigen combines with antibody and forms visible turbidity or a precipitate. The result is seen best in the **equivalence zone**, where the ratio of antigen and antibody is optimal.

**Variants:** ring precipitation (a white ring at the boundary of two liquids in a tube — the Ascoli reaction), **double immunodiffusion (Ouchterlony)** in gel, radial immunodiffusion (Mancini — measuring the amount of immunoglobulin), immunoelectrophoresis, **flocculation** (measuring toxoid activity).

blocks.label: Figure 14.2
blocks.caption: The mechanism of the precipitation reaction: the zones of antibody excess and antigen excess, the equivalence zone and ring precipitation. Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

blocks.text: 5.3. Complement fixation test (CFT)
**It consists of two systems:**

items: **Test system** — patient serum (antibody) + known antigen + complement;
**Indicator (hemolytic) system** — sheep erythrocytes + hemolytic serum.

blocks.text: **Result:** if an antigen–antibody complex forms in the test system, the complement is **bound** there and does not reach the indicator system → **there is no hemolysis** → the reaction is **positive**. If no complex forms, the complement stays free and lyses the erythrocytes → **there is hemolysis** → the reaction is **negative**.

blocks.label: Figure 14.3
blocks.caption: Scheme of setting up the complement fixation test (with the serum of a sick and a healthy person) and the principle of the immunofluorescence reaction. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

parts.text: Remember the result of CFT: **“No hemolysis — reaction present”** (positive); **“Hemolysis — no reaction”** (negative). This is where students make the most mistakes.

blocks.text: 5.4. Reactions based on labeled antibodies

**Immunofluorescence reaction (IF, Coons method)** — the antibody is labeled with a fluorochrome (FITC); in a fluorescence microscope it glows bright green. In the **direct** method the labeled antibody is applied directly to the antigen; in the **indirect** method an ordinary antibody is added first, then a labeled antibody against it (more sensitive).

**Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)** — the antibody or antigen is labeled with an **enzyme**; when substrate is added a color appears, and the color intensity is measured in a photometer. Direct, indirect and “sandwich” variants exist. It is currently the most widespread serological method.

blocks.label: Figure 14.4
blocks.caption: The schematic mechanism of the enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA): a) direct, b) indirect method; the steps of antigen, patient serum, enzyme-conjugated antibody and substrate–chromogen. Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

blocks.text: **Radioimmunoassay (RIA)** — labeling with an isotope; very sensitive, but replaced by ELISA in practice because of the radiation hazard.

**Immunoblot (Western blot)** — antigens are separated by electrophoresis, transferred to a membrane and treated with the patient’s serum; as a result the **antibody against each antigen appears as a separate band**. That is why it is used as a **confirmatory (verification)** test (for example, in HIV diagnosis — topic 29).

blocks.label: Figure 14.5
blocks.caption: The scheme of performing the immunoblot (Western blot) reaction: electrophoresis of the antigens in gel, transfer to a membrane and detection of the antibodies. Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

blocks.text: **Neutralization test (NT)** — the antibody removes the biological activity of a toxin or virus; the result is assessed in a living system (animal, cell culture).

blocks.text: **Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs)** are completely identical antibodies obtained from a single clone of B lymphocytes and directed against **a single epitope**. An ordinary immune serum, by contrast, is **polyclonal** — the product of many clones, a mixture of antibodies against different epitopes.
**Production — hybridoma technology (Köhler and Milstein, 1975):**

items: A mouse is immunized with the required antigen.
**B lymphocytes** are taken from the spleen (they produce the required antibody but do not live long).
They are fused with **myeloma cells** (myeloma cells divide without limit but do not produce the required antibody).
In a special selective medium only the fused cells — **hybridomas** — survive.
The hybridomas are separated into individual clones, the clone that produces the required antibody is selected and multiplied without limit.

blocks.text: As a result a cell line that is **“immortal + produces the required antibody”** is obtained.
**Advantages:** absolute specificity, standardization (the same from batch to batch), and the possibility of obtaining unlimited amounts.
**Uses:**

items: **In diagnosis** — ELISA, immunofluorescence, immunochromatographic rapid tests, detecting CD markers by flow cytometry (topic 15), determining blood groups, measuring hormones and tumor markers;
**In treatment** — targeted therapy (directed at a chosen target): in oncology, autoimmune diseases and some infections; preventing rejection in transplantation;
**In research** — detecting, purifying and studying proteins.

blocks.text: **Types:** mouse, chimeric, humanized and fully human antibodies — progressively “humanized” to reduce the response to the foreign protein (indicated by the corresponding suffixes in their names).

parts.text: **Polyclonal** serum — many kinds of antibodies to many epitopes (the product of natural immunization). **Monoclonal** — one kind of antibody to one epitope (the product of a hybridoma). The accuracy of standard diagnostic test systems is ensured precisely by monoclonality.

skills.title: Practical skill: setting up the extended agglutination reaction

items: Physiological saline is poured into a row of tubes and the patient’s serum is serially **diluted two-fold** (1:50, 1:100, 1:200, 1:400, 1:800...).
The same volume of **diagnosticum** is added to each tube.
Control tubes are set up: a **serum control** (serum + physiological saline, without diagnosticum) and an **antigen control** (diagnosticum + physiological saline).
They are left in a thermostat at 37 °C for 2 hours, then at room temperature for 18–20 hours.
The result is assessed: clearing of the liquid with a granular sediment at the bottom is positive; depending on the amount of sediment it is graded from “++++” to “+”.
The **titer** is the highest dilution that gives a positive result. There must be no reaction in the control tubes.

parts.text: The result can be read **only if the controls are correct**. If there is spontaneous sediment in the antigen control (the diagnosticum is of poor quality), the whole reaction is considered unreliable.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: **IgM** against a known pathogen was detected in the patient’s serum, while IgG is at a low titer.
cases.ask: What does this result mean?
cases.answer: IgM is the class that appears first in the primary response; this is characteristic of a **new (acute) infection**. For confirmation, a rise in IgG titer is looked for in paired sera after 10–14 days.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: In an extended agglutination reaction, the result was negative in the first two tubes (the least diluted) and positive in the following ones.
cases.ask: What is this phenomenon called and what should be done?
cases.answer: **Prozone phenomenon** — because antibody is in excess, the reaction is not visible in the first tubes. The result is read by titer, from the diluted tubes; that is why the reaction is always set up with serial dilution.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A screening ELISA test was positive. The doctor did not make a final diagnosis right away and sent the patient for confirmatory testing.
cases.ask: Why, and which method is used?
cases.answer: Screening tests are tuned for high sensitivity, so a **false-positive** result is possible. For confirmation a method with high specificity — **immunoblot** (or a molecular method) — is used.
