topics.title: Adaptive immunity. T and B lymphocytes, their subpopulations. CD markers. Cytokines, interferons. Immunoprophylaxis

goals.text: To know the formation of adaptive immunity and the mechanisms of the cellular and humoral response;
to explain the subpopulations, CD markers and functions of T and B lymphocytes;
to master the laboratory assessment of lymphocytes (E-RFC, flow cytometry);
Independent work: to know the basics of cytokines and interferons, immunodeficiency states, immunoprophylaxis and immunotherapy.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Th1 — against intracellular pathogens (activates macrophages), Th2 — the antibody and allergy pathway.** These two directions inhibit each other; their balance determines the course of the infection.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Polysaccharide vaccines do not work well in young children — their T-independent response is not sufficiently developed. That is why **conjugate vaccines** were created: the polysaccharide is attached to a carrier protein, and the response becomes T-dependent, strong and with memory.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **The CD4⁺ cell count** is the main indicator for assessing the stage of disease and for starting treatment in HIV infection (topic 29). That is why flow cytometry is the main method of clinical immunology.

blocks.text: Adaptive immunity forms after an encounter with antigen, is **specific** and leaves **immunological memory**. It appears in two forms:

items: **Humoral response** — B lymphocytes → plasma cells → **antibodies**; effective against extracellular bacteria and toxins;
**Cellular response** — T lymphocytes; directed against **intracellular** pathogens (viruses, *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*), tumor cells and the transplant.

blocks.text: **Three stages of the immune response:** recognition and presentation of the antigen (APC) → activation, proliferation and differentiation of lymphocytes → the effector stage (antibody production or destruction of the target cell) and the formation of **memory cells**.

T lymphocytes arise in the bone marrow and mature in the **thymus**. They recognize antigen **only together with MHC** (through the T cell receptor — TCR). The common marker is **CD3** (the complex linked to the TCR).

Marker
Which MHC it works with
Main function
rows: Regulating the immune response, secreting cytokines, helping B cells
Destroying virus-infected and tumor cells (perforin, granzyme, Fas pathway)
Limiting the immune response, maintaining self-tolerance

blocks.title: Table 15.1. The main subpopulations of T lymphocytes

blocks.text: **Directions (polarization) of T helpers:**

items: **Th1** — secretes IFN-γ and IL-2; **activates macrophages**, strengthens the response against intracellular pathogens (tuberculosis, leishmaniasis);
**Th2** — IL-4, IL-5, IL-13; **helps B cells**, strengthens the IgE and eosinophil response (helminths, allergy);
**Th17** — IL-17; recruits neutrophils, protects the mucous membranes against extracellular bacteria and fungi;
**Tfh (follicular helpers)** — in the lymph node they help B cells in class switching of antibodies.

parts.text: **Th1 — against intracellular pathogens (activates macrophages), Th2 — the antibody and allergy pathway.** These two directions inhibit each other; their balance determines the course of the infection.

sections.title: B lymphocytes and the humoral response

blocks.text: In humans B lymphocytes mature in the **bone marrow**. Markers: **CD19, CD20, CD21**; on the surface there is **membrane-bound immunoglobulin (IgM and IgD)** — the B cell receptor.
**Stages of the humoral response:**

items: The receptor on the surface of the B cell recognizes the antigen directly and engulfs it;
It shows a piece of the antigen with **MHC II** to a T helper (Tfh);
With the help of the T helper (cytokines + CD40L), the B cell is activated and multiplies;
Some become **plasma cells** (the antibody “factory”), others remain as **memory B cells**;
In the germinal centers of the lymph node, **class switching** (IgM → IgG, IgA, IgE) and **affinity maturation** take place.

blocks.text: **T-dependent and T-independent antigens.** Protein antigens require the help of a T helper and give a full response (IgG, memory). Polysaccharide antigens (for example, the pneumococcal capsule) provoke a T-independent response: mainly IgM, with weak memory.

parts.text: Polysaccharide vaccines do not work well in young children — their T-independent response is not sufficiently developed. That is why **conjugate vaccines** were created: the polysaccharide is attached to a carrier protein, and the response becomes T-dependent, strong and with memory.

sections.title: CD markers and methods of assessing lymphocytes

blocks.text: **CD (Cluster of Differentiation)** — differentiation markers on the cell surface; detected with the help of monoclonal antibodies.

head: Marker
In which cell
Note
rows: The α chain of the IL-2 receptor
blocks.title: Table 15.2. The main CD markers

blocks.text: **Methods of assessment:**

items: **Flow cytometry** — the modern standard. The cells are stained with monoclonal antibodies labeled with different fluorochromes, passed one by one under a laser beam, and the set of markers is recorded for each cell. As a result the percentage and absolute number of the subpopulations are determined, including the **CD4/CD8 ratio** (normally about 1.5–2.5).

**E-RFC method (rosette formation reaction)** — the classical method: T lymphocytes spontaneously form “rosettes” with sheep erythrocytes; the cells that have formed rosettes are counted. For B lymphocytes, EAC rosettes (with complement and antibody) are used.

**Separation of lymphocytes** — from peripheral blood by the **density gradient** (Ficoll–Verografin) method: after centrifugation the lymphocytes collect in the interphase layer and the erythrocytes settle to the bottom.

blocks.label: Figure 15.1
blocks.caption: Separation of lymphocytes from peripheral blood by the density gradient (Ficoll–Verografin) method: centrifugation and the layer of lymphocytes in the interphase. Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

blocks.label: Figure 15.2
blocks.caption: Determining the number of T lymphocytes — the scheme of the E-RFC (rosette formation) method. Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

parts.text: **The CD4⁺ cell count** is the main indicator for assessing the stage of disease and for starting treatment in HIV infection (topic 29). That is why flow cytometry is the main method of clinical immunology.

blocks.text: **Cytokines** are protein–peptide molecules produced by immune and other cells that provide cell-to-cell communication. Properties: they act in very small amounts, work through receptors, are **pleiotropic** (one cytokine has many effects) and **redundant** (different cytokines have similar effects), and act mainly locally.

head: Group
Representatives
Main effect
rows: Cell-to-cell communication; IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α — inflammation and fever; IL-2 — T cell proliferation; IL-10 — anti-inflammatory
Antiviral (α, β), regulation of immunity and activation of macrophages (γ)
Recruiting leukocytes to the focus of inflammation
Stimulating the formation of blood cells
Repair, suppression of the immune response
blocks.title: Table 15.3. The main groups of cytokines

blocks.text: **Interferons:** IFN-α (leukocytes), IFN-β (fibroblasts) — **type I**, direct antiviral defense; IFN-γ — **type II**, produced by T and NK cells, activates macrophages and increases MHC expression. Production: natural (from donor leukocytes) and **recombinant** (by genetic engineering — the main method now). Use: certain chronic viral hepatitides, some oncological and neurological diseases — only on a physician’s prescription.

parts.text: **IFN-α/β — “antiviral,” IFN-γ — “immune regulator.”** IFN-γ is mainly linked to the Th1 pathway and strengthens the macrophage’s ability to kill intracellular microbes.

blocks.text: **Primary (congenital) immunodeficiency** — the result of a genetic defect; it usually appears in childhood with recurrent and unusual infections. Depending on the impaired link:

items: **B-system (humoral)** defect — recurrent purulent infections with encapsulated bacteria;
**T-system (cellular)** defect — viral, fungal and intracellular infections;
**combined** defects — the most severe course;
**phagocytosis** defects — recurrent abscesses (the NBT test in topic 13);
**complement** defects — susceptibility to *Neisseria* infections.

blocks.text: **Secondary (acquired) immunodeficiency** — much more common; causes: viral infections (the most important — HIV), protein-energy malnutrition, severe chronic diseases, tumors and chemotherapy, irradiation, long-term glucocorticoid and immunosuppressive treatment, extensive surgical interventions, old age, chronic stress.

**Laboratory assessment:** complete blood count and leukocyte differential, immunoglobulin class levels, lymphocyte subpopulations (flow cytometry), phagocytic activity and the NBT test, complement components, and genetic testing when necessary.
**Immunoprophylaxis** — preventing infections with the help of vaccines and immune preparations.

head: Type
Meaning
Examples
rows: A weakened but live pathogen; strong and long-lasting immunity
Measles, rubella, mumps, chickenpox, tuberculosis (BCG), oral poliomyelitis
A killed pathogen; safer, revaccination is needed
Pertussis (whole-cell), inactivated poliomyelitis, rabies, hepatitis A
Pneumococcal, meningococcal and influenza subunit vaccines
An antigen obtained by genetic engineering
*H. influenzae* type b and pneumococcal conjugate vaccines
blocks.title: Table 15.4. The main types of vaccines

blocks.text: **Immunotherapy and passive immunization:** sera and immunoglobulins provide **ready-made antibodies** — protection begins immediately but is short-lived (2–4 weeks). **Antitoxic sera** (tetanus, diphtheria, botulism) neutralize the toxin; that is why they are given as early as possible. When foreign (horse) serum is given, special rules are followed because of the risk of serum sickness and anaphylaxis.

head: Feature
Active (vaccine)
Passive (serum, Ig)
blocks.title: Table 15.5. Active and passive immunization

parts.text: Tetanus prophylaxis in a contaminated wound is determined according to the **vaccination history**: for a vaccinated person, usually an additional dose of toxoid; for an unvaccinated person or one with an unknown history, active and passive immunization are used together (the prescription is by the physician, according to the current protocol).

skills.title: Practical skill: a stepwise approach to assessing immune status

items: **History and clinical picture:** frequently recurring infections, unusual pathogens, severe course, poor response to antibiotics, family history.
**First-stage tests:** complete blood count (absolute numbers of lymphocytes and neutrophils), immunoglobulin classes (IgG, IgM, IgA), the NBT test or phagocytic indices.
**Second-stage tests:** lymphocyte subpopulations (CD3, CD4, CD8, CD19, CD16/56) and the **CD4/CD8 ratio**, complement components, the response of lymphocytes to mitogens.
**Special investigations:** HIV test, genetic analysis, antibody response to specific antigens (assessing the response to vaccination).
**Interpretation:** the results are compared with **age-appropriate norms** and assessed together with the clinical picture.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: In a patient, the CD4⁺ cell count on flow cytometry has fallen sharply and the CD4/CD8 ratio has dropped to 0.4. Infections caused by unusual pathogens have been found in the patient.
cases.ask: What condition does this picture suggest?
cases.answer: Profound deficiency of cellular immunity; selective loss of CD4⁺ cells is very characteristic of HIV infection. For confirmation, HIV-specific testing (screening ELISA + a confirmatory method, viral load) is done.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 2-year-old child has recurrent pneumococcal otitis and pneumonias. Immunoglobulin levels are low and the response to polysaccharide vaccine is weak.
cases.ask: Which link is impaired and which vaccine is preferable in this situation?
cases.answer: The **humoral (B-system)** link is impaired. Polysaccharide vaccines are ineffective at this age and in this condition; **conjugate** vaccines are preferable because they give a T-dependent response. The treatment plan is determined by the physician.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A patient not vaccinated against tetanus came with a deep wound contaminated with soil.
cases.ask: Which of active and passive immunization is needed, and why?
cases.answer: Both: **passive** (ready-made antibodies) gives immediate protection, and **active** (toxoid) builds long-term immunity. The exact scheme is determined by the physician according to the current protocol and the vaccination history.

topics.title: Causative agents of purulent inflammatory diseases: staphylococci, streptococci, *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*

goals.text: To know the morphological, cultural and biochemical properties of staphylococci, streptococci and *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*;
to explain their pathogenicity factors and the diseases they cause;
to master the collection of material in purulent infections, the algorithm of bacteriological diagnosis and the differential tests;
Independent work: to know the significance and laboratory diagnosis of opportunistic anaerobic cocci (*Peptococcus*, *Peptostreptococcus*, *Veillonella*).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **MRSA** (methicillin-resistant *S. aureus*) is an important problem in hospital and community settings. The resistance is linked to an altered penicillin-binding protein, so **all beta-lactams** are considered ineffective (topic 9). Treatment is chosen on the basis of the antibiogram.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Group A streptococcal antigens resemble antigens of heart, joint and kidney tissue (**cross-reactive antigens**). That is why **rheumatic fever** or **acute glomerulonephritis** may develop 2–4 weeks after tonsillitis. For this very reason, complete treatment of streptococcal tonsillitis is important.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Remember the complications of streptococcus: **“High ASO — had tonsillitis.”** The antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer shows a past group A streptococcal infection and helps in the diagnosis of rheumatic fever.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: *P. aeruginosa* is resistant to many disinfectants and persists in wet places (sinks, respiratory equipment, solutions). That is why infection control in hospitals is directed at the regimen related to exactly these wet environments and instruments.

blocks.text: **Morphology:** gram-positive cocci (0.5–1.5 µm); because division occurs in different planes, they form **grape-like clusters**; nonmotile, do not form spores, may have a microcapsule.

blocks.label: Figure 16.1
blocks.caption: Staphylococci: gram-positive cocci forming typical grape-like clusters (pure culture, Gram stain). Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **Cultural properties:** facultative anaerobe; grows on ordinary media, **resistant to a high concentration of NaCl (7.5–10%)** — this property was the basis for creating a selective medium (egg-yolk salt agar). Colonies are round, smooth, convex; *S. aureus* forms a **golden-yellow pigment**. On blood agar it often produces beta-hemolysis.
**The main species and how to distinguish them:**

head: Species
Coagulase
Pigment
Main significance
rows: Purulent infections, food poisoning, toxic shock, osteomyelitis, sepsis
Urinary tract infection in young women
blocks.title: Table 16.1. Clinically significant staphylococci

blocks.text: **Pathogenicity factors:**

items: **Enzymes:** **plasmacoagulase** (a fibrin envelope — protection from phagocytosis, the main marker of *S. aureus*), hyaluronidase, fibrinolysin, lecithinase, DNase, beta-lactamase;

**Toxins:** hemolysins (α, β, γ, δ), **leukocidin**, **exfoliative toxin** (scalded skin syndrome), **toxic shock syndrome toxin (TSST-1)** — a superantigen, **enterotoxins** (A–E; thermostable — food poisoning, topic 23);
**Surface structures:** **protein A** (binds to the Fc part of IgG and disrupts opsonization), teichoic acids, microcapsule.

blocks.text: **Diseases:** skin and soft tissue infections (furuncle, carbuncle, abscess, phlegmon, mastitis), pneumonia, osteomyelitis, endocarditis, meningitis, sepsis, food poisoning, toxic shock syndrome, hospital-acquired infections.

parts.text: **MRSA** (methicillin-resistant *S. aureus*) is an important problem in hospital and community settings. The resistance is linked to an altered penicillin-binding protein, so **all beta-lactams** are considered ineffective (topic 9). Treatment is chosen on the basis of the antibiogram.

blocks.text: **Morphology:** gram-positive cocci, dividing in one plane to form **chains**; nonmotile, nonspore-forming; some species are encapsulated.

blocks.label: Figure 16.2
blocks.caption: Streptococci: gram-positive cocci forming chains in pus. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **Cultural properties:** fastidious — requires medium with added blood or serum; small, transparent colonies; **catalase-negative** (the main difference from staphylococci).
**Classification:**

items: **By type of hemolysis:** beta-hemolytic (a completely clear zone), alpha-hemolytic (a green zone — the viridans group, pneumococcus), gamma (no hemolysis).
**Serological groups by Lancefield** (by the cell wall polysaccharide): A, B, C, D and others.

head: Species/group
Hemolysis
Differential test
Diseases
rows: Tonsillitis, scarlet fever, erysipelas, impetigo, phlegmon, sepsis; complications — **rheumatic fever, acute glomerulonephritis**
Grows in 6.5% NaCl, positive on bile-esculin medium
Urinary tract and abdominal cavity infections; multidrug resistance
blocks.title: Table 16.2. Clinically significant streptococci

blocks.text: **Pathogenicity factors of group A streptococcus:** **M protein** (the main virulence factor — antiphagocytic, type-specific), capsule (hyaluronic acid), **streptolysin O and S**, **erythrogenic (pyrogenic) toxin** (the rash in scarlet fever), streptokinase, hyaluronidase, DNase.

parts.text: Group A streptococcal antigens resemble antigens of heart, joint and kidney tissue (**cross-reactive antigens**). That is why **rheumatic fever** or **acute glomerulonephritis** may develop 2–4 weeks after tonsillitis. For this very reason, complete treatment of streptococcal tonsillitis is important.

Remember the complications of streptococcus: **“High ASO — had tonsillitis.”** The antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer shows a past group A streptococcal infection and helps in the diagnosis of rheumatic fever.

blocks.text: **Morphology:** gram-negative, straight or slightly curved rod; **monotrichous** (a single polar flagellum) — motile; nonspore-forming, with a slime layer.

blocks.label: Figure 16.3
blocks.caption: *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* — gram-negative motile rods. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **Cultural and biochemical properties:** **obligate aerobe**; grows on ordinary media, not demanding of nutrients; **oxidase-positive** (the main difference from Enterobacteriaceae); does not break down lactose. **Pyocyanin** (blue-green) and pyoverdine pigments stain the medium; it has a characteristic **hyacinth-like odor**.
**Pathogenicity factors:** exotoxin A (stops protein synthesis), elastase, proteases, phospholipase C, pyocyanin, LPS, **biofilm formation**.

**Clinical significance:** a typical **opportunistic and hospital-acquired** pathogen. It causes infection in burn patients, in patients on artificial ventilation, in patients with catheters and in the immunocompromised: suppuration of wounds (blue-green pus), pneumonia, urinary tract infection, otitis, eye infections, sepsis.

parts.text: *P. aeruginosa* is resistant to many disinfectants and persists in wet places (sinks, respiratory equipment, solutions). That is why infection control in hospitals is directed at the regimen related to exactly these wet environments and instruments.

blocks.text: **Material:** pus, wound discharge, sputum, blood (in sepsis), urine, cerebrospinal fluid, puncture fluid; in hospital surveillance — a nasal swab (staphylococcal carriage).
**Bacterioscopic method** — a Gram-stained smear: gram-positive clustered cocci (staphylococcus), chained cocci (streptococcus), gram-negative rods (*Pseudomonas*). It gives a preliminary direction.
**Bacteriological method (main):**

items: **Day 1:** the material is inoculated onto blood agar and a selective medium (egg-yolk salt agar for staphylococcus).
**Day 2:** the colonies are studied (hemolysis, pigment, odor), a smear is made, and a pure culture is collected.
**Day 3:** differential tests and antibiogram.
**Day 4:** final report.

head: Test
Result and interpretation
rows: A cloudy zone around the colony in *S. aureus*
Pneumococcus is sensitive ↔ viridans is resistant
blocks.title: Table 16.3. The main differential tests

blocks.text: **Serological method:** determining the ASO titer (assessing a past group A streptococcal infection and its complications).
**Additional:** phage typing (epidemiological investigation), detecting toxin genes by PCR, MALDI-TOF identification.

head: Representative
Gram
Normal location
Clinical significance
rows: Oral cavity infections, mixed anaerobic infections
blocks.title: Table 16.4. Brief characteristics of anaerobic cocci

blocks.text: **General features:** members of the normal microflora; against a background of injury, circulatory disturbance, surgery or reduced immunity they cause an **endogenous** infection. They usually occur as part of a **mixed (polymicrobial)** infection.
**Clinical signs:** a **foul smell** of the pus, gas in the tissue, necrosis, poor response to the usual antibiotics — grounds for suspecting a mixed anaerobic infection.
**Special features of laboratory diagnosis:**

items: **Collecting material** — not with a swab but as a **puncture sample or tissue**, taken with limited contact with air;
**Transport** — in a special anaerobic transport medium, fast;
**Culture** — under anaerobic conditions (anaerostat, gas packs), on enriched blood agar, for 48–72 hours;
**Identification** — Gram stain, oxygen tolerance, biochemical tests, gas-liquid chromatography (fatty acid spectrum), MALDI-TOF, PCR.

parts.text: The most frequent reason for “missing” an anaerobic infection is **incorrect collection and late delivery of the material**. In a sample transported under aerobic conditions the anaerobes die, and the result comes out falsely negative.

skills.title: Practical skill: collecting material from a purulent wound

items: Clean the skin around the wound with an antiseptic (the antiseptic must not get into the sample).
Remove the dried surface layer or crust — the material is taken from the **deep, active** part.
The preferred method is taking a **puncture sample with a syringe** (especially in a closed abscess and when anaerobes are suspected); a swab is a less informative option.
Label the sample: patient, site, time of collection, whether antibiotics have been taken.
Deliver it to the laboratory in a transport medium as fast as possible (within 1–2 hours); a special medium is essential for anaerobic examination.
In the laboratory: Gram smear + blood agar (aerobic) + anaerobic culture + selective medium.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A pus smear from a furuncle showed gram-positive clustered cocci. The culture gave golden-yellow colonies on blood agar, with beta-hemolysis; it was catalase-positive and coagulase-positive.
cases.ask: Which is the pathogen, and which tests were decisive?
cases.answer: *Staphylococcus aureus*. Catalase positivity distinguishes a staphylococcus from a streptococcus, and coagulase positivity distinguishes *S. aureus* from other staphylococci.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: An 8-year-old child developed joint pain and a heart murmur 3 weeks after tonsillitis. The ASO titer is high.
cases.ask: What is this condition linked to?
cases.answer: A complication after group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal infection — acute rheumatic fever. The cause is the similarity between streptococcal antigens and human tissue antigens (cross-reactive antigens). ASO confirms a past streptococcal infection.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A burn patient in intensive care developed blue-green pus and a characteristic smell in the wound. The culture grew an oxidase-positive, lactose-negative gram-negative rod, and the medium turned blue-green.
cases.ask: Which is the pathogen and what measures are important?
cases.answer: *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*. Measures — treatment according to the antibiogram, local treatment of the wound, control of wet equipment and solutions, and strict observance of infection control rules.

topics.title: Wound infections: causative agents of tetanus and gas gangrene. Non-clostridial anaerobic infections

goals.text: To know the morphological, cultural and toxigenic properties of the causative agents of tetanus and gas gangrene;
to explain the main links in their pathogenesis and their clinical expression;
to master the algorithm of laboratory diagnosis in anaerobic wound infections and the principles of specific prophylaxis and treatment;
Independent work: to know the non-clostridial anaerobic pathogens (*Bacteroides*, *Prevotella*, *Fusobacterium*) and their diagnosis.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: In tetanus consciousness **is not impaired** — the patient feels everything. This is because the toxin acts selectively on inhibitory neurons.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: In tetanus **no immunity develops**: the amount of toxin that causes disease is too small for an immune response. That is why **vaccination** is done even after recovery from the disease.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The triad of gas gangrene: **gas** (crepitus) + **necrosis** + **severe intoxication**. In tetanus, by contrast, **convulsions**, with consciousness intact.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In anaerobic wound infections **the time factor** is decisive: the earlier the surgical treatment is done, the better the outcome. Treatment cannot be delayed to wait for the laboratory answer.

blocks.text: **Clostridia** (*Clostridium*) are gram-positive, **spore-forming**, **obligate anaerobic** rods. The position of the spore and the shape of the cell are important signs in preliminary identification (topic 3). The natural habitat is soil and the intestines of humans and animals.

blocks.label: Figure 17.1
blocks.caption: Causative agents of anaerobic wound diseases: a) pure culture of *Cl. perfringens* (Gram stain); b) its growth in a special medium; c) the classic clinical picture of tetanus. Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

sections.title: The causative agent of tetanus — *Clostridium tetani*

blocks.text: **Morphology:** gram-positive, thin, long rod; **peritrichous** (motile); forms a **round, terminally located spore** — the cell takes the shape of a **“drumstick”** or a “matchstick.”

blocks.label: Figure 17.2
blocks.caption: The causative agent of tetanus: gram-positive rods with terminal spores — the “drumstick” appearance. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **Cultural properties:** obligate anaerobe; in Kitt–Tarozzi medium it grows, making the medium turbid and giving a characteristic smell; on blood agar it gives thin, “creeping” growth and hemolysis.
**Pathogenicity factors — two exotoxins:**

items: **Tetanospasmin (neurotoxin)** — the main toxin; it reaches the central nervous system along the nerve fibers and through the blood, and **stops the release of inhibitory mediators (glycine and GABA)**. As a result the inhibition reaching the muscles is lost and a constant **tonic contraction (spasm)** develops;
**Tetanolysin** — lyses erythrocytes and contributes to local tissue damage.

blocks.text: **The main condition of pathogenesis:** the pathogen stays **local** in the wound and does not spread into the blood — the clinical picture is determined only by the **toxin**. That is why tetanus is a disease of **toxinemia**.

**Clinical picture:** contraction of the masseter muscles (**trismus**), drawing of the facial muscles (“risus sardonicus”), difficulty swallowing, then generalized tonic convulsions and arching of the trunk (**opisthotonus**); consciousness is preserved.

parts.text: In tetanus consciousness **is not impaired** — the patient feels everything. This is because the toxin acts selectively on inhibitory neurons.
In tetanus **no immunity develops**: the amount of toxin that causes disease is too small for an immune response. That is why **vaccination** is done even after recovery from the disease.

blocks.text: **The main pathogen — *Clostridium perfringens***; in addition *C. novyi*, *C. septicum* and *C. histolyticum* take part. It often occurs as a **mixed (several species)** infection.

***C. perfringens* features:** large gram-positive rod, **nonmotile** (rare among clostridia), **encapsulated**; in the body it often does not form spores. On blood agar it gives **double-zone hemolysis**, and in milk medium **“stormy fermentation”** (violent gas formation).

**Pathogenicity factors:** numerous toxins and enzymes — **alpha-toxin (lecithinase)** (damages the membrane, the main factor), collagenase, hyaluronidase, proteases, DNase, neuraminidase; **enterotoxin** (in some strains — food poisoning).

**Pathogenesis:** when an oxygen-free environment forms in the tissue (a crushed wound with impaired circulation), clostridia multiply; enzymes dissolve tissue, **gas** forms from the fermentation of carbohydrates (crepitus under the skin), necrosis spreads, and severe intoxication develops.

parts.text: The triad of gas gangrene: **gas** (crepitus) + **necrosis** + **severe intoxication**. In tetanus, by contrast, **convulsions**, with consciousness intact.

blocks.text: **In tetanus the diagnosis is made mainly clinically** — waiting for the laboratory result delays treatment. Laboratory examination has an auxiliary role: wound discharge, necrotic tissue and operative material are examined; detection is possible by bacterioscopy, anaerobic culture and the **toxin neutralization test**.
**Laboratory diagnosis in gas gangrene:**

items: **Material:** a piece of tissue taken from the wound, discharge from the edge of the necrosis, puncture fluid, blood (when generalized).
**Bacterioscopy** — Gram stain: large gram-positive rods, capsule; gives a rapid direction.
**Anaerobic culture** — Kitt–Tarozzi medium, Wilson–Blair medium (black colonies), blood agar; in an anaerostat for 24–48 hours.
**Identification** — morphology, lecithinase activity (a zone on egg-yolk agar), the reaction in milk medium, biochemical tests, determining the toxin type with the neutralization test.
**Modern methods** — detecting toxin genes by PCR, MALDI-TOF.

sections.title: Principles of specific prophylaxis and treatment

blocks.text: **Prevention of tetanus:**

items: **Planned (active)** — **tetanus toxoid** (as part of combination vaccines), according to the national immunization schedule, later with booster vaccinations;

**Emergency (when a wound is received)** — depending on the vaccination history, toxoid and/or ready-made antibodies (passive immunization) are given; the exact scheme is determined by a **physician** on the basis of the current protocol;
**Primary surgical debridement of the wound** — removal of necrotic tissue and foreign bodies is the main part of prophylaxis.

blocks.text: **In gas gangrene:** the main measure is **surgery** (wide surgical debridement, necrectomy); antibacterial therapy and intensive care; oxygen-based methods; antitoxic serum is used in some protocols. All prescriptions are made by the physician.

parts.text: In anaerobic wound infections **the time factor** is decisive: the earlier the surgical treatment is done, the better the outcome. Treatment cannot be delayed to wait for the laboratory answer.

blocks.text: Non-spore-forming (non-clostridial) anaerobes are members of the normal microflora and a frequent cause of endogenous infections.

blocks.label: Figure 17.3
blocks.caption: Morphotinctorial properties of the causative agents of non-spore-forming anaerobic purulent-inflammatory processes: a) *Bacteroides fragilis*; b) *Peptococcus niger*; c) *Peptostreptococcus*; d) *Veillonella parvula*. Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

blocks.text: **General features of pathogenesis:** endogenous origin; a fall in the oxygen level in the tissue (ischemia, necrosis, foreign body, surgery) is the decisive condition; it often occurs **together with aerobes (synergism)**.
**Signs that raise suspicion:** a foul smell of the pus, gas formation, necrosis, no growth on ordinary culture even though the smear shows many microbes, poor response to commonly used antibiotics.

**Diagnosis:** properly collected material (puncture sample/tissue) + anaerobic transport + anaerobic culture; in identification — Gram stain, relation to oxygen, biochemical tests, gas-liquid chromatography, MALDI-TOF, PCR.

parts.text: **Vincent’s angina** (necrotizing ulcerative tonsillitis) — the combined action of oral anaerobes (fusobacteria) and spirochetes; the diagnosis is made by seeing both morphotypes together in a smear.

skills.title: Practical skill: collecting and culturing material for an anaerobic infection

items: The skin around the wound is cleaned with an antiseptic; wait until the antiseptic dries.
The material is taken as a **puncture sample with a syringe** or as a **piece of tissue** from the edge of the necrosis; the syringe must be free of air.
The sample is placed in **anaerobic transport medium**; it is not cooled and is delivered as fast as possible.

In the laboratory the following are inoculated at the same time: anaerobic blood agar, Kitt–Tarozzi medium, Wilson–Blair medium and an **aerobic control** plate (to distinguish whether the culture is aerobic or anaerobic).
In an anaerostat at 37 °C for 48–72 hours; the aerobic plate — 24 hours.
Smears (Gram) and differential tests are made from the colonies that grew; a culture that did not grow on the aerobic plate but grew anaerobically is judged to be an **obligate anaerobe**.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A patient who received a deep puncture wound to the foot during field work developed, after 8 days, difficulty opening the mouth, drawing of the facial muscles, and then generalized convulsions. Consciousness is intact.
cases.ask: What is the probable diagnosis and how is it made?
cases.answer: Tetanus. The diagnosis is **clinical** — typical trismus, risus sardonicus, convulsions and preserved consciousness. Without waiting for laboratory confirmation, urgent measures are taken in the manner prescribed by the physician; the wound is debrided surgically.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A patient with a crush wound developed, on day 2, edema around the wound, crepitus under the skin, a foul smell and rapidly spreading necrosis. The smear shows large gram-positive rods.
cases.ask: What should be considered and what is the first measure?
cases.answer: Gas gangrene (*C. perfringens* and others). The first and decisive measure is **urgent wide surgical debridement**; laboratory examination is carried out in parallel.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: An abscess developed after abdominal surgery. There was no growth on the usual aerobic culture, but the pus smelled foul and the smear showed many gram-negative rods.
cases.ask: Why was the culture negative and how is it corrected?
cases.answer: The pathogen is an obligate anaerobe (probably *Bacteroides fragilis*). The material should have been collected in anaerobic transport medium and cultured under anaerobic conditions for 48–72 hours. The repeat examination is done in this way.

Foul smell, gas, necrosis, no growth on aerobic culture
Puncture sample/tissue + anaerobic transport + anaerobic culture

topics.title: Airborne infections: diphtheria, pertussis, meningococci. Pneumococcus and *Haemophilus influenzae*

goals.text: To know the biological properties of the causative agents of diphtheria, pertussis and meningococcal infection;
to explain their pathogenicity factors and the pathogenesis of the diseases they cause;
to master the algorithm of laboratory diagnosis of each infection (material, medium, identification, determining toxigenicity);
Independent work: to know the description, diseases and diagnosis of pneumococcus and *Haemophilus influenzae*.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The main danger of diphtheria is **asphyxia** (the laryngeal membrane blocks the airway — “true croup”) and the late complications: **myocarditis**, polyneuritis, nephrosis. That is why antitoxic serum is given on clinical suspicion, without waiting for the laboratory answer.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: In the diagnosis of diphtheria, **determining toxigenicity is essential**: nontoxigenic corynebacteria can occur in the throat as carriage and do not cause disease.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In pertussis the effectiveness of the bacteriological method falls sharply depending on the stage of the disease: the best result is obtained **in the catarrhal stage and at the beginning of the spasmodic stage**; later only PCR and serology give information.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Distinguish the Neisseria by carbohydrate: **MeninGoMaltose** — meningococcus: **G**lucose **+ M**altose; gonococcus — only **G**lucose.

sections.title: The causative agent of diphtheria — *Corynebacterium diphtheriae*

blocks.text: **Morphology:** gram-positive, straight or slightly curved rod; the ends are thickened owing to **volutin granules** (resembling a matchstick); the cells lie at an angle to each other, forming the shape of **the Latin letters V, X, Y** (**pleomorphism and pleomorphic arrangement**). Nonmotile, nonspore-forming, noncapsulated.

blocks.label: Figure 18.1
blocks.caption: The diphtheria bacillus stained by the Neisser method: dark volutin granules at the ends of the cells and angular arrangement. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **Staining:** Gram (positive), **Neisser** (the cell is yellow-brown, the volutin granules dark blue-black), **Löffler’s blue**.

**Cultural properties:** facultative anaerobe; fastidious — requires **serum medium** (Löffler’s coagulated serum) and **tellurite-containing medium** (selective; the tellurite is reduced, making the colony **black/gray**).
**Biovars:** *gravis* (large, rough, “resembling a daisy”), *mitis* (small, smooth, black, shiny), *intermedius*.

blocks.label: Figure 18.2
blocks.caption: Colonies of the gravis (left) and mitis (right) biovars of *C. diphtheriae*. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **Pathogenicity factor — diphtheria exotoxin.** The toxin is encoded by **prophage genes**: only **lysogenic (toxigenic)** strains cause disease (phage conversion — topic 11). The toxin’s mechanism of action is blocking **elongation factor EF-2** in the cell by ADP-ribosylation → **stopping of protein synthesis** → cell necrosis.

**Pathogenesis:** the pathogen stays **local** at the portal of entry (throat, nose, rarely the eye, skin, wound); the toxin is absorbed into the blood and damages **the heart muscle, nervous system and kidneys**. The local change is fibrinous inflammation, with formation of a **dense gray-white membrane**; when the membrane is removed, the mucosa bleeds.

parts.text: The main danger of diphtheria is **asphyxia** (the laryngeal membrane blocks the airway — “true croup”) and the late complications: **myocarditis**, polyneuritis, nephrosis. That is why antitoxic serum is given on clinical suspicion, without waiting for the laboratory answer.

blocks.text: **Laboratory diagnosis:**

items: **Material:** a swab from the throat and nose taken **at the edge of the membrane**; before antibiotics and throat rinses are used, on an empty stomach.
**Bacterioscopy** — Neisser method: rods with volutin granules arranged at angles (**presumptive result**).

**Bacteriological (main):** inoculation onto tellurite-containing and serum media → black colonies → pure culture → biochemical identification (cystinase-positive — **Pizu test**; urease-negative — differs from *C. ulcerans*).

**Determining toxigenicity (the decisive step):** **precipitation in gel (Elek method)** — precipitation lines between a paper strip impregnated with antitoxin and the culture; also detecting the **tox gene** by PCR, and the biological test.
**Serological:** assessing the level of antitoxic immunity (PHA).

blocks.label: Figure 18.3
blocks.caption: Scheme of the bacteriological examination of the diphtheria causative agent: collecting material, inoculation onto tellurite and serum media, identification, determining toxigenicity, susceptibility to antibiotics. Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

parts.text: In the diagnosis of diphtheria, **determining toxigenicity is essential**: nontoxigenic corynebacteria can occur in the throat as carriage and do not cause disease.

blocks.text: **Prophylaxis:** planned vaccination with **toxoid** (as part of combination vaccines, according to the national schedule). In treatment, **antitoxic serum** and antibiotics are used (as prescribed by a physician).

sections.title: The causative agent of pertussis (whooping cough) — *Bordetella pertussis*

blocks.text: **Morphology:** very small, ovoid gram-negative rod (coccobacillus); nonmotile, encapsulated.

**Cultural properties:** **obligate aerobe**, extremely fastidious. The classic medium is **Bordet–Gengou** (potato-glycerin blood agar) and **charcoal-casein agar**; growth is slow (3–5 days), the colonies are small and shiny — resembling a **“mercury droplet”** or a pearl.

**Pathogenicity factors:** **pertussis toxin** (disrupts the adenylate cyclase system), filamentous hemagglutinin and pertactin (adhesion), **tracheal cytotoxin** (damages the ciliated epithelium), adenylate cyclase–hemolysin, LPS.

**Pathogenesis:** the pathogen **adheres to the respiratory epithelium** and does not enter the blood; the movement of the cilia is disrupted, mucus is not cleared, and toxins constantly stimulate the cough center. As a result, **spasmodic (paroxysmal) coughing fits** — a series of cough bursts and a deep whooping inspiration (reprises), often ending in vomiting.
**Stages of the disease:** catarrhal (resembling an acute respiratory viral infection — **the most contagious stage**), spasmodic (typical fits), recovery.
**Laboratory diagnosis:**

items: **Material:** a swab taken from the nasopharynx **from the posterior wall** (special swab), the **“cough plate”** method (an open dish is held in front of the patient’s mouth while he coughs).
**Bacteriological** — immediate inoculation onto special medium; the pathogen is very unstable in the external environment, so **inoculation is done at the patient’s bedside**.
**PCR** — currently the most sensitive and practical method, especially in the catarrhal stage.
**Serological** — detecting antibodies by ELISA; significant in the late stage.

blocks.label: Figure 18.4
blocks.caption: Scheme of the microbiological examination of the pertussis causative agent: collecting material, inoculation onto special media, identification and serological examination. Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

parts.text: In pertussis the effectiveness of the bacteriological method falls sharply depending on the stage of the disease: the best result is obtained **in the catarrhal stage and at the beginning of the spasmodic stage**; later only PCR and serology give information.

blocks.text: **Prophylaxis:** vaccine (whole-cell or acellular) — within the complex immunization schedule.

**Morphology:** gram-negative **diplococcus** with flattened facing sides — resembling a **“coffee bean”** or a kidney bean; in cerebrospinal fluid and blood smears it is often located **inside leukocytes** (intracellularly). Encapsulated, nonmotile.

**Cultural properties:** fastidious aerobe; requires **serum agar** and chocolate agar; grows well in an atmosphere with **5–10% CO₂**; **oxidase-positive**, breaks down glucose and maltose (differs from the gonococcus, which breaks down only glucose).

**Pathogenicity factors:** the **capsule** (antiphagocytic; determines the serological groups — A, B, C, W, Y and others), pili (adhesion), **LPS (endotoxin)** — the main cause of severe shock, IgA protease.

**Clinical forms:** inflammation of the nasopharynx (nasopharyngitis) and **healthy carriage** (the most widespread form), **generalized forms** — meningococcemia (heterogeneous rash, shock) and **purulent meningitis**.
**Laboratory diagnosis:**

items: **Material:** cerebrospinal fluid (lumbar puncture), blood, nasopharyngeal swab, scraping from a rash element.
**Transporting the material** — **warm**, without cooling, immediately: the meningococcus is extremely sensitive to low temperature and drying.
**Bacterioscopy** — Gram smear from the CSF sediment: intracellular gram-negative diplococci in leukocytes → a rapid presumptive answer.
**Bacteriological** — serum/chocolate agar, CO₂ conditions; identification — oxidase, carbohydrates (glucose + maltose), serological grouping.
**Rapid methods** — detecting the capsular antigen in CSF by **latex agglutination**, and **PCR**.

parts.text: Distinguish the Neisseria by carbohydrate: **MeninGoMaltose** — meningococcus: **G**lucose **+ M**altose; gonococcus — only **G**lucose.

In meningococcal infection, collecting and culturing the CSF must not be delayed; at the same time, in severe cases antibacterial treatment is started without waiting for the laboratory answer. After antibiotics are started the culture may be negative — in which case **PCR and antigen tests** are valuable.

blocks.text: **Prophylaxis:** conjugate and polysaccharide vaccines (according to serological groups), preventive measures for contacts in a focus — as prescribed by a physician.
5.1. *Streptococcus pneumoniae* (pneumococcus)
**Morphology:** gram-positive **lancet-shaped diplococcus** with the ends pointing in opposite directions; **encapsulated** (clearly visible in pathological material).

blocks.label: Figure 18.5
blocks.caption: Pneumococci: lancet-shaped gram-positive diplococci. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **Cultural and differential properties:** **alpha-hemolysis** on blood agar (green zone); **sensitive to optochin**, **soluble in bile acids** (this distinguishes it from the viridans streptococci); the **“capsular swelling” reaction** (Quellung; with a special serum) is used to detect the capsule.
**Pathogenicity factor:** the main one is the **polysaccharide capsule** (more than 90 serotypes); pneumolysin, IgA protease, teichoic acids.
**Diseases:** acute pneumonia (classic **lobar pneumonia**), otitis media, sinusitis, meningitis, sepsis.

blocks.label: Figure 18.6
blocks.caption: Scheme of the microbiological examination of diseases caused by pneumococcus: material, bacterioscopy, culture, capsule reaction, sensitivity to optochin and bile acid. Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

blocks.text: **Diagnosis:** sputum, cerebrospinal fluid, blood → bacterioscopy (encapsulated diplococci) → blood agar → optochin and bile tests → serotyping; antigen tests and PCR in cerebrospinal fluid.
**Prophylaxis:** polysaccharide and **conjugate** vaccines (for the reason explained in topic 15, the conjugate form is preferable in children).
5.2. *Haemophilus influenzae*
**Morphology:** very small gram-negative coccobacillus, pleomorphic; type b is encapsulated.

**Cultural property:** requires **factor X (hemin)** and **factor V (NAD)** — therefore it does not grow on ordinary blood agar but grows on **chocolate agar** (topic 5). When it grows next to *S. aureus*, the **“satellite” phenomenon** is seen — the staphylococcus lyses erythrocytes and releases factor V.
**Diseases:** type b (Hib) — meningitis, epiglottitis, pneumonia and sepsis in children; nonencapsulated strains — otitis, sinusitis, exacerbations of bronchitis.
**Diagnosis:** cerebrospinal fluid, blood, sputum → chocolate agar + CO₂ → determining the requirement for factors X and V (disk method) → serotyping; PCR and antigen tests.
**Prophylaxis:** the **Hib conjugate vaccine** has sharply reduced the frequency of Hib meningitis in children.

blocks.label: Figure 18.7
blocks.caption: Legionellae — gram-negative rods transmitted by the airborne route (mainly through water aerosol). Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

skills.title: Practical skill: taking a throat and nose swab

items: The patient is examined on an empty stomach, before throat rinses and antibiotics.
The tongue is pressed with a spatula; with a light, the **membrane or the border of the inflamed area** is identified.
With a sterile swab a sample is taken **from the edge of the membrane** (the border between healthy and altered tissue); the swab must not touch the tongue, lips or teeth.
Material is taken from the nose with a separate swab.
The swabs are placed in transport medium; when diphtheria is suspected, inoculation is done **as soon as possible** (within 2–3 hours), in pertussis — **at the patient’s bedside**.
The referral states the clinical diagnosis, vaccination history and whether antibiotics were taken.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: An unvaccinated 6-year-old child has a dense gray-white membrane in the throat that bleeds when removed; the neck is swollen and the condition is severe.
cases.ask: What are the probable diagnosis, the material and the decisive laboratory step?
cases.answer: Diphtheria. The material is a throat and nose swab from the border of the membrane. The decisive step is determining the **toxigenicity** of the culture (the Elek method, or the tox gene by PCR). Antitoxic serum is given by a physician on clinical suspicion, without waiting for the laboratory answer.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 3-month-old infant has had a cough for 2 weeks; in the last few days paroxysmal coughing, a whooping inspiration and vomiting have appeared. The bacteriological culture is negative.
cases.ask: Why might the culture be negative, and which method is preferable?
cases.answer: In pertussis, the chance of isolating the pathogen falls sharply in the spasmodic stage; in addition, *B. pertussis* is unstable in the external environment. The preferable method is **PCR**, and in the late stage, serology.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A Gram smear of the cerebrospinal fluid sediment showed gram-negative diplococci inside leukocytes.
cases.ask: What is the preliminary conclusion and the next step?
cases.answer: Suspected meningococcal purulent meningitis. The next step is inoculation onto serum/chocolate agar under CO₂ conditions, oxidase and carbohydrate tests (glucose + maltose), and serological grouping; in parallel, latex agglutination and PCR. Treatment is not delayed.

summary.text: **Ziehl–Neelsen result:** the acid-fast rods are **red (carbol fuchsin)**; the background and other cells are **blue (methylene blue)**.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: In tuberculosis there is **no exotoxin**. The picture of the disease is determined mainly by the **delayed-type (type IV) hypersensitivity immune response** and the formation of granulomas. That is why tuberculosis runs as an “immunological disease”: tissue damage is largely the result of the body’s own response.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: A positive Mantoux test does not mean **“tuberculosis disease”**: it shows that the body has met mycobacterial antigens. The diagnosis is made from a combination of clinical findings, X-ray and microbiological results.

blocks.text: **Mycobacteria** (*Mycobacterium*) are slender, slightly curved rods; nonmotile, nonspore-forming, noncapsulated. Their main distinguishing feature is the special composition of the cell wall: it contains very large amounts of **mycolic acids**, waxes and lipids (40–60% of the wall is lipid).
**Consequences:**

items: **Acid-fastness (acid resistance)** — after staining they are not decolorized by acid and alcohol; for this reason the Gram method is unsuitable and the **Ziehl–Neelsen** method is used;
resistance to environmental factors, to many disinfectants and to drying;
**slow growth** (generation time 14–24 hours) — in culture the result is obtained in **3–8 weeks**;
the ability to survive inside the phagocyte (**incomplete phagocytosis**).

parts.text: **Ziehl–Neelsen result:** the acid-fast rods are **red (carbol fuchsin)**; the background and other cells are **blue (methylene blue)**.

sections.title: The causative agent of tuberculosis — *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*

blocks.text: **Historical note:** discovered in 1882 by **Robert Koch** (hence it is also called “Koch’s bacillus”).

**Morphology:** a slender, straight or slightly curved rod; in smears it lies singly, in pairs or in groups, sometimes **branching**. Under unfavorable conditions (antibacterial treatment, immune pressure) it can change into **L-forms**, filterable and granular forms — which matters in relapse of the disease.

blocks.label: Figure 19.1
blocks.caption: *M. tuberculosis* in a sputum smear: red rods stained by the Ziehl–Neelsen method on a blue background. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **Cultural properties:** **obligate aerobe**; grown on **egg-based Löwenstein–Jensen** medium with added glycerin, or on Finn-2 medium. Growth takes **3–8 weeks**; the colonies are dry, rough, **“cauliflower”** or “bread-crumb” in appearance, cream-colored (**R-form — a sign of virulence**). In liquid medium, owing to **cord factor**, it grows in “rope”-like (ribbon-like) strands.
**Pathogenicity factors:**

items: **Cord factor** (trehalose-6,6-dimycolate) — the main marker of virulence; it stops phagosome–lysosome fusion and damages macrophages;
**Sulfatides** — block the formation of the phagolysosome;
**Mycolic acids and lipids** — resistance and granuloma formation;
**Tuberculin (a protein antigen)** — causes the immune-allergic response.

parts.text: In tuberculosis there is **no exotoxin**. The picture of the disease is determined mainly by the **delayed-type (type IV) hypersensitivity immune response** and the formation of granulomas. That is why tuberculosis runs as an “immunological disease”: tissue damage is largely the result of the body’s own response.

blocks.text: **Pathogenesis:** mycobacteria that enter by the airborne route are engulfed by alveolar macrophages, but because of **incomplete phagocytosis** they survive and multiply in them. As a result a **specific granuloma** forms (caseous necrosis in the center, surrounded by epithelioid cells and Pirogov–Langhans giant cells, and lymphocytes). In most people the process is contained at this stage — **latent infection**; when immunity falls (HIV, diabetes mellitus, malnutrition, immunosuppressive therapy, old age) **reactivation** occurs.
**Clinical forms:** pulmonary tuberculosis (the most frequent) and extrapulmonary forms — lymph nodes, bone and joint, kidney, intestine, meningitis, disseminated (miliary) tuberculosis.
**Material:** sputum (morning, 2–3 times, with a deep cough), bronchial washings, gastric washings (in children), urine, cerebrospinal fluid, puncture fluid, tissue biopsy.
4.1. Bacterioscopic method

items: Staining by the **Ziehl–Neelsen** method — rapid and inexpensive; its limitation is low sensitivity (about 10⁴–10⁵ cells per 1 ml of material are needed);
**Fluorescence microscopy** (auramine–rhodamine) — more sensitive and convenient for viewing many samples;
**Enrichment methods** — **flotation** (shaking with xylene/benzine and making a smear from the layer that rises to the surface) and **homogenization/sedimentation** — raise the sensitivity.

blocks.label: Figure 19.2
blocks.caption: Scheme of the bacterioscopic examination in tuberculosis: material, Ziehl–Neelsen staining, the fluorescence method, enrichment (flotation and homogenization). Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

blocks.text: 4.2. Bacteriological (cultural) method — the gold standard

items: The material is subjected to **decontamination** with alkali or acid (to remove the accompanying flora; mycobacteria survive because they are resistant), neutralized and centrifuged.
The sediment is inoculated onto **Löwenstein–Jensen** (or Finn-2) medium; modern laboratories use automated **liquid medium systems** (the result comes much faster).
At 37 °C for 3–8 weeks, observed weekly.

Identification: growth rate, colony appearance, **cord factor**, the **niacin test** (positive for *M. tuberculosis*), nitrate reductase, pigment formation; modern methods — molecular identification and MALDI-TOF.
**Antibiotic susceptibility** — by the cultural or molecular method (resistance genes).

blocks.label: Figure 19.3
blocks.caption: Scheme of the bacteriological examination in tuberculosis: decontamination, inoculation onto Löwenstein–Jensen and Finn-2 media, cord factor, niacin test, antibiotic susceptibility. Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

blocks.text: 4.3. Molecular and immunological methods

items: **Rapid molecular tests (PCR-based)** — detect the pathogen and, at the same time, the **genes for resistance to the main drugs** within a few hours; at present one of the first-line methods;

**Tuberculin test (Mantoux)** — tuberculin is injected into the skin and the papule is measured after 72 hours; it shows **infection (sensitization)**, not disease. It can also be positive after BCG vaccination;
**Blood tests based on IFN-γ release (IGRA)** — independent of BCG, used to detect latent infection;
**Biological test** — now rarely used.

parts.text: A positive Mantoux test does not mean **“tuberculosis disease”**: it shows that the body has met mycobacterial antigens. The diagnosis is made from a combination of clinical findings, X-ray and microbiological results.

blocks.text: **Prophylaxis:** **BCG** — a live attenuated vaccine; it is important for protection against severe disseminated forms. Additional measures: early detection, isolation of the source, examination of contacts, social and hygienic measures.

sections.title: The causative agent of leprosy — *Mycobacterium leprae*

blocks.text: **Features:** an acid-fast rod; **it does not grow on artificial nutrient media at all** — this is its main laboratory feature. In experiments it is propagated in armadillos and in the mouse footpad. It multiplies very slowly (generation time 12–14 days), and the incubation period is several years.
**Morphological feature:** in tissue and mucosal scrapings it lies **inside cells, in orderly bundles resembling “cigarettes in a pack”** (globi).

**Clinical forms:** **lepromatous** (weak immune response, many organisms — more contagious) and **tuberculoid** (strong cell-mediated immunity, few organisms), as well as intermediate forms. The skin, peripheral nerves and mucous membranes are mainly affected; nerve damage leads to loss of sensation and deformities.

**Diagnosis:** nasal mucosal scrapings, material from skin lesions, biopsy → **Ziehl–Neelsen** → seeing orderly intracellular bundles; the **lepromin test** (to assess the type of immune response, not for diagnosis); PCR.

sections.title: Independent work: Actinomycosis and atypical mycobacteria

blocks.text: 6.1. Actinomycosis

**Causative agent:** *Actinomyces israelii* and other actinomycetes — gram-positive, branching filamentous **bacteria** (topic 4), members of the normal flora of the oral cavity, intestine and urogenital tract.

**Pathogenesis:** an **endogenous** disease — when the mucosa is damaged (tooth extraction, jaw injury, appendicitis, an intrauterine device) the organism enters the tissue; under anaerobic conditions chronic **granulomatous** inflammation, a dense infiltrate and **fistulas** develop.
**Forms:** orofacial (the most frequent), thoracic, abdominal, urogenital, and central nervous system forms.

**Diagnosis:** fistula discharge or tissue → looking for visible yellow **druses** → microscopy (mycelium in the center of the druse, a radiating structure at the edge) → **anaerobic culture** (grows slowly, 7–14 days) → identification. Because actinomycetes are bacteria, they **respond to antibacterial treatment**.

parts.text: The triad of actinomycosis: **chronic dense infiltrate + fistulas + yellow druses in the pus**.

blocks.text: 6.2. Atypical (nontuberculous) mycobacteria

**General name:** NTM — mycobacteria that do not belong to the tuberculosis group. Their natural habitat is **water, soil, water pipes and moist environments**; they are hardly ever transmitted from person to person (the main epidemiological difference from tuberculosis).

**Classic groups by Runyon:** photochromogens (produce pigment in light — *M. kansasii*), scotochromogens (pigmented even in the dark — *M. scrofulaceum*), nonphotochromogens (*M. avium* complex), and **rapid growers** (*M. fortuitum*, *M. chelonae* — grow within up to 7 days).

**Clinical significance:** disseminated infection in the immunocompromised (especially in HIV infection — *M. avium* complex); pulmonary forms on the background of chronic lung disease; cervical lymphadenitis in children; skin and soft-tissue infections after surgical and cosmetic procedures (rapid-growing species).

**Diagnostic particularity:** finding an acid-fast rod does not in itself mean tuberculosis — **the species must be identified** (molecular methods, MALDI-TOF). Atypical mycobacteria are naturally resistant to most antituberculosis drugs, so the treatment regimen is entirely different.

parts.text: When an acid-fast rod is found in sputum, **two questions** are asked: (1) is it *M. tuberculosis* or an atypical mycobacterium? (2) is it drug-resistant? Modern molecular tests answer both questions quickly.

skills.title: Practical skill: collecting sputum for tuberculosis testing

items: The patient is told: the material needed is **not saliva but sputum brought up by a deep cough**.
The sample is collected **in the morning, on an empty stomach**, after rinsing the mouth with water.
The patient breathes in deeply, coughs forcefully and spits the sputum into a **wide-mouthed sterile container**; the volume is usually 3–5 ml.
The sample is delivered to the laboratory in a tightly closed container, **upright**, cooled (2–8 °C).
Usually **2–3** samples are collected (on different days or according to a set scheme) — this raises sensitivity.
In the laboratory: a smear (Ziehl–Neelsen or fluorescence), decontamination and culture, a rapid molecular test.
Safety: the material can generate aerosols — the work is done **in a special cabinet**, with protective equipment.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: In the sputum of a patient with a cough lasting 3 weeks, evening low-grade fever and weight loss, red rods were found by the Ziehl–Neelsen method.
cases.ask: What are the preliminary conclusion and the next steps?
cases.answer: Acid-fast rods have been found — tuberculosis is suspected. Next steps: **identify the species** (a rapid molecular test, culture), assess **drug resistance**, a chest X-ray and examination by a phthisiologist. An acid-fast rod alone does not prove that it is *M. tuberculosis*.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A patient with HIV infection has a disseminated infection; in culture, acid-fast rods grew in 7 days, and the niacin test is negative.
cases.ask: What should be considered?
cases.answer: Atypical (nontuberculous) mycobacteria — rapid growth and niacin negativity are not characteristic of *M. tuberculosis*. The species is identified by a molecular method; the treatment regimen differs from that for tuberculosis.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A healthy child vaccinated with BCG had a positive Mantoux test; there are no changes in the clinical picture or on X-ray.
cases.ask: How should the result be interpreted?
cases.answer: A positive Mantoux test can also be due to sensitization after BCG; it does not establish a diagnosis of disease. Where necessary the child is assessed with **IGRA** (a blood test independent of BCG) and clinical and radiological follow-up.

summary.text: Two main “filter” tests for enterobacteria: **oxidase negative** (membership of the family) and **lactose** (differentiation within the family). On Endo/Levine medium **lactose-positive organisms give colored** colonies and **lactose-negative organisms give colorless** colonies.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Growth of *E. coli* from stool is not in itself a diagnosis — it is a member of the normal flora. The diarrheagenic variant must be confirmed by **serological and molecular** methods.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: To remember Yersinia: it **“loves the cold”** — it multiplies in the refrigerator, is enriched in the cold, is inoculated at 25–28 °C and is motile at 25 °C.

blocks.text: **General properties:**

items: gram-negative, nonspore-forming rods; most are **peritrichous** (motile), some are nonmotile (Shigella, Klebsiella);
**facultative anaerobes**; grow on ordinary media;
**oxidase negative** (the main difference from Pseudomonas), **catalase positive**;
**they ferment glucose with production of acid (often gas)**; they reduce nitrate to nitrite;
on differential media they are separated by their **fermentation of lactose**.

parts.text: Two main “filter” tests for enterobacteria: **oxidase negative** (membership of the family) and **lactose** (differentiation within the family). On Endo/Levine medium **lactose-positive organisms give colored** colonies and **lactose-negative organisms give colorless** colonies.

blocks.text: **Antigenic structure:** **O** (somatic, LPS, heat-stable), **H** (flagellar, heat-labile), **K** (capsular/surface; in typhoid fever, **Vi**). Serological identification is based on exactly these antigens.

**Pathogenic (diarrheagenic) variants** — strains that have acquired special virulence genes; they differ from the normal flora in their **serovars and virulence factors**.

blocks.text: **Extraintestinal coli infections:** urinary tract infection (the most frequent causative agent), cholecystitis, peritonitis, meningitis and sepsis in newborns, wound infections.

parts.text: In bloody diarrhea associated with EHEC, **caution is exercised in prescribing antibiotics**: according to some data they can increase toxin release and the risk of hemolytic–uremic syndrome. The treatment approach is decided by the physician.

blocks.text: **Laboratory diagnosis of coli infections:**

items: **Material:** stool (in diarrhea), urine (in UTI), blood, cerebrospinal fluid.
**Inoculation:** Endo/Levine/Ploskirev; urine culture — **quantitative** (CFU/ml).
**Identification:** lactose, indole, Kligler, oxidase; then **serological identification** — agglutination with diagnostic O sera.
**Confirming pathogenicity:** detecting virulence genes (toxin, adhesin) by **PCR** — the most reliable way to distinguish a diarrheagenic variant from ordinary *E. coli*.

blocks.caption: Scheme of the microbiological examination in escherichiosis: material, Endo and Kligler media, biochemical properties, serological identification with diagnostic sera. Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

parts.text: Growth of *E. coli* from stool is not in itself a diagnosis — it is a member of the normal flora. The diarrheagenic variant must be confirmed by **serological and molecular** methods.

blocks.text: ***Klebsiella pneumoniae*** — a gram-negative, **nonmotile**, large **encapsulated** rod. The colonies are mucoid, **sticky, stretching into a string behind the loop** (M-form); lactose-positive.

blocks.label: Figure 20.3
blocks.caption: *Klebsiella pneumoniae* — large encapsulated gram-negative rods. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **Clinical significance:** pneumonia (classically severe, destructive), urinary tract infection, sepsis, infections of newborns; **an important causative agent of hospital-acquired infections**, notorious for multidrug resistance (including carbapenemases).
**Causative agents:** *Yersinia enterocolitica* (yersiniosis) and *Y. pseudotuberculosis* (pseudotuberculosis). (*Y. pestis* is covered in topic 24.)

**Features:** gram-negative rods; **psychrophilic** — **multiply at low temperature (4–8 °C)**, so they accumulate in refrigerated products and vegetables (“refrigerator infection”). Motile at 25–28 °C, nonmotile at 37 °C; urease positive.

blocks.label: Figure 20.4
blocks.caption: Results of the indirect hemagglutination reaction (IHA) of *Y. enterocolitica* with an erythrocyte diagnostic reagent. Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

blocks.text: **Clinical picture:** gastroenteritis, mesenteric lymphadenitis (**a picture resembling acute appendicitis** — the “pseudoappendicular form”), terminal ileitis; a generalized form; complications — reactive arthritis, erythema nodosum.
**Diagnosis:**

items: **Material:** stool, blood, surgical material (lymph nodes, appendix).

**“Cold enrichment”** — storing the material in phosphate buffer **at 4 °C for 1–3 weeks**; Yersinia multiply while the accompanying flora is suppressed. It is then inoculated onto selective medium (CIN agar, Endo).
**Incubation** is carried out at 25–28 °C (not 37 °C).
**Identification:** biochemical tests (urease +), testing motility at two temperatures, serological identification.
**Serological method:** dynamics of the titer in paired sera by IHA/ELISA.

parts.text: To remember Yersinia: it **“loves the cold”** — it multiplies in the refrigerator, is enriched in the cold, is inoculated at 25–28 °C and is motile at 25 °C.

blocks.text: 6.1. *Campylobacter jejuni*

**Features:** gram-negative, **“gull-wing”**, S-shaped or “swallow-wing” curved rod; polar flagellum, highly motile; **microaerophilic** (5–10% O₂ + 10% CO₂) and **thermophilic** (grows well at 42 °C); oxidase positive.
**Epidemiology:** the source is poultry and other animals; it is transmitted through undercooked poultry, unpasteurized milk and contaminated water.

**Clinical picture:** acute gastroenteritis (often bloody diarrhea, severe abdominal pain, fever) — one of the main causes of bacterial diarrhea worldwide; a complication is **Guillain–Barré syndrome** (through cross-reactive antigens).

**Diagnosis:** stool → **selective medium** (with added antibiotics) → **microaerophilic conditions, 42 °C** → oxidase and motility; in a wet mount the characteristic “darting” motion; modern methods — antigen tests and PCR.
6.2. *Helicobacter pylori*
**Features:** gram-negative, **spiral/S-shaped** curved rod; a tuft of flagella at one end (highly motile); **microaerophilic**; its most important feature is **strong urease activity**.

blocks.label: Figure 20.5
blocks.caption: *Helicobacter pylori* — spiral-shaped gram-negative bacteria in the gastric mucosa. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **Pathogenesis:** urease splits urea to form **ammonia** — it neutralizes the acid around the bacterium and allows it to survive in the acidic gastric environment; motility and the spiral shape ensure penetration into the mucous layer; adhesins and the **CagA** and **VacA** factors damage the epithelium.
**Clinical significance:** chronic gastritis, gastric and duodenal ulcer disease; in the long term, it is linked to the risk of gastric cancer and MALT lymphoma.

parts.text: Before breath and stool tests, proton pump inhibitors, antibiotics and bismuth preparations are stopped for a set period — otherwise the result will be a **false negative**. Serology stays positive for a long time even after treatment, so it is not suitable for monitoring eradication.

skills.title: Practical skill: examining stool for intestinal infection

items: Stool is collected **before antibiotics**, if possible in the first days of the illness, into a sterile container; if there are pathological admixtures (mucus, blood), the sample is taken from exactly that part.
The sample is delivered within 2 hours; if delayed, **transport medium** (Cary–Blair) is used.
Inoculation: Endo/Levine (general), Ploskirev and bismuth sulfite agar (Salmonella/Shigella), selective media (for Campylobacter — 42 °C under microaerophilic conditions).
After 18–24 hours the colonies are assessed: lactose-positive (colored) and lactose-negative (colorless) colonies are separated.
A pure culture is picked from suspicious colonies → Kligler, the biochemical series → **serological identification** (diagnostic sera).
Where necessary, PCR (diarrheagenic *E. coli*, Campylobacter, viral diarrheas) and an antibiogram.
The final answer states the species of the causative agent, its serovar (if any) and its antibiotic susceptibility.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A child has bloody diarrhea; on stool culture lactose-positive colonies grew on Endo medium, biochemically *E. coli*.
cases.ask: Does this result prove a diarrheagenic strain? What should be done?

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A patient operated on with suspected acute appendicitis has an almost unchanged appendix and enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes. In recent days the patient ate a vegetable salad that had been stored in the refrigerator for a long time.
cases.ask: Which pathogen should be considered, and what is special about the examination?
cases.answer: Yersiniosis (*Y. enterocolitica*) — the “pseudoappendicular” form. The examination uses **cold enrichment**, inoculation is done at 25–28 °C; the dynamics of the titer in paired sera are assessed serologically.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A patient with chronic gastritis was prescribed a urea breath test; the patient had been taking a proton pump inhibitor up to the day of the test. The result was negative, but the symptoms persist.
cases.ask: How should the result be assessed?
cases.answer: A **false negative** is highly likely: PPIs and antibiotics should have been stopped for a set period before the test. The test is repeated after the drugs are stopped, or another method is chosen (stool antigen, biopsy).

topics.title: Causative agents of shigellosis and cholera. Amebic dysentery

goals.text: To know the classification and biological properties of Shigella and the pathogenesis of dysentery;
to explain the properties of *Vibrio cholerae*, its toxin and the pathogenesis of cholera;
to master the algorithm of microbiological diagnosis of shigellosis and cholera;
Independent work: to know the causative agent of amebic dysentery and its laboratory diagnosis.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Dysentery is an **invasive** diarrhea: the stool is scanty but **mucous and bloody**, with tenesmus. Cholera is a **secretory (toxin-mediated)** diarrhea: the stool is very copious and watery, with little pain or fever.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: *Sh. sonnei* can ferment lactose **late (after 48 hours)**. If the result is read late, it may be wrongly assessed as “lactose-positive” and the organism may fail to be identified as Shigella (recall the situational case in topic 7).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The basis of treatment in cholera is **rehydration** (replacing water and electrolytes): oral rehydration solutions and, in severe cases, intravenous infusion solutions. Antibiotics play a supporting role (they shorten the course of the disease and the shedding of the vibrio). It is carried out as prescribed by a physician.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Cholera toxin: **“cAMP goes up — water pours out.”** That is why the stool is watery, resembling “rice water.”

blocks.text: **Morphology and properties:** gram-negative rods; **nonmotile** (no flagella — a distinguishing feature among enterobacteria), nonspore-forming, noncapsulated. **Lactose-negative** (colorless colonies on Endo medium), **H₂S negative**, usually **produce no gas**, lysine decarboxylase negative.

blocks.text: **Pathogenicity factors:**

items: **Invasiveness** — the main mechanism: Shigella **penetrate** the epithelium of the large intestine, multiply inside the cell and spread to neighboring cells → erosion and ulcers form;
**Shiga toxin** (in *Sh. dysenteriae* serovar 1) — stops protein synthesis (cytotoxic), has neurotoxic and enterotoxic effects; it can be linked to hemolytic–uremic syndrome;
**Endotoxin (LPS)** — general intoxication.

blocks.text: **Pathogenesis and clinical picture:** the infectious dose is very low (a few dozen cells) — so it spreads easily by the **contact-household** route. The process is mainly in the **distal large intestine**; the clinical picture: frequent, scanty, **stool mixed with mucus and blood**, **tenesmus** (a painful false urge to defecate), spasmodic abdominal pain, fever.

parts.text: Dysentery is an **invasive** diarrhea: the stool is scanty but **mucous and bloody**, with tenesmus. Cholera is a **secretory (toxin-mediated)** diarrhea: the stool is very copious and watery, with little pain or fever.

blocks.text: **Laboratory diagnosis:**

items: **Material:** stool (the mucous-bloody part), rectal swab; the sample is delivered **as quickly as possible** or in **Cary–Blair** transport medium (Shigella are unstable in the external environment).
**Inoculation:** Endo, Ploskirev (selective), Levine → **colorless (lactose-negative) colonies**.
**Identification:** Kligler (slant red, butt yellow, **no gas, no H₂S**), nonmotility (in semisolid agar), the biochemical series.
**Serological identification:** agglutination with diagnostic sera specific to group and type.
**Additional:** antibiogram; PCR (invasiveness and toxin genes); the colonoscopic picture — clinically supportive.
