blocks.caption: Scheme of the microbiological examination in dysentery: material, Ploskirev and Endo media, biochemical properties and serological identification. Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

parts.text: *Sh. sonnei* can ferment lactose **late (after 48 hours)**. If the result is read late, it may be wrongly assessed as “lactose-positive” and the organism may fail to be identified as Shigella (recall the situational case in topic 7).

sections.title: The causative agent of cholera — *Vibrio cholerae*

blocks.text: **Morphology:** gram-negative, **comma-shaped** curved rod (a vibrio); **monotrichous** — highly motile thanks to a single polar flagellum (directed movement like a “shoal of fish”); nonspore-forming, noncapsulated.

blocks.label: Figure 21.3
blocks.caption: Cholera vibrios — comma-shaped motile gram-negative bacteria. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **Cultural and biochemical properties:**

items: **alkaliphilic (alkali-loving)** — grows well at pH 8.5–9.0; therefore **alkaline peptone water** is used as the enrichment medium: the vibrio forms a **thin pellicle** on the surface and outgrows the accompanying flora;
the selective solid medium is **TCBS agar** (yellow colonies) or alkaline agar (transparent, bluish colonies);
**oxidase positive** (unlike enterobacteria!), ferments sucrose and mannose, does not ferment arabinose.

blocks.text: **Serological groups:** O1 (classical and **El Tor** biovars; Ogawa and Inaba serovars) and **O139** — of epidemic significance. Other (non-O1) vibrios usually cause mild gastroenteritis.

**The main pathogenicity factor — cholera toxin (choleragen):** it consists of A and B subunits; the B subunit binds to a receptor on the intestinal epithelium, and the A subunit enters the cell and **permanently activates adenylate cyclase** → **cAMP** rises sharply → **water and electrolytes** (Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, HCO₃⁻) leave the cell into the intestinal lumen.
**Pathogenesis:** the vibrio **does not enter the epithelium**, stays in the intestinal lumen and produces toxin. Therefore:

items: the stool looks like **“rice water”** — watery, odorless, with whitish flecks; no blood or mucus;
inflammation and high fever are usually absent;
the main danger is **severe dehydration**, loss of electrolytes, metabolic acidosis and hypovolemic shock.

parts.text: The basis of treatment in cholera is **rehydration** (replacing water and electrolytes): oral rehydration solutions and, in severe cases, intravenous infusion solutions. Antibiotics play a supporting role (they shorten the course of the disease and the shedding of the vibrio). It is carried out as prescribed by a physician.
Cholera toxin: **“cAMP goes up — water pours out.”** That is why the stool is watery, resembling “rice water.”

blocks.text: **Laboratory diagnosis (rapid and staged):**

items: **Material:** stool, vomit; in fatal cases — a piece of intestine; water and environmental samples (in epidemiological investigation). The requirements of the **especially dangerous infection** regime are observed.
**Rapid methods:** seeing **motility** in a wet mount (dark-field/phase-contrast) and the **cessation of motility** with specific serum; immunofluorescence, latex agglutination, PCR.
**Enrichment:** **alkaline peptone water**, 37 °C, 6–8 hours → subculture from the pellicle on the surface.
**Inoculation:** TCBS or alkaline agar.

**Identification:** oxidase, biochemical properties, agglutination with O1/O139 sera; additional tests to determine the biovar (classical/El Tor) (phage susceptibility, hemagglutination, polymyxin susceptibility).

parts.text: Cholera is an **especially dangerous (quarantine) infection**: when it is suspected, the material is collected and transported in a special manner, and the health system is notified immediately. Laboratory work is carried out under the prescribed biosafety regime.

blocks.text: **Causative agent:** *Entamoeba histolytica* — a protozoan (class Sarcodina).
**Life cycle and forms:**

items: **Cyst** — resistant in the external environment, the **infective** form (4 nuclei); it is swallowed with water and food;
**Trophozoite** — the vegetative form: *forma minuta* (in the intestinal lumen, harmless) and **forma magna (the tissue form)** — the form that has ingested erythrocytes and invades tissue.

blocks.label: Figure 21.4
blocks.caption: Protozoa: microscopic appearance of *Entamoeba* cysts and other parasites. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **Pathogenesis and clinical picture:** the tissue form penetrates the mucosa of the large intestine and forms **“flask-shaped” ulcers**; through the bloodstream it can reach the liver and cause a **liver abscess**. Clinically: a gradual onset, **blood and mucus in the stool** resembling “raspberry jelly,” abdominal pain; fever is often mild.

blocks.text: **Laboratory diagnosis:**

items: **Wet mount** — from **warm, fresh** stool; seeing motile **trophozoites with ingested erythrocytes** (the main sign of the tissue form);
**Staining with Lugol’s solution** — to see the cysts and the number of nuclei in them;
**Antigen detection (ELISA)** and **PCR** — distinguish *E. histolytica* from the morphologically identical but nonpathogenic *E. dispar*;
**Serology** — important in tissue forms, especially in **liver abscess**;
In liver abscess — imaging methods (ultrasound, CT) and examination of the aspirate.

parts.text: Finding an amebic **cyst** in stool may also mean carriage. The sign that proves disease is a **trophozoite with ingested erythrocytes** (the tissue form) or a positive antigen/PCR result.

skills.title: Practical skill: choosing a method when examining stool for intestinal infections

items: **Mucous-bloody stool + tenesmus** → inoculation for shigellosis (Ploskirev, Endo) + excluding invasive variants of *E. coli*; in parallel — a wet mount (to exclude amebae).
**Watery, odorless, copious stool (rice water)** → **suspect cholera**: enrichment in alkaline peptone water, TCBS, rapid methods; the especially dangerous infection regime.
**Gradual onset, no fever, “raspberry jelly”** → examination for amebiasis: warm wet mount, antigen test, PCR.
**Bloody diarrhea + impaired kidney indices in a child** → excluding EHEC and Shiga toxin.
In all cases: the sample is taken **before antibiotics**, from the part with pathological admixtures, and delivered quickly; if delay is likely, transport medium is used.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A patient passes scanty stool mixed with mucus and blood 15–20 times a day, with severe tenesmus and a temperature of 38.5 °C. On stool culture colorless colonies grew on Endo medium; the culture is nonmotile, H₂S negative and produces no gas.
cases.ask: What are the probable causative agent and the method of final confirmation?
cases.answer: Shigella — the features (nonmotility, lactose-negative, no H₂S or gas) fit. The final confirmation is **agglutination with group- and type-specific diagnostic sera** (serological identification), followed by an antibiogram.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: In the hot season, several patients have very copious watery, odorless stool many times a day; there is almost no abdominal pain or fever, and rapid dehydration is developing.
cases.ask: What should be suspected, and what are the first measure and the laboratory tactics?
cases.answer: Suspected cholera. The first measure is to start **rehydration** immediately. Laboratory: the material is collected under the especially dangerous infection regime, enriched in alkaline peptone water and inoculated onto TCBS; rapid methods in parallel (cessation of motility, PCR). The health system is notified.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A patient has had diarrhea that gradually worsened over several weeks, with mucus and blood in the stool; no fever. The stool culture is negative for pathogenic bacteria. A space-occupying lesion was found in the liver.
cases.ask: What should be considered, and what examination is needed?
cases.answer: Amebiasis and its complication — a liver abscess. Examination: looking for **trophozoites with ingested erythrocytes** in a warm wet mount, a stool antigen test and PCR, serology (important in tissue forms), imaging methods.

topics.title: Causative agents of typhoid fever and paratyphoid A and B. Opportunistic enterobacteria and viral diarrheas

goals.text: To know the biological properties and antigenic structure of the causative agents of typhoid fever and paratyphoid;
to explain the stages of the pathogenesis of typhoid fever and the corresponding examination methods;
to master the concepts of hemoculture, coproculture, urinoculture and biliculture and the Widal reaction;
to know the principle of detecting bacterial carriage;
Independent work: to have an understanding of opportunistic intestinal bacteria (Citrobacter, Klebsiella, Enterobacter) and viral diarrheas (rotavirus, adenovirus).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The Vi antigen is the **“virulence” antigen**: it protects the live bacterium from agglutination with O serum. Therefore, if there is no O agglutination in serological identification, the culture is heated (the Vi antigen is destroyed) and the reaction is repeated.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: In typhoid fever the rule **“stage — material”** is basic: **week 1 — blood** (hemoculture), **from week 2 — stool and urine** (coproculture, urinoculture), **from week 2 — serum** (Widal/PHA), **after recovery — bile** (biliculture, detecting carriage).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: A single positive Widal reaction is not enough for a final diagnosis: it can be positive in a vaccinated person or one who has had the disease before. The sign that has diagnostic value is **at least a 4-fold rise in titer in paired sera** (topic 11).

sections.title: The causative agents of typhoid fever and paratyphoid

blocks.text: **Causative agents:** *Salmonella* Typhi (typhoid fever), *S.* Paratyphi A and *S.* Paratyphi B.

**Morphology and properties:** gram-negative, **peritrichous** (motile) rods; nonspore-forming, noncapsulated (the Vi antigen is present). **Lactose-negative**, they ferment glucose; *S.* Typhi **produces no gas**, whereas the paratyphoids **produce gas**; *S.* Typhi produces little H₂S, paratyphoid B a lot.
**Antigenic structure (based on the Kauffmann–White scheme):**

items: **O antigen** — somatic, heat-stable; determines the group (*S.* Typhi — group D, Paratyphi A — A, Paratyphi B — B);
**H antigen** — flagellar, heat-labile;
**Vi antigen** — a surface (capsule-type) antigen; associated with **virulence** and “masks” the O antigen; especially important **in detecting carriage**.

parts.text: The Vi antigen is the **“virulence” antigen**: it protects the live bacterium from agglutination with O serum. Therefore, if there is no O agglutination in serological identification, the culture is heated (the Vi antigen is destroyed) and the reaction is repeated.

blocks.text: **Pathogenesis — the stages (this determines diagnostic tactics!):**

items: **Entry and multiplication in the intestine** (incubation period, 7–14 days): the bacteria enter the mucosa of the small intestine and multiply in Peyer’s patches and the mesenteric lymph nodes.
**Bacteremia** (week 1): the bacteria pass into the blood — the clinical picture begins (fever, headache, intoxication, relative bradycardia, a roseolar rash on the abdomen).
**Parenchymatous dissemination** (week 2): they settle in the liver, spleen, bone marrow and gallbladder.

**Excretion stage** (weeks 2–3): they are excreted from the gallbladder with bile into the intestine and through the kidney into the urine; **necrosis and ulcers** form in Peyer’s patches owing to sensitization — complications (intestinal bleeding, perforation) occur precisely in this period.
**Recovery or transition to carriage:** the pathogen can persist for a long time in the gallbladder (especially in gallstone disease), and **chronic carriage** may develop.

parts.text: In typhoid fever the rule **“stage — material”** is basic: **week 1 — blood** (hemoculture), **from week 2 — stool and urine** (coproculture, urinoculture), **from week 2 — serum** (Widal/PHA), **after recovery — bile** (biliculture, detecting carriage).

blocks.text: **Hemoculture technique:** 5–10 ml of blood is drawn from a vein and inoculated into a **10-fold larger** volume of liquid medium (Rappoport — a medium containing bile, glucose and an indicator). Dilution reduces the bactericidal action of the blood serum. After 18–24 hours at 37 °C, it is assessed by color change and gas, then subcultured onto Endo/Ploskirev or bismuth sulfite agar.

blocks.text: **Identification:** lactose-negative colonies → Kligler (slant red, butt yellow; in *S.* Typhi no gas, little H₂S; on bismuth sulfite agar a **black colony**) → the biochemical series → agglutination with **O, H and Vi sera**.

blocks.caption: Scheme of the bacteriological examination of the causative agents of typhoid fever and paratyphoid A and B: I — hemoculture; II — coproculture; III — serological examination (Widal reaction). Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

blocks.text: **The Widal reaction** — an extended agglutination test: the patient’s serum is serially diluted and set up with O, H and Vi diagnosticums.
**Interpretation:**

items: **O antibodies** appear early and fall quickly → they indicate an **active (acute)** process;
**H antibodies** appear later and persist for a long time → they may be positive after past disease or after vaccination;
**Vi antibodies** → an indicator of **chronic carriage**.

parts.text: A single positive Widal reaction is not enough for a final diagnosis: it can be positive in a vaccinated person or one who has had the disease before. The sign that has diagnostic value is **at least a 4-fold rise in titer in paired sera** (topic 11).

blocks.text: **Rapid and modern methods:** PCR (blood, stool), antigen tests; MALDI-TOF in identification.
**Prophylaxis:** sanitary and hygienic measures (water supply, sewage, food control), detecting and monitoring carriers, vaccination on indication (Vi-polysaccharide and live vaccines).
**Types of carriage:** acute (up to 3 months), **chronic** (over 3 months), transitory.
**Detection scheme:**

items: Repeated **coproculture** and **urinoculture** (by a set scheme, several times);
**Biliculture** — inoculation of bile portions obtained by duodenal intubation (the most reliable, because the main habitat of the pathogen is the gallbladder);
Detecting **Vi antibodies** (PHA) — as a screening test;
PCR where necessary.

parts.text: Chronic carriers are one of the main sources of the disease; therefore people who work in food, water supply, and children’s and medical institutions are examined by a set procedure.

blocks.text: **Representatives:** *Citrobacter*, *Klebsiella*, *Enterobacter*, *Serratia*, *Proteus*, *Morganella*, *Providencia*.
**General features:** members of the normal flora or of the external environment; they cause infection **endogenously** or in hospital settings; often **multidrug-resistant**.

blocks.text: **Rule of interpretation in diarrhea:** these bacteria can be present in stool even in health. To judge them as the causative agent: other pathogens must have been excluded, the **quantity must be high** (massive growth), it must fit the clinical picture, and it must persist on follow-up.
6.1. Rotavirus
**Features:** the family **Reoviridae**; double-stranded, **segmented RNA**; nonenveloped, resistant; on electron microscopy it has a **“wheel”** appearance (Latin *rota* — wheel).

**Epidemiology and clinical picture:** in children (especially 6 months to 2 years) **the most frequent cause of acute gastroenteritis**; fecal-oral route; seasonality — the cold period. Clinically: vomiting, **watery diarrhea**, fever; the main danger is **dehydration**.
**Diagnosis:** **antigen detection (ELISA, immunochromatographic rapid tests)** in stool — the main method in practice; PCR; electron microscopy (research).
**Prophylaxis:** **live oral rotavirus vaccine** — in infancy; it significantly reduces severe forms and hospitalizations.
6.2. Adenovirus (enteric types)
**Features:** **Adenoviridae**; double-stranded DNA, nonenveloped, icosahedral capsid, with projections (fibers).

blocks.text: **Clinical picture:** the enteric types (40, 41) cause longer-lasting diarrhea in children; other types — respiratory infection, conjunctivitis, pharyngoconjunctival fever.
**Diagnosis:** stool antigen test, PCR.

parts.text: In acute watery diarrhea in children, **viruses are considered first** (especially rotavirus); in mucous-bloody diarrhea — invasive bacteria (Shigella, invasive *E. coli*, Campylobacter). The basis of treatment is **rehydration**.

skills.title: Practical skill: collecting a hemoculture

items: Blood is taken **during a rise in fever** and **before antibiotics**.
The skin is treated according to aseptic rules (wait until the antiseptic has dried) — this prevents **contamination**.
5–10 ml of blood (an age-appropriate volume in children) is drawn from a vein with a sterile syringe.
The blood is immediately inoculated into a **10-fold larger** volume of medium (Rappoport or bile broth; in modern settings, automated bottles).
The bottle is placed at 37 °C; it is observed for signs of growth (turbidity, color change, gas), or the automated system gives a signal.
From a positive bottle a smear (Gram) and a subculture onto solid medium are made; then identification and an antibiogram.
For reliability, usually **several samples from different sites** are taken.

parts.text: Inoculating blood into a small volume of medium or failing to treat the skin are the two most frequent mistakes: the first leads to a false-negative, the second to a false-positive (skin flora) result.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A patient has had a stepwise rising fever since day 6, with headache and intoxication; single roseolas on the abdomen. The stool culture was negative.
cases.ask: What error might there be in the examination, and what is the correct tactic?
cases.answer: In week 1 of the disease the pathogen is mainly **in the blood**; excretion into the stool begins later. The correct tactic is **hemoculture** (before antibiotics), later coproculture/urinoculture, and from week 2 serology (paired sera).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A woman who works in a canteen has no complaints, but a preventive examination detected **Vi antibodies** by PHA.
cases.ask: What does this mean, and what is the next step?
cases.answer: Possible chronic carriage. The next step is repeated coproculture, urinoculture and **biliculture** (by duodenal intubation). If confirmed, the questions of employment and monitoring are resolved by the set procedure.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 1-year-old child has vomiting, up to 10 watery stools a day and a low-grade fever. No pathogenic bacteria were found on stool culture; the stool antigen rapid test was positive.
cases.ask: What are the probable causative agent and the basis of treatment?
cases.answer: Rotavirus gastroenteritis. The basis of treatment is **rehydration** (oral rehydration solutions, intravenous if necessary). Antibiotics are not indicated. The rotavirus vaccine is important in prophylaxis.

topics.title: Foodborne infections and food poisonings: salmonellosis, botulism

goals.text: To know the difference between foodborne infectious diseases (toxicoinfections) and intoxications;
to explain the properties, pathogenesis and diagnosis of the causative agents of salmonellosis;
to master the mechanism of action of the botulism causative agent and its toxin, the clinical expression of the disease and its diagnosis;
Independent work: to know poisonings associated with Proteus, Campylobacter, *E. coli* and Listeria, and the serological identification of bacteria of the enteric group.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **The incubation period — the first indicator:** very short (1–6 hours), with vomiting predominating — **preformed toxin** (staphylococcal enterotoxin); 12–48 hours, with fever — **multiplication of live microbes** (a toxicoinfection of the salmonellosis type).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: In ordinary gastrointestinal salmonellosis an antibiotic is **not indicated**: it does not shorten the course of the disease and may, on the contrary, prolong the shedding of bacteria. Antibiotics are used on a physician’s prescription in generalized forms and in risk groups (newborns, the elderly, the immunocompromised). The basis of treatment is **rehydration**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Salmonella in Kligler: **“red/yellow + gas + black”** (slant alkaline, butt acidic, gas and H₂S present). In Shigella, neither gas nor H₂S is present — **absent** (topic 21).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Listeriosis** can be linked to products stored in the refrigerator, because the causative agent multiplies at low temperature. It is dangerous for pregnant women, newborns and the immunocompromised; in diagnosis, blood and cerebrospinal fluid culture is decisive.

rows: **Live microbes** enter with the food, multiply in the intestine and release toxin
**Preformed toxin** enters in the product; a live microbe is not required
**Short** (30 min–6 hours), or longer in botulism
A classic infection; food is only a transmission factor
blocks.title: Table 23.1. Main groups of food-related conditions

parts.text: **The incubation period — the first indicator:** very short (1–6 hours), with vomiting predominating — **preformed toxin** (staphylococcal enterotoxin); 12–48 hours, with fever — **multiplication of live microbes** (a toxicoinfection of the salmonellosis type).

blocks.text: **Staphylococcal enterotoxin** (topic 16) is **heat-stable**: reheating a product kills the bacteria but does not inactivate the toxin. For this reason even “reheated” food can cause poisoning.
**Causative agents:** the many serovars of *Salmonella enterica*, the most frequent being **Enteritidis** and **Typhimurium**. (The typhoid–paratyphoid group was covered in topic 22.)

**Properties:** gram-negative, peritrichous (motile) rods; **lactose-negative**, they ferment glucose with production of **acid and gas**, **H₂S positive** (the Kligler butt blackens), urease negative, indole negative.

**Epidemiology:** the main source is **animals and poultry**; transmission factors are undercooked eggs and egg dishes, poultry and beef, dairy products; in addition, the contact-household route (especially in children) and contact with reptiles.
**Pathogenicity factors:** adhesins, **invasion factors** (entry into the intestinal epithelium), enterotoxin and cytotoxin, **endotoxin (LPS)**; virulence plasmids in *S.* Typhimurium and others.
**Clinical forms:**

items: **Gastrointestinal (common)** — fever, abdominal pain, vomiting, watery or mucous diarrhea;
**Generalized** — typhoid-like and septic forms; in newborns, the elderly and the immunocompromised;
**Bacterial carriage** — acute or chronic.

parts.text: In ordinary gastrointestinal salmonellosis an antibiotic is **not indicated**: it does not shorten the course of the disease and may, on the contrary, prolong the shedding of bacteria. Antibiotics are used on a physician’s prescription in generalized forms and in risk groups (newborns, the elderly, the immunocompromised). The basis of treatment is **rehydration**.

blocks.text: **Laboratory diagnosis:**

items: **Material:** stool, vomit, gastric lavage, remains of suspect food; in a generalized form — **blood** (hemoculture), urine.
**Enrichment:** selenite or magnesium medium (for stool).
**Inoculation:** Endo, Ploskirev, **bismuth sulfite agar** (black colonies).
**Identification:** Kligler (slant red, butt yellow, **gas +, H₂S +**), the biochemical series, motility.
**Serological identification:** agglutination with O and H sera according to the **Kauffmann–White scheme** — first polyvalent, then group-specific and type-specific sera.
**Additional:** antibiogram, PCR; in epidemiological investigation — examination of food and environmental samples.

parts.text: Salmonella in Kligler: **“red/yellow + gas + black”** (slant alkaline, butt acidic, gas and H₂S present). In Shigella, neither gas nor H₂S is present — **absent** (topic 21).

blocks.text: **Causative agent:** *Clostridium botulinum* — a gram-positive, **obligate anaerobe**, **subterminal spore**-forming rod (“tennis racket” shape); motile.

blocks.label: Figure 23.1
blocks.caption: The causative agent of botulism — gram-positive rods with subterminal spores (“tennis racket” appearance). Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **Botulinum toxin:** one of the most potent biological poisons in nature; **protein in nature**, **heat-labile** (broken down on boiling), but resistant to gastric acid and proteases. Serological types A, B, E, F (more common in humans) and others.

**Mechanism of action:** the toxin binds to peripheral cholinergic nerve endings and **stops the release of acetylcholine** → neuromuscular transmission is impaired → **flaccid (peripheral) paralysis** develops.

parts.text: Compare the two clostridial neurotoxins: **tetanus toxin — blocks inhibitory mediators → spastic (tonic) convulsions**; **botulinum toxin — blocks acetylcholine → flaccid paralysis**. In both, consciousness is preserved.

blocks.text: **Routes of transmission and forms:**

items: **Foodborne botulism** — toxin accumulates in products in which anaerobic conditions have been created, such as home-canned sealed preserves, smoked fish and sausage;
**Wound botulism** — multiplication of the pathogen in a wound;
**Infant botulism** — germination of spores in the intestine in children under 1 year (therefore **honey is not recommended before age 1**).

blocks.text: **Clinical picture:** the incubation period is usually 12–36 hours (from 2 hours to several days, depending on the dose of toxin). At first nausea and abdominal discomfort may occur, then the typical **neurological signs**:

items: **visual disturbance** — “a net before the eyes,” double vision (diplopia), drooping of the eyelid (ptosis), dilated pupil;
**swallowing and speech disturbance** — dysphagia, dysphonia, dry mouth;
**symmetric, descending flaccid paralysis**; in severe cases — **paralysis of the respiratory muscles** (the main cause of death).

blocks.text: **Fever is usually absent and consciousness is preserved** — this distinguishes botulism from many infections.
**Laboratory diagnosis:**

items: **Material:** blood serum, vomit, gastric lavage, stool, **remains of suspect food**.

**The main method — detecting the toxin:** the classic variant is the **biological test (neutralization test)**: the material is mixed with type-specific antitoxic sera and injected into a laboratory animal; the serum that protects shows the type to which the toxin belongs. Modern variants — ELISA and other in vitro methods.
**Isolating the pathogen** — anaerobic culture (Kitt–Tarozzi and others); detecting toxin genes by PCR.
**In practice diagnosis rests on clinical and epidemiological data** — waiting for the laboratory answer must not delay treatment.

parts.text: The decisive treatment in botulism is giving **antitoxic serum** as **early** as possible: the serum neutralizes only toxin **in the blood that is not bound to nerve**. The effect of bound toxin cannot be reversed — so no time is lost. In severe cases breathing is supported. All prescriptions are made by a physician.

blocks.text: **Prophylaxis:** following the technology of home canning, not using suspect preserves (with a bulging lid or a changed smell), heating the product sufficiently before consumption (the toxin is heat-labile), not giving honey to children under 1 year.

parts.text: **Listeriosis** can be linked to products stored in the refrigerator, because the causative agent multiplies at low temperature. It is dangerous for pregnant women, newborns and the immunocompromised; in diagnosis, blood and cerebrospinal fluid culture is decisive.

blocks.text: **Serological identification of bacteria of the enteric group.** The isolated culture is tested with **diagnostic agglutinating sera**:

items: **A preliminary (orienting) reaction on a glass slide** — first with **polyvalent** serum: if it is positive, the group is determined;
Then it is clarified with **group** and **monoreceptor (type-specific)** O sera;
Then it is typed by the **H antigen** (in a motile culture);
Where necessary the **Vi serum** is used; if the Vi antigen interferes with O agglutination, the culture is heated;
The result is recorded as a serovar formula according to the **Kauffmann–White scheme**.

blocks.text: Serological identification is also important for epidemiological analysis: the same serovar shows that the cases spread from one source.

skills.title: Practical skill: investigating a focus of food poisoning

items: **Epidemiological history:** who ate what and when; the number of cases; the **incubation period** and the dominant signs (vomiting or diarrhea; whether there are neurological signs).
**Collecting material:** from patients — vomit, gastric lavage, stool, blood (if a generalized form is suspected); **remains of the suspect product**, hand swabs from the people who prepared it.
**Choosing the direction:**

blocks.text: - short incubation + predominant vomiting → **staphylococcal enterotoxin**;
- 12–48 hours + fever + diarrhea → **salmonellosis** and other toxicoinfections;
- neurological signs (vision, swallowing, flaccid paralysis), no fever → **botulism**;
- bloody diarrhea → Shigella, Campylobacter, EHEC.

items: **Inoculation:** enrichment medium + Endo/Ploskirev/bismuth sulfite agar; salt egg-yolk agar for staphylococcus; when botulism is suspected — anaerobic culture and **detecting the toxin**.
**Identification and serological identification**, antibiogram.
**Conclusion:** the causative agent, the probable source and factor; sanitary and epidemiological measures.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: 3 hours after a wedding feast, several guests developed severe nausea and repeated vomiting; there was almost no fever and little diarrhea. Among the dishes was a creamy dessert.
cases.ask: What is the probable cause, and what points to it?
cases.answer: Intoxication with **staphylococcal enterotoxin**: a very short incubation period, predominant vomiting, absence of fever and a product such as cream — the typical picture. In the examination, vomit, remains of the product and hand swabs of the people who prepared it are cultured; the toxin can be detected.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: In a family, 20 hours after eating home-canned preserves, several people developed “a net before the eyes,” double vision and difficulty swallowing; no fever, consciousness intact.
cases.ask: What are the diagnosis, the first measure and the laboratory tactics?
cases.answer: Botulism. The first measure is to give **antitoxic serum as early as possible** (by a physician) and to monitor breathing. Laboratory: **detecting the toxin** (neutralization test/ELISA) in blood serum, gastric lavage, stool and the remains of the product, anaerobic culture and PCR.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: 18 hours after eating an undercooked egg dish, a patient developed fever, abdominal pain and diarrhea. On stool culture lactose-negative colonies; in Kligler, gas and H₂S positive.
cases.ask: What are the probable causative agent and the final confirmation?
cases.answer: Salmonella (probably *S.* Enteritidis). The final confirmation is serological identification with O and H sera according to the **Kauffmann–White scheme**; the basis of treatment is rehydration.

topics.title: Zoonotic infections: anthrax and brucellosis. Plague and tularemia

goals.text: To know the concept of zoonotic infections and their epidemiological features;
to explain the biological properties, pathogenesis and clinical forms of the causative agents of anthrax and brucellosis;
to master the algorithm of laboratory diagnosis of these infections and the biosafety requirements;
Independent work: to know the diseases caused by *Yersinia pestis* and *Francisella tularensis*, their diagnosis and prophylaxis.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The causative agents of anthrax, plague and tularemia belong to the group of **especially dangerous infections**. When they are suspected, the material is collected in a special manner, transported in a prescribed container, and processed **in specially authorized laboratories** under a high biosafety regime; the health system is notified immediately. Such cultures are not handled in an ordinary diagnostic laboratory.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Anthrax toxin is **three-component**: PA is the carrier and “door-opener,” while LF and EF are the effector parts. The protective antigen (PA) is the main component of vaccines.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The **Ascoli reaction** is the classic way of making a diagnosis in material in which the causative agent cannot be grown or is dead (dried skin, wool, old meat): the antigen persists because it is heat-stable.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: To remember brucellosis: **“milk + undulant fever + sweating + joint pain”**; in serology — **Wright** (tube, titer) and **Huddleson** (slide, rapid).

blocks.text: **Zoonoses** are diseases whose source of infection is **animals**. A human is often the “final host,” and person-to-person transmission is limited or absent.
**Routes of transmission:** direct contact (a sick animal, its skin and wool products), alimentary (meat, milk), airborne (dust, aerosol), vector-borne (arthropods).
**Occupational risk groups:** livestock breeders, shepherds, veterinary workers, workers at meat-processing plants and in the hide-and-wool industry, hunters, laboratory workers.

parts.text: The causative agents of anthrax, plague and tularemia belong to the group of **especially dangerous infections**. When they are suspected, the material is collected in a special manner, transported in a prescribed container, and processed **in specially authorized laboratories** under a high biosafety regime; the health system is notified immediately. Such cultures are not handled in an ordinary diagnostic laboratory.

blocks.text: **Morphology:** a large gram-positive rod (1–1.5 × 3–10 µm) with blunt (“cut-off”) ends; in smears it forms **chains** (“bamboo cane”); **nonmotile** (rare among bacilli); it forms a **capsule** (polypeptide) in the body and a **central spore** in the external environment.

blocks.label: Figure 24.1
blocks.caption: The anthrax bacillus: large gram-positive rods, encapsulated chains in a blood smear. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **Cultural properties:** aerobe; grows on ordinary media; the colonies are **R-form** — rough, with thread-like projections at the edges (“**lion’s mane**” or “Medusa head” appearance); in gelatin it grows in the shape of an **“inverted fir tree.”**
**Pathogenicity factors:**

items: **Capsule** (polypeptide) — antiphagocytic;

**Exotoxin** — three-component: **protective antigen (PA)**, **lethal factor (LF)** and **edema factor (EF)**. Each alone is inactive; the combination of two acts: PA + EF → edema, PA + LF → tissue necrosis and death.

parts.text: Anthrax toxin is **three-component**: PA is the carrier and “door-opener,” while LF and EF are the effector parts. The protective antigen (PA) is the main component of vaccines.

blocks.text: **Clinical forms:**

items: **Cutaneous form (the most frequent)** — a spot at the entry site → papule → vesicle → it bursts, leaving a **black eschar ulcer (carbuncle)** in the center; edema around it; **painlessness** is characteristic;
**Pulmonary form** — inhalation of spores; severe course;
**Intestinal form** — from eating infected meat; severe course.

blocks.text: **Laboratory diagnosis:**

items: **Material:** discharge from the ulcer and fluid under the eschar, sputum, stool, blood; material from dead animals; samples of skin, wool and meat.
**Bacterioscopy** — Gram stain and capsule stain: encapsulated, blunt-ended chains.
**Bacteriological** — culture, colony appearance (R-form), nonmotility, the “string of pearls” test (under the action of penicillin the cells become spherical), **susceptibility to bacteriophage**.
**Biological test** — in a laboratory animal (in special laboratories).

**Ascoli precipitation reaction** — detecting the heat-stable antigen in materials such as **skin, wool and meat**; the material is boiled (the antigen persists even if the bacteria are dead), then a ring reaction is set up with precipitating serum.
**Skin allergy test (anthraxin)** and PCR.

blocks.label: Figure 24.2
blocks.caption: Scheme of the microbiological examination in anthrax: bacterioscopic, bacteriological, biological and serological examinations. Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

parts.text: The **Ascoli reaction** is the classic way of making a diagnosis in material in which the causative agent cannot be grown or is dead (dried skin, wool, old meat): the antigen persists because it is heat-stable.

blocks.text: **Prophylaxis:** veterinary control and vaccination of livestock, destruction of material from sick animals by the prescribed procedure, vaccination of risk groups (live vaccine), occupational hygiene.
**Causative agents:** *Brucella melitensis* (sheep, goats — the most pathogenic for humans), *B. abortus* (cattle), *B. suis* (pigs), *B. canis* (dogs).
**Morphology:** very small gram-negative coccobacilli; nonmotile, nonspore-forming; with a microcapsule.

blocks.label: Figure 24.3
blocks.caption: Brucellae — very small gram-negative coccobacilli. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **Cultural properties:** aerobes, **fastidious and slow-growing** — growth may take 5–30 days; some species (*B. abortus*) require **additional CO₂ (5–10%)** for growth; they are grown in liver-broth and special media.

**Routes of transmission:** unpasteurized milk and dairy products (especially fresh cheese, cream), direct contact with a sick animal and its birth products, aerosol (in laboratories and on livestock farms).

**Pathogenesis:** brucellae spread through the lymphatic pathways and **live inside macrophages** (incomplete phagocytosis) → **granulomas** form in organs of the reticuloendothelial system (lymph nodes, liver, spleen, bone marrow) → repeated release into the blood produces **undulant fever**. Delayed-type hypersensitivity develops.

**Clinical picture:** prolonged **undulant fever**, profuse sweating, joint and muscle pain, enlargement of the lymph nodes, liver and spleen; when it becomes chronic — arthritis, spondylitis, damage to the nervous system and reproductive organs.
**Laboratory diagnosis:**

items: **Bacteriological** — blood and bone marrow aspirate are cultured; because growth is slow, it is observed for **up to 30 days**. Because of the high hazard it is done only in a special laboratory.
**Serological (the main one in practice):**

blocks.text: - **Wright reaction** — extended agglutination (in a tube), with a titer;
- **Huddleson reaction** — rapid screening on a glass slide;
- **Coombs reaction** — detecting incomplete antibodies (in the chronic form);
- ELISA (IgM/IgG) — a modern method.

items: **Skin allergy test (Bürnet test)** — with brucellin; it shows sensitization and is important in the chronic form.
**PCR** — fast and safer.

parts.text: To remember brucellosis: **“milk + undulant fever + sweating + joint pain”**; in serology — **Wright** (tube, titer) and **Huddleson** (slide, rapid).

Working with a Brucella culture is **highly hazardous for laboratory staff**: it is transmitted by aerosol. Therefore when brucellosis is suspected the laboratory is warned in advance and the work is carried out under a special regime.

blocks.text: 5.1. Plague — *Yersinia pestis*
**Morphology:** a gram-negative, short, oval rod; it **stains bipolarly** (both ends darker — a “safety pin” appearance, clearly seen with Romanowsky–Giemsa); nonmotile, encapsulated.

blocks.label: Figure 24.4
blocks.caption: The causative agent of plague — gram-negative rods that stain bipolarly. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **Epidemiology:** a natural-focal, **vector-borne** infection; the reservoir is rodents, the vector is **fleas**; in the pulmonary form it spreads **from person to person by the airborne route**.
**Pathogenicity factors:** the F1 capsular antigen, the V and W antigens, “plague toxin,” plasminogen activator, LPS; they ensure resistance to phagocytosis and rapid spread.

**Clinical forms:** **bubonic** (the most frequent — severe inflammation of the lymph node nearest the entry site and a painful “bubo”), septic and **pulmonary** form (the most dangerous, spreading rapidly).

**Diagnosis:** bubo aspirate, sputum, blood, lymph nodes → bacterioscopy (bipolar rods) → culture → typing with phages → biological test; rapid methods — immunofluorescence, antigen tests, PCR. All work is done under the **especially dangerous infection** regime.
**Prophylaxis:** epidemiological surveillance in natural foci, measures against rodents and fleas, vaccination of risk groups, quarantine measures.
5.2. Tularemia — *Francisella tularensis*
**Morphology:** a very small gram-negative coccobacillus; nonmotile, encapsulated.

blocks.label: Figure 24.5
blocks.caption: The causative agent of tularemia (*Francisella tularensis*) — very small gram-negative coccobacilli. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **Epidemiology:** the reservoir is rodents and hares; the routes of transmission are **very varied**: vector-borne (ticks, horseflies), contact (the skin of a sick animal), alimentary (contaminated water and food), airborne (dust). **The infectious dose is very low** — which is why it poses a high risk for laboratory staff.
**Features:** does not grow on ordinary medium — it requires a special medium **supplemented with cysteine/cystine** (a medium enriched with egg yolk); lives intracellularly.
**Clinical forms:** bubonic, ulceroglandular, oculoglandular, oropharyngeal (anginal-bubonic), pulmonary and generalized forms.
**Diagnosis (mainly by indirect methods):**

items: **Serological** — agglutination reaction (Wright type), PHA, ELISA; the dynamics of the titer in paired sera;
**Skin allergy test (tularin)** — becomes positive early (from day 3–5 of the illness);
**PCR** and antigen tests;
**Bacteriological method** — only in special laboratories.

blocks.text: **Prophylaxis:** surveillance in natural foci, protection of water sources, measures against rodents, vaccination of risk groups with the **live vaccine**.

skills.title: Practical skill: procedure when a zoonosis is suspected

items: **Establish the epidemiological history:** occupation, contact with animals, consumption of unpasteurized milk and fresh cheese, hunting, a tick or flea bite, travel to a natural focus.
**Assess the clinical syndrome:** a painless black-eschar ulcer → anthrax; undulant fever + sweating + joint pain → brucellosis; acute fever + a painful bubo → plague/tularemia.
**Warn the laboratory in advance** — this is essential for staff safety and helps to plan the examination correctly.
**Collect the material in the prescribed manner:** a sealed, unbreakable container, double packaging, a clearly completed requisition.
**Choose the examination method:** in especially dangerous infections preference is given to **serological and molecular** methods; culture work is done only in a specially authorized laboratory.
**Notify the epidemiological service** and begin the measures for the focus.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A patient who works at a hide-and-wool plant has a painless sore on the hand: a black eschar in the center, vesicles around it and wide edema. The smear shows large gram-positive, blunt-ended, chain-forming rods.
cases.ask: What are the probable diagnosis and the laboratory tactics?
cases.answer: Cutaneous anthrax. The laboratory is **warned in advance**; the material is collected in a special manner. The examination: bacterioscopy, culture and identification in a special laboratory, the **Ascoli reaction** on raw-material samples, PCR. The epidemiological service is notified.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A livestock breeder has had undulant fever for 2 months, profuse sweating and joint pain; the spleen and liver are enlarged. The patient ate cheese made from fresh (unpasteurized) milk.
cases.ask: What should be considered, and which examinations are informative?
cases.answer: Brucellosis. In practice **serological methods** are the main ones: Huddleson (rapid screening), **Wright** (with a titer), Coombs and ELISA; the skin allergy **Bürnet** test; PCR. A blood culture is possible but slow and hazardous — only in a special laboratory.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A patient who hunted in a natural focus developed acute fever and a painful enlarged lymph node in the armpit.
cases.ask: Which infections should be excluded, and what is the first measure?
cases.answer: Plague and tularemia should be excluded (both produce a bubo). The first measure is to **notify the laboratory and the epidemiological service immediately** and to collect the material in a special manner; the examination — bacterioscopy (bipolar rods), rapid antigen tests and PCR, and in tularemia additionally serology and the tularin test. Treatment is not delayed.

topics.title: Dermatovenereal infections: causative agents of syphilis and gonorrhea. Chlamydiosis, mycoplasmosis, trichomoniasis, chancroid

goals.text: To know the biological properties of the causative agents of syphilis and gonorrhea;
to explain the periods of the course of syphilis and the laboratory method suited to each period;
to master the serological reactions (nontreponemal and treponemal tests) and their interpretation;
to know the diagnostic tactics in the acute and chronic forms of gonorrhea;
Independent work: to know the description and diagnosis of urogenital chlamydiosis, mycoplasmosis, trichomoniasis and chancroid.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **“In the primary period — the microscope; in the secondary and later periods — serology.”** This is the basic rule of syphilis diagnosis.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Rule of interpretation: **screening — nontreponemal; confirmation — treponemal; monitoring of treatment — the dynamics of the nontreponemal test titer.** If only the treponemal test is positive, it may also be a past (treated) infection.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The gonococcus dies quickly after the material is collected, so inoculation is done **as quickly as possible** (at the patient’s bedside or in transport medium). The material must not be cooled.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Two Neisseria: **Gonococcus — Glucose** (only); **Meningococcus — glucose + Maltose**. The gonococcus is noncapsulated, the meningococcus is encapsulated.

blocks.text: **Morphology:** a delicate spirochete; **8–14 uniform, regular coils**; length 6–14 µm, thickness 0.1–0.2 µm. It takes up ordinary dyes poorly (its name means “pale”); with **Romanowsky–Giemsa** it stains pale pink, with **Morozov’s method (silver impregnation)** black-brown. Its motility is varied: rotating, flexing, undulating.

blocks.label: Figure 25.1
blocks.caption: *T. pallidum* in a smear from a hard chancre and in dark field: bacterioscopic methods in syphilis. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **Cultural properties:** **it does not grow on artificial nutrient media** (pathogenic strains). Therefore the classic bacteriological method is not used; diagnosis rests on **bacterioscopy and serology**.
**Resistance:** very unstable in the external environment — sensitive to drying, high temperature, antiseptics and soap; it survives briefly when moisture and temperature are maintained.
**Routes of transmission:** mainly **sexual**; also contact-household (rare), **transplacental (congenital syphilis)**, through blood (transfusion, syringe).

parts.text: **“In the primary period — the microscope; in the secondary and later periods — serology.”** This is the basic rule of syphilis diagnosis.

blocks.text: 2.2. Serological diagnosis
**Two groups of tests:**

items: **Nontreponemal (lipoidal) tests** — **MPR, RPR, VDRL**; cardiolipin is used as the antigen; they detect **reagins** in the body.

blocks.text: - *Advantage:* cheap, fast, **quantitative (with a titer)** — therefore used for **monitoring the effect of treatment** (the titer should fall);
- *Disadvantage:* **false-positive** results are possible (pregnancy, autoimmune diseases, some infections, old age).

items: **Treponemal tests** — **TPHA, ELISA, immunoblot, IF**; the antigen is the treponeme itself or its proteins.

blocks.text: - *Advantage:* high specificity — a **confirmatory test**;
- *Disadvantage:* they remain positive for many years even after treatment → **unsuitable for monitoring treatment**.

parts.text: Rule of interpretation: **screening — nontreponemal; confirmation — treponemal; monitoring of treatment — the dynamics of the nontreponemal test titer.** If only the treponemal test is positive, it may also be a past (treated) infection.

blocks.text: **The Wassermann reaction (CFT)** — the historical classic method; it has now been replaced by modern tests.

blocks.label: Figure 25.2
blocks.caption: Scheme of the bacterioscopic methods in syphilis: taking material from a hard chancre, dark field, the Romanowsky–Giemsa and Morozov methods, immunofluorescence, PCR. Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

blocks.text: **Morphology:** a gram-negative **diplococcus** with concave facing sides (“coffee bean”); in **acute gonorrhea it lies inside leukocytes in the pus** — a classic diagnostic sign. Nonmotile, nonspore-forming; it has pili and a microcapsule.

blocks.label: Figure 25.3
blocks.caption: Gonococci: gram-negative diplococci inside leukocytes in a pus smear. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **Cultural properties:** a fastidious aerobe; **serum or chocolate agar**, **5–10% CO₂**; **oxidase positive**; it ferments **only glucose** (the difference from the meningococcus — topic 18). Very unstable in the external environment (sensitive to drying and cold).

**Pathogenicity factors:** **pili** (adhesion; because of antigenic variability immunity is not durable), **Opa proteins**, LPS (lipooligosaccharide), **IgA protease**, beta-lactamases (in some strains).

**Clinical picture:** in men — acute urethritis (purulent discharge, pain on urination); in women — often **with few or no symptoms** (cervicitis), so it is detected late and causes complications (pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, ectopic pregnancy); in newborns — **blennorrhea** (conjunctivitis of the eye); in the disseminated form — arthritis, skin rash.
**Laboratory diagnosis:**

items: **Material:** a urethral, cervical canal, rectal or throat swab, conjunctival discharge.
**Bacterioscopy** — Gram and methylene blue: **gram-negative diplococci inside leukocytes**. Sensitivity is high in men with acute urethritis; low in women and in the chronic form.
**Bacteriological** — serum/chocolate agar + CO₂; identification: oxidase, carbohydrates (glucose only), **antibiogram** (important because resistance is widespread).
**Molecular (NAAT/PCR)** — currently the most sensitive method, especially in women, in the chronic form and in extragenital localization; it can also be done on urine.
**In the chronic form** — provocation methods (physiological, chemical, dietary) were used; in current practice **molecular methods** have largely taken their place.

parts.text: The gonococcus dies quickly after the material is collected, so inoculation is done **as quickly as possible** (at the patient’s bedside or in transport medium). The material must not be cooled.
Two Neisseria: **Gonococcus — Glucose** (only); **Meningococcus — glucose + Maltose**. The gonococcus is noncapsulated, the meningococcus is encapsulated.

blocks.text: 4.1. Urogenital chlamydiosis
**Causative agent:** *Chlamydia trachomatis* (serovars D–K) — an obligate intracellular parasite (topic 4).

**Clinical picture:** often **asymptomatic or with few symptoms** — a “silent” infection; urethritis, cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, reactive arthritis; conjunctivitis and pneumonia in newborns.

**The key to diagnosis:** the material must contain **epithelial cells** (a scraping, not the discharge itself). Methods: **PCR/NAAT (the main one)**, direct immunofluorescence, ELISA; cell culture — the gold standard, but rarely used in practice.
4.2. Urogenital mycoplasmosis
**Causative agents:** *Mycoplasma hominis*, *M. genitalium*, *Ureaplasma urealyticum*.

**Features:** no cell wall → **naturally resistant to beta-lactams** (topic 4); some species also occur in the normal flora, so finding them does not always mean disease. *M. genitalium* — a definite pathogen (urethritis, cervicitis).
**Diagnosis:** **PCR** (the main one), growth in special media (by urease and arginine), quantitative assessment.
4.3. Trichomoniasis
**Causative agent:** *Trichomonas vaginalis* — a flagellated protozoan; pear-shaped, with 4 free flagella and an undulating membrane; **it does not form cysts**.

blocks.label: Figure 25.4
blocks.caption: *Trichomonas vaginalis* — a flagellated, pear-shaped protozoan (under the electron microscope). Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **Clinical picture:** in women — foamy, yellowish-green discharge, itching; in men often asymptomatic (carriage).
**Diagnosis:** **warm wet mount** — seeing the motile parasite immediately (topic 4); a stained smear (Romanowsky–Giemsa), culture in special medium, **PCR** (the most sensitive), antigen tests.
4.4. Chancroid
**Causative agent:** *Haemophilus ducreyi* — a gram-negative coccobacillus; in smears it lies as a **“school of fish” or in chains**.

**Clinical picture:** a **painful**, soft ulcer with a purulent base and painful suppurating lymphadenitis — these signs are decisive in differential diagnosis from the **hard chancre of syphilis** (painless, dense).
**Diagnosis:** a smear from the ulcer discharge (Gram), culture on specially enriched medium (fastidious, difficult), PCR.

skills.title: Practical skill: the examination algorithm when syphilis is suspected

items: **Determine the clinical period:** ulcer (primary), rash (secondary), late signs (tertiary).

**In the primary period:** cleanse the ulcer with physiological saline and take tissue fluid from its base → **examine it immediately in dark field** (a live, unstained preparation). If necessary — PCR.
**Serology:** the **nontreponemal test (MPR/RPR)** — screening, **with a titer**; if the result is positive or the clinical suspicion is strong — confirm with the **treponemal test (TPHA/ELISA)**.
**Interpret the result:**

blocks.text: - nontreponemal (+) and treponemal (+) → active or past infection (assessed with the clinical picture and history);
- nontreponemal (+), treponemal (−) → probably a **false positive**;
- nontreponemal (−), treponemal (+) → past/treated infection or the late period.

items: **Monitoring of treatment:** only by the dynamics of the **nontreponemal test titer**.
**Epidemiological work:** examination and registration of sexual partners — by the set procedure.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A patient has a painless ulcer with firm edges on the genitals and painless enlargement of a regional lymph node. MPR is negative.
cases.ask: Can the diagnosis be ruled out? What should be done?
cases.answer: No. At the beginning of primary syphilis serology may still be negative (the “seronegative” stage). **Dark-field** microscopy (or PCR) of the ulcer discharge is performed and serology is repeated at the set time.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: On a screening examination RPR is positive (at a low titer) and TPHA is negative. The patient has no clinical signs of syphilis; she is pregnant.
cases.ask: How should the result be interpreted?
cases.answer: Probably a **false-positive** nontreponemal result (pregnancy is one of the known causes). Because the confirmatory treponemal test is negative, a diagnosis of syphilis is not made; follow-up and, if necessary, repeat testing are carried out by the set procedure.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A male patient has acute purulent urethritis. Gram-negative diplococci were found inside leukocytes in the smear.
cases.ask: What are the preliminary diagnosis and the next step?
cases.answer: Gonorrhea (gonococcal urethritis). The next step is culture (serum/chocolate agar, CO₂) and an **antibiogram** (because resistance is widespread), and PCR to exclude chlamydia; examination of sexual partners.

topics.title: Vector-borne infections: rickettsiae, epidemic typhus, Q fever, relapsing fever borreliae. Lyme disease and leptospirosis

goals.text: To know the concept of vector-borne infections and the feature of natural focality;
to explain the biological properties of rickettsiae and the pathogenesis and diagnosis of epidemic and endemic typhus and of Q fever;
to know the characteristics of borreliae and relapsing fever and the mechanism of “relapse”;
Independent work: to know the causative agents of Lyme disease and leptospirosis and their laboratory diagnosis.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Brill–Zinsser disease** — the recrudescence of epidemic typhus after years: the rickettsiae persist latent in the body and become active when immunity falls. Therefore isolated cases may occur even in a louse-free area.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In rickettsioses, diagnosis rests in practice on **serology and PCR**. The aerosol risk is taken into account when collecting material from the patient and when working in the laboratory.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: In Lyme disease **negative serology in the early stage is normal** — antibodies appear in 2–6 weeks. Therefore, with a typical erythema, treatment is started without waiting for serology (by a physician’s prescription).

blocks.text: **Vector-borne infections** are diseases in which the causative agent is transmitted by **arthropods (vectors)**. Vectors: lice, fleas, ticks, mosquitoes, horseflies.
**Two groups:**

items: **Anthroponoses** — the source is a human (epidemic typhus, epidemic relapsing fever);
**Zoonoses (natural-focal)** — the source is animals (endemic typhus, Lyme disease, tick-borne relapsing fever, Q fever).

blocks.text: **Natural focality** (the doctrine of E.N. Pavlovsky) — the causative agent, the vector and the reservoir animals circulate in a certain landscape even without human participation; a person falls ill on entering the focus.
**Rickettsiae** (topic 4) are small, pleomorphic gram-negative bacteria; **obligate intracellular parasites** (they multiply mainly in endothelial cells); they do not grow on artificial media.

Causative agent

Vector/transmission
rows: **Body louse**; not by the bite — the louse’s feces are rubbed into scratched skin

blocks.title: Table 26.1. Main rickettsial infections

blocks.text: **Pathogenesis of epidemic typhus:** the rickettsiae multiply in the **endothelium** of blood vessels → the vessel wall is damaged, thrombi and **vasculitis** develop → a skin rash (roseolar-petechial), damage to the nervous system and internal organs, severe intoxication.

**Clinical picture:** acute onset, high fever, severe headache, insomnia, excitement; from day 4–5 a **roseolar-petechial rash** (on the trunk and the inner surfaces of the limbs); cardiovascular and nervous system disturbances.

parts.text: **Brill–Zinsser disease** — the recrudescence of epidemic typhus after years: the rickettsiae persist latent in the body and become active when immunity falls. Therefore isolated cases may occur even in a louse-free area.

blocks.text: **The particularity of Q fever:** *C. burnetii* is **highly resistant** in the external environment (it forms a spore-like form); it is transmitted mainly by the **airborne route** (dust, animal birth products), a rash is usually absent; the clinical picture — fever, atypical pneumonia, hepatitis; in the chronic form, endocarditis.
**Laboratory diagnosis of rickettsioses:**

items: **Serological (the main one)** — CFT, **PHA**, **ELISA** (IgM/IgG); the dynamics of the titer in paired sera. The historical method — the **Weil–Felix reaction** (a cross-reaction with *Proteus* OX antigens; low specificity, no longer used in practice).
**PCR** — in blood and biopsy material; important in the early period.
**Bacterioscopy** — Romanowsky–Giemsa, the **Zdrodovsky** method (rickettsiae red, the cell cytoplasm blue).
**Isolating the pathogen** — chick embryo, cell culture, laboratory animal; because of the **high hazard** only in special laboratories.

parts.text: In rickettsioses, diagnosis rests in practice on **serology and PCR**. The aerosol risk is taken into account when collecting material from the patient and when working in the laboratory.

blocks.text: **Prophylaxis:** louse control and sanitation, epidemiological surveillance in the focus; in Q fever — veterinary control of livestock, pasteurization of milk, occupational protection.

**Morphology:** *Borrelia* — a group of spirochetes; **3–8 large, irregular coils**; stains **blue-violet** with Romanowsky–Giemsa (the spirochete that takes ordinary dyes best — so it is visible in a blood smear).

blocks.label: Figure 26.1
blocks.caption: Borreliae — large spirochetes with irregular coils (blood smear). Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

head: Feature
**Epidemic (lice)**
**Endemic (ticks)**
blocks.title: Table 26.2. The two forms of relapsing fever

blocks.text: **The “relapse” mechanism:** during the fever period borreliae are numerous in the blood; the body produces antibodies against them and they disappear (the apyrexia period). But a new population with a **changed antigenic structure (antigenic variation)** multiplies and produces the next wave of fever. For this reason the disease runs with **recurrent attacks of fever**.

parts.text: In relapsing fever the **blood smear is taken at the peak of fever** — exactly when borreliae are numerous in the blood. During apyrexia the smear is negative.

blocks.text: **Laboratory diagnosis:**

items: **Bacterioscopic (the main one)** — a **thick drop** and a thin blood smear taken **at the peak of fever**, stained with Romanowsky–Giemsa; live borreliae can also be seen in dark field.
**Biological test** — was used to distinguish the endemic form from the epidemic form (infecting mice).
**Serological and molecular** methods — additional.

blocks.text: **Causative agent:** the *Borrelia burgdorferi* group; the vector is **Ixodes ticks**; the reservoir is rodents and large mammals; a natural-focal zoonosis.
**Clinical stages:**

items: **Early localized** — at the site of the tick bite a **migrating annular erythema** (a spot with a pale center and red edge that keeps expanding) — the most characteristic sign;
**Early disseminated** — after several weeks to months: the nervous system (neuroborreliosis — neuritis, meningitis), the heart (atrioventricular block), migrating joint and muscle pain;
**Late (chronic)** — chronic arthritis, acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans, chronic damage to the nervous system.

blocks.text: **Diagnosis:**

items: **If there is a typical erythema — the diagnosis is made clinically**, and serology is not awaited (antibodies may not yet be present in the early stage);
**In later stages — two-tier serology:** first **ELISA (screening)**, and with a positive or equivocal result **immunoblot (confirmation)** (topic 14);
PCR — important in joint fluid and biopsy material;
Culture — difficult and rarely used in practice.

parts.text: In Lyme disease **negative serology in the early stage is normal** — antibodies appear in 2–6 weeks. Therefore, with a typical erythema, treatment is started without waiting for serology (by a physician’s prescription).

blocks.text: **Causative agent:** *Leptospira interrogans* — a delicate spirochete; **very many fine coils**, with hooked ends (**S, C or “S” letter** appearance); highly motile.

**Epidemiology:** a natural-focal zoonosis; the reservoir is rodents (mainly rats), dogs, pigs and cattle. Transmission: **through water** (swimming, working in an irrigation ditch), and through soil and food contaminated with animal urine; the pathogen enters through **mucous membranes and damaged skin**.

**Clinical picture:** acute fever, severe **muscle (especially calf) pain**, redness of the conjunctiva; in the severe form — **jaundice, renal failure, hemorrhagic syndrome** (Vasiliev–Weil disease).
**Diagnosis — depends on the period:**

head: Period
Material
Method
rows: Seeing in dark field, culture, PCR
**Microscopic agglutination test (the gold standard)**, ELISA; paired sera
blocks.title: Table 26.3. Choice of material and method in leptospirosis

blocks.text: **Additional:** leptospirae grow slowly in special liquid media (weeks), so culture gives its result late; for staining, Romanowsky–Giemsa and **silver impregnation (Morozov)** are used.
**Prophylaxis:** rodent control, protection of water bodies and water supply, occupational protective equipment, vaccination on indication (animals are also vaccinated).

skills.title: Practical skill: examination when a vector-borne infection is suspected

items: **Epidemiological history:** travel to a natural focus, **a tick/louse/flea bite**, contact with livestock, swimming in a water body, occupation.

**Determine the syndrome:** fever + rash → rickettsiosis; **recurrent waves of fever** → relapsing fever; **migrating erythema** at the site of a tick bite → Lyme disease; fever + calf muscle pain + jaundice → leptospirosis; fever + atypical pneumonia + contact with livestock → Q fever.
**Collect the material at the right time:**

blocks.text: - in relapsing fever — **a thick drop and smear at the peak of fever**;
- in leptospirosis — **blood** in week 1, **urine** from week 2, **serum** in parallel;
- in rickettsioses — **paired sera** and PCR in the early period.

items: **Choose the method:** microscopy (borrelia, leptospira), serology (rickettsiosis, leptospirosis, Lyme disease), PCR (informative in all in the early period).
**Safety:** an aerosol and contact risk when working with rickettsiae and leptospirae; warn the laboratory.
**Epidemiological measure:** identifying the focus, vector control, monitoring of contacts.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A patient had a high fever for 4 days, then 7 days of normal temperature, and the fever rose again. In a blood smear taken at the peak of fever, large spirochetes with irregular coils, stained blue-violet with Romanowsky–Giemsa, were found.
cases.ask: What is the diagnosis, and why was the timing of the smear important?
cases.answer: Relapsing fever (borreliae). Borreliae are numerous in the blood **precisely at the peak of fever**; during apyrexia the smear is negative. The waves of fever are explained by antigenic variation.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A patient who worked in an irrigation ditch in summer developed acute fever and severe calf muscle pain 5 days ago; now jaundice and reduced urine output have been added.
cases.ask: What are the probable diagnosis and the material suited to the period of the disease?
cases.answer: Leptospirosis (severe form). In week 1 — **blood** (dark field, culture, PCR), from week 2 — **urine**; in parallel, the **microscopic agglutination test** in serum (paired sera).

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: 10 days after a rest in the forest, a patient developed at the tick bite site an expanding, pale-centered annular red spot. ELISA is negative.
cases.ask: Can the diagnosis be ruled out?
cases.answer: No. In the early stage of Lyme disease antibodies may not yet have formed. A **typical migrating erythema** is sufficient basis for a clinical diagnosis; treatment is started by a physician without waiting for serology.

topics.title: RNA viruses — causative agents of respiratory disease: orthomyxoviruses, paramyxoviruses, coronaviruses

goals.text: To know the structure, antigens and mechanisms of variability of the influenza virus;
to explain the properties of the paramyxoviruses (parainfluenza, measles, mumps, RS virus) and of coronaviruses;
to master the algorithm of collecting material and of virological, serological and molecular diagnosis in respiratory viral infections;
Independent work: to know the current problems of avian and swine influenza, RS virus and rhinoviruses.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Drift — a small change (epidemic), shift — a big jump (pandemic).** Shift occurs only in **type A**, because it also circulates in animals and creates conditions for reassortment.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The main danger of influenza is **secondary bacterial pneumonia**, especially in the elderly, in pregnant women and in people with chronic diseases. Therefore a renewed worsening after influenza (a second wave of fever) always demands attention.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **RS virus — “Syncytium”**: both its name and its main sign in cell culture. The main cause of bronchiolitis in infants.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The clinical picture of respiratory viruses is largely similar; **only the laboratory determines the type**. Therefore in practice **multiplex PCR panels**, which cover several causative agents at once, are often used.

blocks.text: **Structure:** a medium-sized (80–120 nm), **enveloped (with a supercapsid)** virus; the genome is **single-stranded, negative-sense, segmented RNA** (8 segments in types A and B). The nucleocapsid has **helical** symmetry.

blocks.label: Figure 27.1
blocks.caption: The structure of the influenza virus: the envelope (supercapsid), hemagglutinin and neuraminidase spikes, matrix protein, segmented RNA and nucleoprotein. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **Main antigens:**

items: **Internal antigens** — nucleoprotein (NP) and matrix protein (M): they determine the **type (A, B, C)** and are stable;
**Surface antigens (spikes):**

blocks.text: - **Hemagglutinin (H)** — provides binding to the cell receptor (sialic acid) and agglutinates erythrocytes; **the main protective antigen** — neutralizing antibodies form against it;
- **Neuraminidase (N)** — provides the release of new virions from the cell and their spread through mucus; the target of several antiviral drugs.
**Types:** A (in humans and animals; capable of pandemics), B (mainly in humans; epidemics), C (mild course).
2.1. Mechanisms of variability

head: Mechanism
Meaning
Consequence
rows: Gradual change of H and N through point mutations
Seasonal **epidemics**; the vaccine composition is updated every year
Redistribution of segments (reassortment) when two strains infect one cell, owing to the **segmented genome** — entirely new H and/or N
Risk of **pandemic**: no immunity in the population
blocks.title: Table 27.1. Variability of the influenza virus

parts.text: **Drift — a small change (epidemic), shift — a big jump (pandemic).** Shift occurs only in **type A**, because it also circulates in animals and creates conditions for reassortment.

blocks.text: **Pathogenesis:** the virus multiplies in the ciliated epithelium of the respiratory tract → epithelial necrosis and disruption of the clearance mechanism → viremia and intoxication (toxic effect, increased vascular permeability) → conditions for **secondary bacterial complications**.

**Clinical picture:** sudden onset, high fever, severe intoxication (headache, muscle pain), tracheitis (dry cough, retrosternal burning); catarrhal signs are relatively few. Complications: viral and **bacterial pneumonia** (often pneumococcus, *S. aureus*, *H. influenzae*), otitis, sinusitis, myocarditis, encephalopathy.

parts.text: The main danger of influenza is **secondary bacterial pneumonia**, especially in the elderly, in pregnant women and in people with chronic diseases. Therefore a renewed worsening after influenza (a second wave of fever) always demands attention.

blocks.text: 2.2. Diagnosis of influenza

items: **Material:** a nasal and throat swab/wash — **in the first 3 days** of the illness; in severe cases — material from the lower respiratory tract.
**Rapid methods:**

blocks.text: - **PCR (real-time)** — currently the main method: it determines the type and subtype;
- **Immunochromatographic rapid antigen tests** — fast, but less sensitive;
- **Immunofluorescence** — detecting viral antigen in epithelial cells.

items: **Virological method:** infection of a **chick embryo** (into the amniotic/allantoic cavity) or of a cell culture → indication by the **hemagglutination reaction (HA)** → identification by the **hemagglutination inhibition test (HI)** (topic 12). Mainly for epidemiological surveillance and for choosing vaccine strains.
**Serological method:** HI, CFT, ELISA in **paired sera** — a ≥4-fold rise in titer; of retrospective importance.

blocks.text: **Prophylaxis:** an annually updated **seasonal vaccine** (inactivated, subunit or live), vaccination of risk groups; nonspecific measures — hand hygiene, a mask, ventilation.

**General features:** enveloped, **single-stranded, negative-sense, nonsegmented RNA**; helical nucleocapsid. Because it is nonsegmented, **there is no antigenic shift** — so the measles and mumps viruses are antigenically stable and the vaccines are long-lasting.

Salivary glands; complications — orchitis, pancreatitis, meningitis
Forms **syncytia** (multinucleated clumps) in cell culture; has no hemagglutinin

blocks.text: **Diagnosis:** PCR (the main one), antigen tests and immunofluorescence (especially for RS virus), serology (IgM — a fresh infection; important in measles and mumps), isolation in cell culture (CPE — syncytium).
**Prophylaxis:** the **live combined vaccine** against measles, mumps and rubella — in the national immunization schedule; special immunoprophylaxis products exist against RS virus for risk groups.

parts.text: **RS virus — “Syncytium”**: both its name and its main sign in cell culture. The main cause of bronchiolitis in infants.

blocks.text: **Structure:** enveloped, **single-stranded, positive-sense RNA** viruses; the genome is the largest among RNA viruses. The **S (spike) protein** in the envelope forms crown-like projections — hence the name.
**Members:** seasonal coronaviruses (mild ARVI), **SARS-CoV**, **MERS-CoV** and **SARS-CoV-2** (COVID-19).

**Pathogenesis and clinical picture:** the S protein binds to the cell receptor; the epithelium of the respiratory tract and other tissues are damaged. The clinical picture ranges from mild ARVI to severe pneumonia and systemic complications; in severe forms, excessive activation of the immune response and disturbance of the coagulation system are important.
**Diagnosis:**

items: **PCR (real-time)** — the gold standard; material: a nasopharyngeal swab;
**Rapid antigen tests** — convenient for screening, with lower sensitivity;
**Serology (IgM/IgG)** — for assessing past infection and the immune response; not the main method for acute diagnosis;
**Isolation in cell culture** — only in special laboratories.

blocks.text: **Prophylaxis:** vaccination, a mask, hand hygiene, ventilation, isolation measures.

parts.text: The clinical picture of respiratory viruses is largely similar; **only the laboratory determines the type**. Therefore in practice **multiplex PCR panels**, which cover several causative agents at once, are often used.

sections.title: Independent work: Avian and swine influenza, RS virus, rhinoviruses

blocks.text: **Avian influenza (for example, A/H5N1, A/H7N9):** the natural reservoir is wild waterfowl; it is transmitted to humans mainly **by direct contact with sick birds**; person-to-person transmission is limited. It can run with severe lung damage. The main danger is the appearance, as a result of **reassortment**, of a new variant easily transmitted from person to person (antigenic shift).

**Swine influenza (A/H1N1pdm09):** the strain of the 2009 pandemic — the product of **redistribution** of segments of human, swine and avian influenza viruses. It now circulates among the seasonal influenza strains and is included in the seasonal vaccine.
**The pig — the “mixing vessel”:** because pig cells carry receptors for both avian and human influenza viruses, the pig is a favorable environment for reassortment.

**RS virus:** **the main cause of bronchiolitis and pneumonia** in children under 1 year; it causes seasonal rises; immunity is incomplete — reinfection is possible. Diagnosis — antigen tests and PCR; special immunoprophylaxis is used in risk groups.

**Rhinoviruses (*Picornaviridae*):** **nonenveloped**, single-stranded positive RNA; there are more than 100 serotypes — so durable immunity does not form and a person falls ill several times a year. The optimal temperature for multiplication is **33–35 °C** — so they multiply mainly **in the upper respiratory tract** (the nasal mucosa). The most frequent cause of the common cold; diagnosis is usually not required.

parts.text: **Rhinovirus — many serotypes + loves low temperature → a frequently recurring “common cold”; a vaccine is hard to develop.**

skills.title: Practical skill: collecting material for a respiratory virus

items: The material is taken **in the first days of the illness** (best on day 1–3) — viral shedding is highest in this period.

**Nasopharyngeal swab:** the swab is advanced along the nasal passage **to the posterior wall**, held for a few seconds and withdrawn with rotation; a throat swab is taken from the tonsils and the posterior wall.
The swab is placed in **viral transport medium** and its tip is broken off.
The sample is kept at **2–8 °C** and delivered quickly; if prolonged storage is needed, it is frozen by the set procedure (repeated freezing and thawing is prohibited).
On the requisition: the date of onset, vaccination status, travel/contact history.
In the laboratory: PCR (often a multiplex panel), an antigen test where necessary, and in epidemiological surveillance — virological isolation.
**Safety:** aerosols may form — protective equipment and the prescribed regime are observed.
