cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A patient with influenza had his temperature return to normal on day 5, but on day 7 it rose again to 39 °C, the cough worsened with purulent sputum, and focal changes were found on X-ray.
cases.ask: What has happened, and what examination is needed?
cases.answer: **Secondary bacterial pneumonia** (often pneumococcus, *S. aureus*, *H. influenzae*). Examination: sputum culture and **antibiogram**, blood culture; treatment is decided by a physician.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: As part of epidemiological surveillance, the virus from a patient’s material was propagated in a chick embryo; the allantoic fluid agglutinated erythrocytes. When specific serum was added, the agglutination stopped.
cases.ask: Which reactions were set up, and what does the result mean?
cases.answer: First the **hemagglutination reaction (HA)** — an indication that the virus is present; then the **hemagglutination inhibition test (HI)** — the type/subtype of the virus was determined (identification).

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 4-month-old infant has shortness of breath, wheezing and tachypnea; the season is winter. The antigen test on a nasopharyngeal swab was positive, and multinucleated cells (syncytia) formed in cell culture.
cases.ask: Which causative agent, and what is its clinical significance?
cases.answer: **RS virus** — the main cause of bronchiolitis in infants. Treatment is mainly supportive; special immunoprophylaxis products are used in risk groups.

blocks.text: **General features:** very small (22–30 nm), **nonenveloped**, with an icosahedral capsid, **single-stranded, positive-sense RNA** viruses. Because they are nonenveloped they are **resistant** to the external environment, acid and bile acids — which is why most are transmitted by the **fecal-oral** route.

blocks.text: 2.1. Poliomyelitis
**Causative agent:** poliovirus (serotypes 1, 2, 3).
**Transmission:** **fecal-oral** (the main route), less often airborne; the source is a sick person and a virus excretor.
**Pathogenesis (stages):**

items: **Alimentary stage** — the virus multiplies in the lymphoid tissue of the pharynx and intestine (tonsils, Peyer’s patches);
**Viremia** — it enters the blood; in most cases the process ends here;
**Neural stage** — the virus crosses the blood–brain barrier and infects the **motor neurons in the anterior horns of the spinal cord**.

blocks.text: **Clinical forms:** inapparent (asymptomatic, the most frequent), abortive (general infectious signs), meningeal (serous meningitis) and the **paralytic** form — **asymmetric, flaccid (peripheral) paralysis**, often in the legs; sensation is preserved.

parts.text: In poliomyelitis the paralysis is **asymmetric and flaccid**, and **sensation is not impaired** — this is related to the selective damage to the motor neurons.

blocks.text: **Diagnosis:**

items: **Material:** stool (the virus is shed longest there), throat wash, cerebrospinal fluid; paired sera.
**Virological method** — infection of a cell culture → **cytopathic effect** → typing by the neutralization reaction; **molecular typing** to distinguish it from the vaccine strain.
**PCR** — fast and sensitive.
**Serological** — the dynamics of the titer in paired sera by neutralization or ELISA.

blocks.text: **Prophylaxis — two kinds of vaccine:**

head: A vaccine
Type
Advantage
Property
rows: Also gives intestinal (local, IgA) immunity; cheap and easy to administer
In very rare cases vaccine-associated conditions may occur
Safe; also used in the immunocompromised
blocks.title: Table 28.2. Poliomyelitis vaccines

parts.text: In the poliomyelitis eradication program both vaccines are used: OPV interrupts the circulation of the virus, while IPV gives safe individual protection. They are used according to the national immunization schedule.

blocks.text: **Structure:** a **bullet-shaped**, enveloped virus; the genome is **single-stranded, negative-sense, nonsegmented RNA**; helical nucleocapsid; the envelope bears **G glycoprotein** spikes (the main protective antigen, receptor binding).

blocks.label: Figure 28.1
blocks.caption: The structure of the rabies virus: a bullet-shaped virion, supercapsid, G glycoprotein spikes, matrix protein and helical nucleoprotein. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **Epidemiology:** a zoonosis; the source is wild and domestic animals (dog, cat, fox, wolf, bats). Transmission — through **a bite by a sick animal or saliva getting on a mucous membrane**.

**Pathogenesis:** the virus multiplies at the entry site → moves **along peripheral nerves to the center** → multiplies in the central nervous system (especially the hippocampus and brainstem) and causes encephalitis → then spreads **along nerves outward**, including to the **salivary glands** (which is why saliva is infectious).
**Incubation period** — usually 1–3 months; **it is shorter if the bite is near the head and deep**.

**Clinical picture:** a prodromal period (discomfort at the bite site, restlessness) → an excitation period (**hydrophobia** — fear of water and spasm on swallowing, aerophobia, photophobia, excitability) → a paralytic period. Once clinical signs have developed, the disease is considered practically untreatable.
**Morphological sign:** in the cytoplasm of nerve cells **Babes–Negri bodies** (topic 12) — viral inclusions; found on examining brain tissue after death.
**Diagnosis:**

items: **In animals:** examination of brain tissue — immunofluorescence (the standard method), detection of Babes–Negri bodies, PCR;

**In humans (during life):** immunofluorescence on a nuchal skin biopsy, **PCR** on saliva and cerebrospinal fluid, a smear from the cornea; the methods have limited sensitivity, so repeat samples are taken;
After death — examination of brain tissue.

blocks.text: **Emergency prophylaxis (postexposure):** **wash the wound immediately with soap and plenty of water** and treat it with an antiseptic; then, as prescribed, the **vaccine** and, when indicated, **specific immunoglobulin** are used. The animal is placed under observation. All measures are determined by a physician on the basis of the current protocol.

parts.text: In rabies **time is the decisive factor**: prophylaxis must begin before clinical signs appear. Therefore in any case of a bite it is necessary to seek medical help immediately.

sections.title: Hepatitis viruses transmitted by the fecal-oral route

blocks.text: 4.1. Hepatitis A virus (HAV)

**Features:** the family *Picornaviridae* (hepatoviruses); **nonenveloped**, single-stranded positive RNA; **resistant** in the external environment (to acid, bile, drying and the usual disinfection regimes).

blocks.label: Figure 28.2
blocks.caption: The structure of the hepatitis A virus and the papillomavirus (schematic image). Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **Transmission:** **fecal-oral** — contaminated water and food (especially unwashed vegetables and fruit, seafood), contact-household. Viral shedding is **highest before jaundice appears** — so the patient is most infectious until jaundice begins.

**Clinical picture:** the incubation period is 2–6 weeks; a pre-icteric period (fever, loss of appetite, nausea), an icteric period, recovery. In children it often runs **asymptomatically**. It **does not become chronic**, carriage does not develop; acute liver failure is rare.
**Diagnosis:** **anti-HAV IgM** — a sign of acute infection (the main marker); **anti-HAV IgG** — past infection or immunity after vaccination; PCR (stool, blood) — in epidemiological investigation.
**Prophylaxis:** sanitary and hygienic measures (water supply, food control, hand hygiene), the **inactivated vaccine**; immunoglobulin for contacts on indication.
4.2. Hepatitis E virus (HEV)

**Features:** *Hepeviridae*; nonenveloped, single-stranded positive RNA; transmitted by the fecal-oral route, mainly **through water**; some genotypes are zoonotic (pigs and others, via undercooked meat).

**Clinical picture:** resembles hepatitis A; usually does not become chronic (an exception may occur in the severely immunocompromised). **The main feature is a severe course in pregnant women** and a high risk of acute liver failure.
**Diagnosis:** anti-HEV IgM and IgG, PCR (blood, stool).

blocks.text: **General principles:** work with these viruses requires laboratories of the **highest biosafety level**; diagnosis is made mainly by **PCR and antigen tests**; care and isolation measures are carried out according to strictly set protocols. parts.text: In a patient who presents with fever and who has **traveled to an epidemic area** in recent weeks, establishing the travel history is of decisive importance: it makes it possible to consider malaria, hemorrhagic fevers and other imported infections in good time.

skills.title: Practical skill: the sequence of examination when hepatitis is suspected

items: **Clinical and epidemiological information:** jaundice, loss of appetite, darkening of the urine; a link with water/food, travel, parenteral interventions, sexual history.
**Biochemical tests:** transaminases and bilirubin — they confirm liver damage (but do not show the causative agent).
**Marker panel:** **anti-HAV IgM**, **HBsAg** and **anti-HBc IgM**, **anti-HCV**, and if necessary **anti-HEV IgM** (to be viewed together with topic 29).
**Interpret the result:** IgM — an **acute** process; IgG — past infection or immunity.
**Confirmation and assessment:** PCR (viral RNA/DNA), and viral load where necessary.
**Epidemiological measure:** in A and E — examining the source of water and food, monitoring contacts, hygiene rules; reporting by the set procedure.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A child developed asymmetric flaccid paralysis of the leg after a fever; sensation is preserved.
cases.ask: What are the probable diagnosis and the material to be examined?
cases.answer: The paralytic form of poliomyelitis. The material is **stool** (the virus is shed longest there), throat wash, cerebrospinal fluid and paired sera. Methods: virological isolation, **PCR** and molecular typing (to distinguish a wild strain from a vaccine strain). The case is reported by the set procedure.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A patient was bitten on the street by an unknown dog; the wound is in the facial area and is deep.
cases.ask: What is the first measure, and why is it urgent?
cases.answer: **Wash the wound immediately with soap and plenty of water** and treat it with an antiseptic; then the vaccine and, when indicated, specific immunoglobulin are used by the procedure set by a physician. The reason for urgency: with a wound near the head and a deep one, **the incubation period is shortened**, and once clinical signs appear the disease is practically untreatable.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: Several children in a group have jaundice; the common feature is that they drank water from the same place. anti-HAV IgM is positive.
cases.ask: What are the diagnosis, the route of transmission and the measures?
cases.answer: Acute hepatitis A; fecal-oral (waterborne) transmission. Measures: examining and disinfecting the water source, a hygiene regime, monitoring of contacts, vaccination/immunoglobulin on indication, reporting of cases.

goals.text: To know the structure of retroviruses and the particularity of their replication cycle;
to explain the pathogenesis, stages and algorithm of laboratory diagnosis of HIV infection;
to master the properties of the hepatitis B, D and C viruses and the interpretation of their serological markers;
Independent work: to know the causative agents, pathogenesis and laboratory diagnosis of fungal diseases.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Modern antiretroviral therapy targets exactly these stages of the cycle: there are groups of drugs that stop **entry**, **reverse transcriptase**, **integrase** and **protease**. Treatment is given in a combination regimen, determined by a physician.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The **“window period” (serological window)** is the period after infection when antibodies cannot yet be detected. During this period **ELISA may be negative**, but the person is infectious. Therefore after a risky contact the test is **repeated** at set intervals; PCR is used for early detection.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: In an infant born to an HIV-positive mother, **the mother’s IgG antibodies** cross the placenta and may persist up to 18 months. Therefore up to this age the diagnosis is made **not by antibodies but by PCR**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **Only anti-HBs positive → vaccinated.** **anti-HBs + anti-HBc positive → recovered from the disease.** Because the vaccine consists only of HBsAg, core antibodies are not formed after vaccination.

blocks.text: **Retroviruses** (*Retroviridae*) are enveloped viruses containing **two copies of single-stranded positive-sense RNA**; their main feature is the enzyme **reverse transcriptase (revertase)**: it synthesizes DNA from RNA, and this DNA is then **integrated** into the host chromosome (**provirus**).

**HIV (human immunodeficiency virus)** is the causative agent of AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome); there are two types: **HIV-1** (widespread worldwide) and **HIV-2** (mainly West Africa, with a slower course).
**Structure:**

items: **Genome** — two copies of RNA; the main genes: *gag* (internal proteins — p24 and others), *pol* (enzymes: reverse transcriptase, integrase, protease), *env* (envelope glycoproteins — **gp120 and gp41**);
**Conical capsid** (p24 — an important diagnostic antigen);
**Supercapsid** — from the host cell membrane; **gp120** binds to the receptor, **gp41** provides membrane fusion.

blocks.label: Figure 29.1
blocks.caption: The structure of HIV (HIV-1 and HIV-2): the envelope, gp120 and gp41 glycoproteins, matrix protein, p24 capsid protein, RNA and reverse transcriptase. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **Target cells:** **CD4⁺ T lymphocytes** (the main ones), macrophages, dendritic cells, microglia. The virus binds to the **CD4 molecule** (the main receptor) and to **chemokine coreceptors** (CCR5, CXCR4).

**Replication cycle:** adsorption (gp120 + CD4 + coreceptor) → membrane fusion (gp41) → **reverse transcription** (RNA → DNA) → formation of the provirus with the help of **integrase** → transcription and translation → maturation of proteins by **protease** → release by **budding**.

blocks.label: Figure 29.2
blocks.caption: The replicative cycle of HIV: entry into the cell, reverse transcription, integration, formation of new virions. Source: Aliyev Sh.R. et al., 2013.

parts.text: Modern antiretroviral therapy targets exactly these stages of the cycle: there are groups of drugs that stop **entry**, **reverse transcriptase**, **integrase** and **protease**. Treatment is given in a combination regimen, determined by a physician.

blocks.text: **Routes of transmission:** sexual; parenteral (blood, syringe, medical and nonmedical manipulations); **vertical** (pregnancy, delivery, breastfeeding). It is **not transmitted** through household contact, air or insects.

**Pathogenesis:** the virus gradually destroys CD4⁺ cells → cell-mediated immunity is deeply impaired → **opportunistic infections** and tumors develop. Stages of the disease: acute retroviral syndrome → the **latent (asymptomatic) period** (lasting years) → persistent lymphadenopathy → the **AIDS stage**.

**AIDS indicator conditions:** Pneumocystis pneumonia, toxoplasma encephalitis, cryptococcal meningitis, disseminated forms of candidiasis, tuberculosis and atypical mycobacterioses, cytomegalovirus retinitis, Kaposi sarcoma and others.

parts.text: The **“window period” (serological window)** is the period after infection when antibodies cannot yet be detected. During this period **ELISA may be negative**, but the person is infectious. Therefore after a risky contact the test is **repeated** at set intervals; PCR is used for early detection.

In an infant born to an HIV-positive mother, **the mother’s IgG antibodies** cross the placenta and may persist up to 18 months. Therefore up to this age the diagnosis is made **not by antibodies but by PCR**.

blocks.text: **Prophylaxis:** safe sexual behavior, disposable medical instruments and blood safety, programs for preventing mother-to-child transmission, postexposure and preexposure prophylaxis (by a physician’s prescription), early detection and treatment (a person on treatment whose viral load is undetectable does not transmit the infection).
3.1. Hepatitis B virus (HBV)

**Features:** *Hepadnaviridae*; **partially double-stranded DNA**; enveloped; its distinctive enzyme is **DNA polymerase with reverse transcriptase activity**. The complete virion is the **Dane particle**.

blocks.label: Figure 29.4
blocks.caption: The structure of the hepatitis B virus: HBsAg (surface antigen), HBcAg and HBeAg, DNA polymerase, partially double-stranded DNA. Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **Antigens:**

items: **HBsAg** — the surface (Australia) antigen; **the main marker of infection**; the vaccine is made from this antigen;
**HBcAg** — the core antigen; not detected free in the blood, only in liver cells;
**HBeAg** — a marker of active replication and **high infectivity**.

blocks.text: **Transmission:** parenteral (blood, medical manipulations, syringe), **sexual**, **vertical**. The infectious dose is very low, and the virus is resistant in the external environment.

**Clinical picture:** acute hepatitis (often with a gradual onset); in adults in most cases complete recovery, but in a proportion **chronicity**; in newborns and young children the likelihood of chronicity is much higher. In a chronic course — the risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.

head: Marker
Meaning
rows: **Acute** infection (or a flare of chronic infection)
Has met the virus (past or chronic)
blocks.title: Table 29.2. Interpretation of hepatitis B markers

parts.text: **Only anti-HBs positive → vaccinated.** **anti-HBs + anti-HBc positive → recovered from the disease.** Because the vaccine consists only of HBsAg, core antibodies are not formed after vaccination.

blocks.text: 3.2. Hepatitis D virus (HDV)
**Features:** a **defective** virus — it cannot multiply independently and uses **HBsAg** as its envelope. Therefore it occurs only together with HBV:

items: **coinfection** — HBV and HDV are acquired at the same time;
**superinfection** — HDV is added to a chronic HBV carrier; it usually runs more severely and increases the risk of cirrhosis.

blocks.text: **Diagnosis:** anti-HDV (IgM/IgG), HDV RNA (PCR) — tested in HBsAg-positive patients.
**Prophylaxis:** vaccination against hepatitis B — indirectly also protects against D (D does not develop without B).
3.3. Hepatitis C virus (HCV)

**Features:** *Flaviviridae*; enveloped, **single-stranded positive-sense RNA**; high genetic **variability** (many genotypes and quasispecies) — therefore **there is no vaccine** and immunity does not protect.

blocks.label: Figure 29.5
blocks.caption: The structure of adenovirus and hepatitis C virus (schematic image). Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **Transmission:** mainly **parenteral** (blood, syringe, medical manipulations); the sexual and vertical routes are relatively less common.

**Clinical picture:** the acute phase often runs **asymptomatically**; **the likelihood of chronicity is high** → the risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Therefore HCV is often found incidentally, during screening.
**Diagnosis:** **anti-HCV** (screening, ELISA) → confirmation with **HCV RNA (PCR)** and determination of active infection; genotyping — to choose the treatment regimen.

parts.text: **A positive anti-HCV does not prove a current infection**: it also stays positive in a past infection that has cleared spontaneously or as a result of treatment. Active infection is confirmed only by **HCV RNA**.

blocks.text: **Important mycoses associated with HIV infection:** Pneumocystis pneumonia (*Pneumocystis jirovecii*), cryptococcal meningitis (*Cryptococcus neoformans* — an encapsulated yeast-like fungus; viewed in the cerebrospinal fluid **with India ink**, and the **capsular antigen** test), esophageal and disseminated forms of candidiasis.
**Laboratory diagnosis (see also topic 3):**

items: **Microscopic:** the material (skin scrapings, hair, nails, sputum, cerebrospinal fluid) is cleared in **10–20% KOH**; staining — Gram, Romanowsky–Giemsa, PAS, calcofluor; for cryptococcus in the cerebrospinal fluid, an **India ink preparation**.
**Culture:** inoculation on **Sabouraud** medium, at 22–28 °C and 37 °C; identification by colony appearance and microscopic structure; for dimorphic fungi both temperatures are important.
**Antigen detection:** cryptococcal capsular antigen (cerebrospinal fluid, blood), galactomannan in aspergillosis.
**Molecular:** PCR, sequencing; MALDI-TOF.
**Antifungal susceptibility** — in disseminated cases and when resistance is suspected.

parts.text: The fungal membrane contains **ergosterol** (absent in bacteria) — this is the target of most antifungal drugs; the cell wall consists of **chitin and glucan**. Therefore antibacterial antibiotics do not act on fungi and may, on the contrary, create conditions for their growth.

skills.title: Practical skill: interpreting the markers of parenteral hepatitis and HIV

items: **Screening panel:** HBsAg, anti-HCV, HIV (4th-generation ELISA).
**If HBsAg is positive:** anti-HBc IgM (is it acute?), HBeAg and anti-HBe (degree of replication), **HBV DNA**; in an HBsAg-positive patient **anti-HDV** is also tested.
**If anti-HCV is positive:** **HCV RNA (PCR)** — to confirm active infection; if positive, genotyping.
**If the HIV screening is positive:** a **confirmatory test** by the set algorithm (immunoblot and/or a molecular method); after confirmation, the **CD4⁺ count** and **viral load**.
**If a negative result was obtained after a risky contact:** taking the “window period” into account, the test is repeated at set intervals.
**At all stages:** confidentiality, counseling (before and after the test), observing safe care rules.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A patient who came 2 weeks after a risky contact had a negative ELISA for HIV.
cases.ask: How should the result be interpreted?
cases.answer: This may be the **“window period”** — antibodies have not yet formed. The result does not rule out infection. The test is repeated at set intervals; **PCR** is used for early detection. Counseling is given to the patient.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: On a preventive examination: HBsAg negative, anti-HBs positive, anti-HBc negative.
cases.ask: What does this picture mean?
cases.answer: **Immunity after vaccination**. The vaccine consists only of HBsAg, so core antibodies (anti-HBc) are not formed; in a person who recovered from the disease, anti-HBc would also be positive.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A patient is anti-HCV positive, but HCV RNA was not detected; liver tests are normal.
cases.ask: What is the conclusion?
cases.answer: Probably a **past infection** (cleared spontaneously or as a result of treatment). anti-HCV persists for a long time and does not prove active infection. The result may be repeated at a set interval and assessed together with clinical information.

topics.title: Herpes and pox viruses. Monkeypox. Nosocomial (hospital-acquired) infections

goals.text: To know the classification, general properties and subfamilies of the herpesvirus family;
to explain the mechanism of latency and recurrence of herpes infections;
to master the structure and diagnosis of poxviruses (smallpox, monkeypox);
Independent work: to know the causative agents, causes, diagnosis and preventive measures of hospital-acquired (nosocomial) infections.

summary.text: Remember the herpesviruses by their site of latency: **α — in nerve ganglia** (HSV, VZV), **β — in monocytes/secretory cells** (CMV), **γ — in lymphocytes** (EBV, HHV-8).

summary.text: Tell poxviruses apart: **the largest + brick-shaped + multiply in the cytoplasm** — other DNA viruses (herpes, adeno, papilloma) multiply in the **nucleus**.

blocks.text: **General properties:** these are large (150–200 nm), **enveloped** viruses with **double-stranded linear DNA**; an icosahedral capsid, with a layer of **tegument** between the capsid and the envelope. They multiply in the nucleus.

blocks.text: **The main biological property — latency and recurrence:** after the primary infection the virus does not leave the body completely, but is kept in certain cells in a **latent** state and **is reactivated** when immunity falls (stress, another illness, immunosuppression, UV light, menstruation).

parts.text: Remember the herpesviruses by their site of latency: **α — in nerve ganglia** (HSV, VZV), **β — in monocytes/secretory cells** (CMV), **γ — in lymphocytes** (EBV, HHV-8).

blocks.text: **Routes of transmission:** direct contact (saliva, vesicle fluid), sexual (HSV-2), airborne (VZV), vertical and transfusion (CMV), through saliva — the “kissing disease” (EBV).
**Clinically important conditions:**

items: **Neonatal herpes** — infection with HSV-2 in the birth canal; it may give a severe, disseminated form;
**Congenital CMV infection** — hearing loss, damage to the nervous system;
**Infectious mononucleosis (EBV)** — fever, tonsillitis, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, **atypical mononuclear cells** in the blood;
**Shingles (reactivation of VZV)** — a painful vesicular rash along a nerve, on one side.

blocks.text: **Laboratory diagnosis:**

items: **Material:** vesicle fluid and scrapings from the base, saliva, cerebrospinal fluid, blood, biopsy; in newborns — from several sites.
**PCR — the main modern method**: especially in encephalitis (HSV in the cerebrospinal fluid), neonatal infection and CMV; **quantitative PCR** to monitor viral load in transplant patients.
**Cytologic method** — the Tzanck preparation: in a smear taken from the base of the rash, **multinucleated giant cells** and intranuclear inclusions.
**Serologic** — IgM (new infection), IgG (past infection); in EBV, the heterophile antibody test (for mononucleosis) and a panel of specific antibodies.
**Virus isolation** — in cell culture (CPE: rounding, syncytia, inclusions); rarely used in practice.
**Immunofluorescence and antigen tests** — rapid methods.

blocks.text: **Prophylaxis and control:** **vaccines against chickenpox and shingles** are available; there is no widely used vaccine against HSV and CMV. Antiviral drugs control reactivation but do not eliminate the latent virus — treatment is prescribed by a physician.

parts.text: **Suspected herpes encephalitis** is an emergency: **HSV PCR** is done immediately on the cerebrospinal fluid; treatment may be started on clinical suspicion, without waiting for the result, because treatment started in time significantly improves the outcome.

blocks.text: **General properties:** **the largest viruses** (250–300 nm), visible under the light microscope with special staining; **double-stranded DNA**; **complex symmetry**, brick-shaped. Unlike other DNA viruses, they **multiply in the cytoplasm** (because they have their own enzymes).

blocks.label: Figure 30.3
blocks.caption: The structure of the smallpox virus: the outer envelope, tubular structures, lateral bodies and the nucleocapsid (DNA + protein). Source: Muhamedov I.M. et al., 2019.

blocks.text: **Smallpox (variola):** historically one of the most severe infectious diseases; **declared eradicated worldwide by the World Health Organization in 1980** — the first and only complete eradication in the history of medicine. The main reasons: the virus circulates only in humans, a stable antigenic structure, an effective vaccine and a mass vaccination strategy.

**Monkeypox (mpox):** a zoonotic infection of the genus *Orthopoxvirus*; the reservoir is rodents and primates (West and Central Africa). Transmission: contact with a sick animal, from person to person by **close direct contact** (rash lesions, body fluids, prolonged face-to-face contact), contaminated objects; the vertical route is also possible.

**Clinical picture:** fever, headache, muscle pain and **enlargement of lymph nodes** (a sign that differs from smallpox), then a rash: macule → papule → vesicle → pustule → scab. The rash lesions in a given area are usually **at the same stage**.
**Diagnosis:**

items: **PCR (the main method)** — scrapings from a rash lesion, vesicle fluid, scab;
electron microscopy (brick-shaped virions), antigen tests — supplementary;
serology — of limited value because of cross-reactivity among orthopoxviruses;
work is carried out under the set biosafety regime.

blocks.text: **Control:** isolation of the patient, monitoring of contacts, protective equipment; smallpox vaccines give cross-protection against orthopoxviruses and are used in risk groups on indication.

parts.text: Tell poxviruses apart: **the largest + brick-shaped + multiply in the cytoplasm** — other DNA viruses (herpes, adeno, papilloma) multiply in the **nucleus**.

blocks.text: **Definition:** **healthcare-associated infections** — infections that were not present in the patient at hospital admission and were not in the incubation period, and that were acquired in a medical institution (also the occupational infections of medical staff).
**Main causes:**

items: **patient factor** — reduced immunity, severe underlying disease, age, diabetes mellitus;
**invasive procedures** — catheters, artificial ventilation, operations, drains (breach of natural barriers);
**microbial factor** — **multidrug-resistant** “hospital strains”; biofilm formation;
**organizational factors** — breaches of hand hygiene, breaches of the sterilization and disinfection regime, crowded rooms, unjustified use of antibiotics.

blocks.text: **Features of “hospital strains”:** multidrug resistance, resistance to disinfectants, long survival in a moist environment, biofilm formation, circulating in a ward for a long time.
**Diagnosis and control:**

items: **Microbiological monitoring** — identification of the isolated strains, following the **antibiogram** and the resistance profile;
**Epidemiologic typing** — phage typing, molecular typing: whether the strains come from one source or are independent;
**Control of the environment** — samples of swabs, air, instruments and equipment, solutions (topic 8);
**Examination of staff** — detecting carriage (for example, *S. aureus* in the nose);
**Control of sterilization and disinfection** — biological indicators (topic 9).

blocks.text: **Preventive measures:**

items: **hand hygiene** — the most effective and cheapest measure;
strict observance of the rules of asepsis and antisepsis;
placing invasive devices only on indication and **removing them as early as possible**;
isolation and contact measures;
**rational antibiotic use** programs;
staff training, vaccination and the work of the infection control service.

parts.text: In catheter- or prosthesis-associated infections, bacteria inside the biofilm are much more resistant to antibiotics. Therefore treatment is often ineffective without **removing the foreign body** or replacing it.

skills.title: Practical skill: collecting material from a vesicular rash

items: The **newest, still unruptured vesicle** of the rash is chosen (it contains the highest amount of virus).
The skin is wiped with an antiseptic and one waits **until it is dry** (so that the antiseptic does not get into the sample).
The vesicle is opened with a sterile needle or the tip of a scalpel; the fluid is collected with a swab, and a **scraping from the base of the vesicle** is also taken (cells are needed).
The material is placed in **virological transport medium**; for PCR a dry swab may also be used (according to the laboratory’s requirements).
The sample is stored at **2–8 °C** and delivered quickly.
In parallel, a **Tzanck preparation** can be made (to see multinucleated giant cells).
The requisition states: the date the rash began, its stage, its spread, vaccination and travel history, and immune status.
**Safety:** gloves and protective equipment; when monkeypox is suspected — the set procedure for isolation and packaging.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A patient suddenly developed fever, confusion and seizures; MRI showed changes in the temporal lobe.
cases.ask: Which causative agent should be excluded first, and which test is needed?
cases.answer: **HSV-1 encephalitis**. **HSV PCR** is done urgently on the cerebrospinal fluid. If clinical suspicion is strong, treatment may be started by a physician without waiting for the result, because early treatment significantly improves the outcome.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 60-year-old patient developed a painful vesicular rash along a nerve on one side of the chest. As a child he had chickenpox.
cases.ask: What are the diagnosis and the mechanism?
cases.answer: **Shingles** — reactivation of VZV. After the primary infection the virus stays latent in the nerve ganglia and, when immunity falls, is reactivated and produces a rash along the nerve.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In the intensive care unit, a patient on a ventilator developed pneumonia; the isolated *Acinetobacter* proved multidrug resistant. A similar strain was found in two more patients in the same unit.
cases.ask: What conclusion and what measures are needed?
cases.answer: A hospital-acquired infection; the strains were probably spread from one source — this is determined by **molecular typing**. Measures: contact isolation, **hand hygiene**, checking the disinfection regime, monitoring instruments, equipment and solutions, rational antibiotic use, involving the infection control service.
